facts.label: Where should I park at Anderson Point Park?
facts.value: Route to 20 Anderson Point Drive. The main lot serves the shelters, playground, restrooms, fields, cottage, and greenway access, but the City warns that parking is limited when multiple areas are in use. Overflow parking is in the lot before crossing the bridge; a rental does not guarantee a main-lot space.

facts.label: Which entrance should I use at Anderson Point Park?
facts.value: Use 20 Anderson Point Drive for the developed park. Greenway users can treat Anderson Point as the eastern end of the 18-mile Crabtree Creek Trail and a connection to the Neuse River Trail. For a cottage, shelter, field, or amphitheater event, confirm the assigned meeting point because the 89.6-acre site is spread out.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Anderson Point Park?
facts.value: Yes. A restroom facility is beside the large picnic shelter and convenient to the small shelter and playground. The cottage also has men's and women's restrooms during approved cottage access. Outdoor restroom availability can change for maintenance or winterization, so verify before a restroom-dependent event.

facts.label: What time does Anderson Point Park close?
facts.value: Use outdoor park and greenway areas from dawn to dusk unless a confirmed rental or City program states otherwise. Cottage, amphitheater, shelter, and field reservations follow their approved contract times; event access does not make the entire park an after-hours public facility.

facts.label: Is Anderson Point Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, greenway travel, playground use, and casual open-space use are free. Rentals charge: the large shelter is listed at $25 per hour, small shelter $15, fields and open space $45, amphitheater $60, and cottage $150 per hour for residents. Minimums, deposits, and nonresident surcharges apply.

facts.label: Is Anderson Point Park wheelchair and stroller accessible?
facts.value: The developed park has paved approaches, in-park restrooms, shelters near parking, and paved greenway connections. The historic cottage, amphitheater terrain, fields, canoe areas, and natural habitat routes can differ in grade and surface. Contact Barwell Road staff at 919-996-5994 for the exact destination and accommodation needed.

facts.label: What ages is the Anderson Point playground for?
facts.value: The playground serves ages 2-12 and includes slides, swings, monkey bars, and climbing elements. The City lists woodchip, sand, and rubberized surfaces, toddler swings, and restrooms in the park. It sits near the small shelter and open space rather than at every greenway entrance.

facts.label: Which greenways connect at Anderson Point Park?
facts.value: Anderson Point is where the paved 18-mile Crabtree Creek Greenway reaches the Neuse River Greenway. This makes it a useful through-ride and turnaround point, not just a park loop. Check Raleigh's greenway alerts before a long trip because flooding, bridge work, fallen trees, or maintenance can break a corridor.

facts.label: Can I reserve a shelter at Anderson Point Park?
facts.value: Yes. The large shelter seats up to 200 at 28 tables and has two charcoal grills; the small shelter seats about 50 at 12 tables with one grill. Neither has electricity. Reservations require approval and payment, and the main parking lot is not guaranteed when several park areas are active.

facts.label: What is the historic cottage at Anderson Point Park?
facts.value: The Anderson Homestead cottage dates to the early 1900s and is now primarily a rental and program space. It holds up to 70 people, includes a warming kitchen, porch, tables, chairs, and restrooms, and is not an always-open visitor center. Enter only for an approved rental, program, or scheduled access.

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Opens 10 a.m. Tuesday-Saturday and 1 p.m. Sunday; closes at a published dusk time that changes monthly; closed Monday.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General entry, exhibits, monthly crafts, nature play, trails, and loaner equipment are free. Registered programs and eligible educational rentals may charge.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: The preserve has an Education Center, comfort station, pedestrian walkways, and a mostly flat field-and-pine loop option. Natural-surface routes vary; contact Raleigh Parks Inclusion Services when a program modification is needed.

facts.label: Amenities
facts.value: Education Center, Live animals and exhibits, Accessible comfort station, Drinking fountain, Nature library, Nature play areas, Pollinator gardens, Five loop trails, Wildlife watching, Picnic shelter, EV charging, Free loaner equipment

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 5229 Awls Haven Drive, Raleigh, NC

facts.label: Where should I park at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Navigate to 5229 Awls Haven Drive and use one of the preserve's designated parking lots. Dog-waste dispensers are provided in both lots. Start near the Education Center when you need staff, exhibits, loaner equipment, or the comfort station; use the park map before choosing a loop from the other access area.

facts.label: Where do I start at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: First-time visitors should begin at the Welcome and Education Center off Awls Haven Drive. Staff can answer nature and route questions while the park is open, and the building contains hands-on children's displays, live animals, monthly crafts, a Nature Library, and the loaner-equipment desk.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Yes. The preserve lists a comfort station with restrooms and a water fountain. Use it before beginning a natural-surface loop, especially with young children, because the trails pass through forest, field, pond, and rock-outcrop habitat rather than additional staffed facilities.

facts.label: What time does Wilkerson Nature Preserve open and close?
facts.value: The preserve opens at 10 a.m. Tuesday-Saturday and 1 p.m. Sunday and is closed Monday. Closing follows a published dusk schedule: 5:30 p.m. January, 6 p.m. February, 6:30/7:30 p.m. March, 8 p.m. April, 8:30 p.m. May-July, 8 p.m. August, 7:30 p.m. September, 7/6:30 p.m. October, 6:30/5:30 p.m. November, and 5 p.m. December.

facts.label: Is Wilkerson Nature Preserve free?
facts.value: Yes. General admission, trails, exhibits, live-animal viewing, monthly nature crafts, nature play, and available loaner equipment are free. Some scheduled programs charge. The picnic shelter is limited to eligible nature-education or conservation groups and is listed at $15 per hour with a two-hour minimum.

facts.label: Which Wilkerson Nature Preserve trail is best for limited mobility?
facts.value: The mostly flat Overflow Loop and Overflow-to-Office Connector can form an approximately 0.45-mile route through the east field and pine forest. Other loops are natural surface and may include roots, rocks, grades, or wet areas. The Education Center, comfort station, and developed walkways offer the most predictable access; contact the park for route-specific conditions.

facts.label: What are the best short trails at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Five loop choices serve different interests: Epps Forest is 0.65 mile through old oak-hickory woods; Hidden Rocks is 0.81 mile past rock outcrops; Pond Loop is 0.54 mile around the beaver pond; Prairie Loop is 0.31 mile around the west field; and the Overflow route can make a mostly flat 0.45-mile loop.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: There are nature-play areas and borrowable outdoor play kits rather than a conventional swing-and-slide playground. The Welcome Center lends a Woodland Village backpack, sandbox kit, kites, binoculars, explorer and art backpacks, and other items that encourage open-ended play and observation.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Yes, but they must remain leashed, under control, and on designated trails. Pick up waste using the dispensers in both parking lots. The rules emphasize that off-trail pets can disturb rare plants, nesting birds, turtles, rabbits, and other wildlife and can encounter ticks or copperheads.

facts.label: Can I ride a bike at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: No. Bicycles are not allowed on the preserve's trails. The park is managed primarily for nature education, conservation research, wildlife habitat, and walking. Choose a Raleigh greenway or a park with designated mountain-bike trails for a cycling visit.

facts.label: Can I fish in the pond at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: No. Fishing in the preserve's pond is prohibited. The one-acre pond and active beaver dams are wildlife and education features; observe them from the Pond Loop and leave plants, animals, rocks, fungi, and artifacts where they are.

facts.label: What can I borrow at Wilkerson Nature Preserve?
facts.value: The Welcome Center offers free first-come loaners including explorer, Woodland Village, and art backpacks; a sandbox kit; binoculars; kites; and other nature-play items. Ask staff what is available that day and return equipment before the preserve's changing dusk closing time.

facts.label: What athletic fields are at Baileywick Park?

facts.label: What dogs are allowed at Baileywick Dog Park?

facts.label: Can I bring toys, treats, or a chair into Baileywick Dog Park?

facts.label: Can children enter Baileywick Dog Park?

facts.label: Is Biltmore Hills Park free?

facts.label: Is Biltmore Hills Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The renovated Community Center and paved developed routes provide the best current access. Shelter 1 is explicitly listed as lacking ADA access, and woodchips can complicate playground access. The tennis project will add accessible walks, parking, lighting, and viewing, but construction will temporarily alter routes through fall 2027.

facts.label: What is the playground like at Biltmore Hills Park?
facts.value: The playground is designed for ages 2-12 and includes slides, swings, and climbing equipment over woodchip surfacing. It remains open under the City's current park notice. Bring wheels suitable for woodchips if using a stroller and contact the Center when a specific accessible play route is important.

facts.label: Are the Biltmore Hills tennis courts open?
facts.value: The City currently says the park's existing tennis courts remain open, but construction closures are expected to begin on a still-unannounced date in August 2026. When open, eight courts have backboards and push-button lighting until 10 p.m. Check the bond-project FAQ or contact the Center before traveling specifically for tennis.

facts.label: What will close during Biltmore Hills Park construction?
facts.value: The upcoming project will close the existing tennis courts, lower parking lot and entrance, and small ballfield while eight new courts, accessible routes, parking, lighting, and large-field improvements are built. The large ballfield, basketball, pool, most shelters, playground, walking trail, and indoor Center programming are expected to continue, subject to changing work zones.

facts.label: What ballfields are at Biltmore Hills Park?
facts.value: The current listing includes a lighted 190-foot youth baseball field and a lighted 300-foot softball field. The small field is planned for conversion into eight new tennis courts and will close during construction; the large field is expected to remain available while receiving new lighting, scoreboard, and later movable bases.

facts.label: Is there a swimming pool at Biltmore Hills Park?
facts.value: Yes, but the pool uses its own entrance at 701 Crown Crossing Lane rather than the Community Center address. It has a seasonal baby pool and main lap-and-recreation pool. Opening dates, daily hours, admission, swim lessons, and weather closures are controlled by Raleigh Aquatics and should be checked separately on the pool page.

facts.value: Outdoor park entry and ordinary playground use are free. Indoor open play varies by activity: current City programming lists some free basketball and volleyball blocks and a small fee for adult pickleball. Fitness access, classes, camps, rentals, and reserved field use may charge; check RecLink for the exact session.

facts.label: Is Brier Creek Park wheelchair and stroller accessible?
facts.value: Both playgrounds use rubberized safety surfacing, and the developed campus has paved approaches to the Community Center and main outdoor amenities. The indoor building and restrooms offer the most predictable access. Contact staff at 919-996-3301 when an exact field edge, transfer feature, fitness machine, or program accommodation is essential.

facts.label: What ages are the Brier Creek Park playgrounds for?
facts.value: There are two separate playgrounds: one designed for ages 2-5 and one for ages 5-12. Both use rubberized safety surfacing, which is generally easier for strollers and mobility devices than loose woodchips. The tot lot sits near the shelter, comfort station, and Field 1.

facts.label: What fields are at Brier Creek Park?
facts.value: The park has two open multipurpose fields used for recreation, practices, programs, and rentals. Reserved and school activities have priority over casual play. The City currently lists field rental at $45 per hour, but a request is not final until staff approval and payment confirmation.

facts.label: Can I play basketball or volleyball at Brier Creek Park?
facts.value: Yes, primarily in the indoor air-conditioned gymnasium, which has six goals, a rubberized sports floor, and volleyball nets. Open-play blocks and programs change through the season. The City park page does not list public outdoor tennis courts here, so check the current indoor schedule before traveling for a specific sport.

facts.label: What equipment is in the Brier Creek fitness room?
facts.value: The fitness room includes treadmills, recumbent and spin bikes, an elliptical, StairMaster, Smith machine, multi-stack weight machine, dumbbells from 5 to 80 pounds, benches, a preacher-curl bench, dip rack, and scales. Ask the front desk about current access rules, age limits, orientation, and fees.

facts.label: Can I reserve the shelter at Brier Creek Park?
facts.value: Yes. The shelter is beside Field 1, the tot lot, and the comfort station and has eight tables, one grill, and capacity around 60-80. The current listing is $25 per hour with a two-hour minimum. Requests require staff approval and payment confirmation, so submitting RecLink information alone does not secure the date.

facts.label: Is Brier Creek Park part of the elementary school?
facts.value: The park is a formal partnership between the City of Raleigh and Wake County Public School System, sharing school and community-use spaces on the Brier Creek Elementary campus. Public access is real, but school operations, student safety, and scheduled programs can control particular spaces at particular times.

facts.label: What hours is Buffaloe Road Athletic Park open?

facts.label: Is Buffaloe Road Athletic Park free?

facts.label: Is Buffaloe Road Athletic Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The campus has paved parking and field approaches, an eight-lane asphalt track, paved Neuse River Greenway access, and zero-depth pool entry at the Aquatic Center. facts.label: What fields are at Buffaloe Road Athletic Park?
facts.value: The complex has five halogen-lit baseball and softball diamonds with skinned infields, hybrid-grass outfields, irrigation, enclosed dugouts, scoreboards, and bleachers. Fields 1-3 are 200 feet, Field 4 is 350 feet for older youth and adults, and Field 5 is 250 feet. A multipurpose field sits inside the track.

facts.label: Can the public use the Buffaloe Road outdoor track?
facts.value: The park has an eight-lane, 400-meter asphalt track. Casual use depends on scheduled leagues, tournaments, practices, maintenance, and special events; reserved activities have priority. Check field status and avoid the track when the infield or complex is closed for an event.

facts.label: What is the dog park at Buffaloe Road like?
facts.value: The free fenced dog park has separate areas for large and small dogs, a woodchip base, shade, and drinking fountains for dogs and people. Dogs may be off leash only inside the appropriate enclosure. Remain with your dog, remove waste, and leave if behavior or crowding becomes unsafe.

facts.label: What ages are the Buffaloe Road playgrounds for?
facts.value: There are separate playgrounds for ages 2-5 and 5-12. The younger area uses sand surfacing, while the older playground uses woodchips. Neither surface is as predictably rollable as poured rubber, so contact Raleigh Parks if accessible equipment or a continuous firm route is essential.

facts.label: Can I access the Neuse River Greenway from Buffaloe Road Athletic Park?
facts.value: Yes. The 27.5-mile paved Neuse River Greenway connects at the athletic park. From here the trail runs north toward Horseshoe Farm and Wake Forest connections and south toward Milburnie Dam, Anderson Point, Knightdale, and Johnston County links. It is part of Raleigh's regional system, not a trail to Charlotte.

facts.label: What is inside Buffaloe Road Aquatic Center?
facts.value: The year-round indoor facility includes a three-story waterslide, lazy river, water vortex, three lap lanes, zero-depth entry, toddler water-play features, and a tot slide. The large yellow slide requires a measured height of at least 48 inches; children under 48 inches must stay within arm's reach of a responsible adult in the water.

facts.label: Can Buffaloe Road Aquatic Center reach capacity?
facts.value: Yes. Admission is first-come and capacity can change with staffing and programs. If full, staff may use a front-desk waiting list. Call 919-996-5600 on the day of your visit, especially on weekends or school breaks, and do not assume purchasing or holding a general pass guarantees immediate entry.

facts.label: Can I bring food to Buffaloe Road Aquatic Center?
facts.value: Yes. Outside food and nonalcoholic drinks are allowed, and coolers may be inspected. Glass and alcohol are prohibited. The facility does not sell food or drinks, although water fountains are available. Delivery is allowed only if you meet the driver in the lobby; staff will not receive it for you. Bring your own towel.

facts.value: Keep your dog leashed from the vehicle through the athletic park and into the gated entry. Pause if dogs are crowding the gate, remove choke, prong, pinch, or spike collars, close the outer gate, then unleash before entering the play area. Reverse the process when leaving and never open both gates together.

facts.label: What hours is Buffaloe Road Dog Park open?
facts.value: The dog park is open dawn to dusk daily, regardless of later field-light or Aquatic Center schedules. Posted closures for weather, saturated wood chips, maintenance, or safety take priority. Check Raleigh Parks Status after rain and leave before dusk.

facts.label: Is Buffaloe Road Dog Park free?
facts.value: Yes. The fenced dog park is free with no day pass or public membership fee. The adjacent Aquatic Center, athletic programs, leagues, field rentals, and special events have separate admission or registration costs; those fees do not apply to ordinary dog-park use.

facts.label: Is Buffaloe Road Dog Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The athletic campus has developed parking and paved internal approaches, but Raleigh does not publish a dog-enclosure-specific accessible-route guarantee. Wood chips, mud, gates, slopes, and a busy vestibule can create barriers. Contact Raleigh Athletics at 919-996-6836 for current parking-to-gate and surface details.

facts.label: Which Buffaloe Road dog area should I use?
facts.value: Use the small-dog enclosure for dogs weighing 30 pounds or less and the large-dog enclosure for dogs over 30 pounds. Follow posted gate signs rather than choosing by temperament alone. Size separation lowers mismatch risk, but handlers must still remove dogs that become aggressive, uncontrollable, or overwhelmed.

facts.label: Is water available at Buffaloe Road Dog Park?
facts.value: Yes. The City lists a drinking fountain for both dogs and humans. Fountain availability can change because of freezing weather, maintenance, or damage, so carrying backup water and a portable bowl is still wise. Do not bring food, treats, or toys into the off-leash area.

facts.label: What is the surface at Buffaloe Road Dog Park?
facts.value: The enclosure uses wood chips and includes shade and benches. Wood chips can shift, hide holes, or become wet and muddy after rain. Wear closed shoes, inspect play areas before running, stop your dog from digging and fill holes, and bring a towel or paw-cleaning supplies.

facts.label: What dogs are allowed at Buffaloe Road Dog Park?
facts.value: Dogs must be healthy and fully vaccinated. Puppies younger than four months, females in season, and aggressive or uncontrollable dogs are prohibited. All breeds are welcome when rules are met. A handler may supervise no more than three dogs and remains responsible for their behavior.

facts.label: Can I bring toys, treats, or a chair into Buffaloe Road Dog Park?
facts.value: No. Raleigh prohibits food, treats, toys, and outside furniture inside dog parks because they can provoke guarding or conflict. Remove choke, prong, pinch, and spike collars; pick up waste; stop digging; fill holes; and actively watch your dog throughout the visit.

facts.label: Can children enter Buffaloe Road Dog Park?
facts.value: Children under 12 must be closely supervised. The enclosure is not a playground: children should not run, carry food or toys, approach unfamiliar dogs, or stand in the gate vestibule. Buffaloe Road has separate playgrounds outside the dog park for child-centered activity.

facts.label: What should I do about a dog bite at Buffaloe Road?
facts.value: Separate and remove dogs before conflict escalates. For an aggressive or uncontrollable dog, call Animal Control at 919-831-6311. After a bite, provide medical care, identify the dog and owner, and report the incident; call 911 for serious injury. Report enclosure or fountain maintenance problems at 919-996-4115.

facts.label: What else is near Buffaloe Road Dog Park?
facts.value: The larger 165.6-acre campus includes playgrounds, athletic fields, an outdoor track, the separately operated Buffaloe Road Aquatic Center, and access to the Neuse River Greenway. Dogs must be leashed outside the fenced enclosure and are prohibited on athletic fields and courts, even when those areas appear unused.

facts.label: Where should I park for Raleigh's Capital Area Greenway?
facts.value: There is no single greenway parking lot. Choose an individual trail and trailhead first, then use Raleigh's Greenway Explorer to locate official parking near that route. The Explorer also identifies restrooms, bike repair stations, parks, and other amenities. Never improvise parking in a neighborhood, business, or apartment lot.

facts.label: Where is the best entrance to the Raleigh greenway system?
facts.value: The best entrance depends on the trail and destination; the Capital Area Greenway has many trailheads rather than one gateway. Start with a named route such as Neuse River, Walnut Creek, Crabtree Creek, Reedy Creek, or a lake loop, then select a documented trailhead close to the distance and amenities you need.

facts.label: Are there restrooms along Raleigh greenways?
facts.value: Some trailheads and connected parks have restrooms, but many trail segments do not. Use the Greenway Explorer to find the nearest documented restroom and check the host park or building hours. A restroom marker does not guarantee it is unlocked after hours, during winterization, or during maintenance.

facts.label: What hours are Raleigh greenways open?
facts.value: Capital Area Greenway trails are open from dawn to dusk daily. Connected parks, parking gates, restrooms, museums, and neighboring jurisdictions can follow different schedules. Plan enough time to return to your trailhead before dusk and do not rely on trail lighting for a late return.

facts.label: Is the Capital Area Greenway free?
facts.value: Yes. Raleigh's public greenway trails are free to use. Costs may arise for parking at a connected destination, bike or scooter rental, transit, an organized event, or a museum, pool, program, or other facility reached from the trail. Check the destination separately.

facts.label: Are Raleigh greenways wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Many paved segments can support wheelchairs and mobility scooters, and Raleigh presents the network for those users, but the system is not uniformly accessible. Trail grade, pavement condition, curb transitions, bridge approaches, flooding, construction, and natural-surface segments vary. Verify the exact trailhead and segment rather than relying on the system-wide label.

facts.label: How many miles of greenway trails does Raleigh have?
facts.value: The City's current public trail list describes 28 trails totaling more than 100 miles. Other planning documents may use larger figures because they count newer construction, connectors, proposed routes, or open-space holdings differently. For trip planning, use the current named-trail list and each route's stated mileage.

facts.label: Does Raleigh's greenway system go to Charlotte?
facts.value: No. The Capital Area Greenway is Raleigh's local and regional network and does not provide a continuous trail to Charlotte, about 160 road miles away. Raleigh trails connect with nearby systems and long-distance routes such as the East Coast Greenway and Mountains-to-Sea Trail, but those do not turn the city network into a Raleigh-to-Charlotte greenway.

facts.label: What is the best map for Raleigh greenways?
facts.value: Use the mobile-friendly Capital Area Greenway Explorer for nearby trailheads, parking, restrooms, repair stations, dog parks, playgrounds, and parks. It is an amenity-finding tool, not turn-by-turn navigation. Use the downloadable City map or a navigation app alongside it for route planning and confirm closure alerts before leaving.

facts.label: What is the speed limit on Raleigh greenways?
facts.value: The trail speed limit is 10 mph. People riding bicycles, skating, or skateboarding must yield to pedestrians, keep right except to pass, approach cautiously, and call out before passing on the left. Slow further near children, dogs, blind corners, bridges, wet pavement, and crowded trailheads.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed on Raleigh greenways?
facts.value: Yes. Dogs must remain on a leash no longer than six feet, keep to the right with their handler, and owners must remove pet waste. Greenways are shared transportation and recreation routes, not off-leash areas; use a designated public dog park when off-leash exercise is the goal.

facts.label: How do I check Raleigh greenway closures and flooding?

facts.label: Is water available at Carolina Pines Dog Park?

facts.label: Does Carolina Pines Dog Park have agility equipment?

facts.label: Is Carolina Pines Dog Park shaded or muddy?

facts.label: What dogs are allowed at Carolina Pines Dog Park?

facts.label: Can I bring toys, treats, or a chair into Carolina Pines Dog Park?

facts.label: Can children enter Carolina Pines Dog Park?

facts.label: What should I do about a dog bite at Carolina Pines?

facts.value: Use the lot for the section you intend to explore. facts.label: Which end of Crabtree Creek Greenway should I start from?
facts.value: Use 4000 Lindsay Drive for the west end near Umstead and 22 Anderson Point Drive for the east end at the Neuse River junction. Kiwanis Park and Lassiter Mill are useful intermediate starts. Choose by destination and total distance; the Lindsay Drive address is not a central visitor center or the only entrance.

facts.label: Are there restrooms along Crabtree Creek Greenway?
facts.value: Restrooms are available at some connected parks, including Anderson Point and Kiwanis during applicable hours, but not continuously along 18 miles. facts.label: What hours is Crabtree Creek Greenway open?
facts.value: The trail is open dawn to dusk daily. Umstead State Park, Anderson Point, Kiwanis Park, Crabtree Valley Mall, restrooms, and parking areas can have different operating or gate hours. Plan to finish before dusk and verify any connected facility you need.

facts.label: Is Crabtree Creek Greenway free?
facts.value: Yes. The City greenway is free to walk, run, or cycle. Separate charges or parking conditions can apply at private destinations, organized events, rentals, programs, or facilities reached from the trail. General access at City park trailheads is free.

facts.label: Is Crabtree Creek Greenway wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The official route is paved and many sections can work for wheelchairs and mobility devices, but the whole corridor is not uniform. Grades, trailhead transitions, street interfaces, flooding, construction, and surface conditions vary. Confirm the exact trailhead and segment in the City map and current alerts.

facts.label: How long is Crabtree Creek Greenway and is it paved?
facts.value: The City lists Crabtree Creek Greenway as an 18-mile paved trail from the Umstead State Park area to Anderson Point Park. It follows the creek through multiple neighborhoods and destinations, so a short visit should be planned around one trailhead rather than the full route.

facts.label: Is Crabtree Creek Greenway a loop?
facts.value: No. It is a long linear route. For an out-and-back, turn around after half your desired total distance. A full one-way trip requires a planned pickup or shuttle and confirmed legal parking at both ends; do not assume transit or rideshare availability at every access point.

facts.label: What does Crabtree Creek Greenway connect to?
facts.value: It connects the Umstead State Park area with Crabtree Valley Mall, Kiwanis Park, historic Lassiter Mill, North Hills Park, Mine Creek Trail, House Creek Trail, Anderson Point Park, and the Neuse River Greenway. Check each connected park separately for facilities and hours.

facts.label: Can I reach Crabtree Valley Mall from the greenway?
facts.value: Yes, the City identifies Crabtree Valley Mall as a trail connection. Treat the mall as a private destination with its own hours, entrances, parking rules, and construction conditions; a greenway connection does not guarantee after-hours building access or permission to leave a vehicle there for a trail trip.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed on Crabtree Creek Greenway?
facts.value: Yes. Dogs must stay controlled on a leash no longer than six feet, keep right, and owners must remove waste. Use extra care around cyclists, wildlife, children, bridges, narrow sections, and busy park or mall connections.

facts.label: Can I bike Crabtree Creek Greenway?
facts.value: Yes. The 18-mile paved route is a major cycling corridor shared with walkers, runners, mobility devices, children, and dogs. Raleigh's greenway speed limit is 10 mph. Keep right, yield, announce passes on the left, and slow near curves, trailheads, road crossings, and crowded destinations.

facts.label: Does Crabtree Creek Greenway flood or close?
facts.value: Yes. The creek corridor is vulnerable to flooding, debris, maintenance, and construction. Lassiter Mill-area improvements are also scheduled to affect nearby access beginning in 2026. Check Raleigh's Greenway Alerts before every longer outing and never cross a barricade or moving water.

For the central park, Stone Houses, and many events, 1030 Richardson Drive is the general park address. For the sunflower and Magnolia Room area, official directions commonly use Umstead Drive from Lake Wheeler Road. Check the park map before leaving because Dix is 308 acres.

facts.label: Are any parts of Dix Park closed or under construction?
facts.value: Dix Park remains open daily from dawn to dusk, but active projects can affect individual areas. Adams, Ashby, Kirby, and Williams buildings on the west campus are being removed through late summer 2026, and the Pullen-to-Bain water project is scheduled to continue through winter 2028. Large events can also close fields, roads, parking lots, or entrances. Check the Dix Park event calendar and posted signs before a time-sensitive visit.

facts.label: Can I take a bus to Dix Park?
facts.value: GoRaleigh Route 21 Caraleigh serves Dix Park along Lake Wheeler Road. The park is very large, so use GoRaleigh's current trip planner to choose a stop near your destination rather than assuming one stop is convenient for Gipson Play Plaza, the Big Field, and the Stone Houses.

facts.label: What are the walking surfaces like at Dix Park?
facts.value: Expect a mix of paved roads and sidewalks, greenway, mown grass, rolling hills, and uneven natural ground. Gipson Play Plaza has accessible entrances and pathways, including ADA-grade routes beside the Grand Stair. The Big Field, troll approaches, and sunflower area can include grass, slopes, and uneven surfaces, so they may not work for every wheelchair, walker, or stroller.

facts.label: Where is the main playground at Dix Park?
facts.value: The main playground destination is Gipson Play Plaza at 715 Biggs Drive. Its play areas include Slide Valley, Watermill Mountain, Sand Bowl, Sensory Maze, Swing Terrace, and a Traffic Garden. The playground is listed as open from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m.; adult supervision is required, and pets must stay off playground equipment and surfaces.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad at Dix Park?
facts.value: Yes. The interactive waterfall and splash pad are at Fountain Plaza within Gipson Play Plaza. Watermill Mountain, the waterfall, and splash pad start at 10 a.m.; the splash pad operates through October, while the waterfall can operate year-round as weather permits. Water features shut down when lightning is detected within 10 miles and can restart 20 minutes after the lightning clears.

facts.label: Where can I picnic at Dix Park?
facts.value: For tables and grills near the playground, use the Picnic Grove at Gipson Play Plaza, which has 22 tables and benches under umbrellas plus first-come charcoal grills. Magnolia Room and Oak Room each have six shaded picnic tables, a grill, seating for 36, water, and temporary restrooms; rentals take priority. Big Field, Flowers Field, Harvey Hill, and the Grove are also popular for informal picnics.

facts.label: Where can I find shade at Dix Park?
facts.value: Harvey Hill and the Grove have mature oak trees and are the strongest officially described natural-shade areas. Magnolia Room and Oak Room have shade structures over picnic tables, and Gipson Play Plaza's Picnic Grove uses umbrellas. Big Field and Flowers Field are primarily open lawns, so bring sun protection if those are your destination.

facts.label: What hours is Dix Park open?
facts.value: Dix Park is open seven days a week from dawn to dusk. Individual indoor restrooms, House of Many Porches Market, Stone Houses, programs, rentals, and events use separate schedules, so general park hours do not guarantee that every building or service is open.

facts.label: Is Dix Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, designated parking, Gipson Play Plaza, lawns, gardens, walking areas, and the dog park are free. Some classes, festivals, private rentals, food, merchandise, and ticketed partner events can have separate charges. Check the specific event listing rather than assuming every scheduled activity is free.

facts.label: What accessibility details should I know at Dix Park?
facts.value: Gipson Play Plaza has accessible play routes and facilities, and developed park destinations provide paved approaches and designated parking. Dix Park is 308 acres with slopes, long distances, grass, gravel, and widely separated destinations, so route to the exact area rather than the general park. Contact Raleigh Parks Inclusion Services at 919-996-2147 for program modifications or destination-specific assistance.

facts.label: Where can I get food, coffee, beer, or wine at Dix Park?
facts.value: House of Many Porches at Gipson Play Plaza is the dependable daily market, open 9 a.m.-8 p.m., with sandwiches, wraps, salads, baked goods, snacks, coffee, tea, ice cream, draft beer, prosecco, wine, canned beer and seltzer, and nonalcoholic options. Alcohol stays in its designated area. Flowers Cottage plans Cottage Coffee and Park Bar service, but should not be treated as open until the park confirms the launch.

facts.label: What events are coming up at Dix Park?
facts.value: AuditMap shows current official Dix Park events in the Today section. The flagship 2026 Kirby Derby is scheduled for August 22 from 3:30-8 p.m. at Harvey Hill, with soapbox racing, a parade, kids pinecars, temporary restrooms, and event-specific road closures. Always open the official event entry for weather and arrival changes.

facts.label: Where is Kirby Derby and how should I arrive?
facts.value: Kirby Derby is at Harvey Hill. For the August 22, 2026 event, Umstead Drive closes between South Boylan Avenue and Lake Wheeler Road and the Lake Wheeler entrance to Umstead closes. The park recommends entering from South Boylan/Hunt, Goode Street, or Blair Drive depending on traffic and posted operations.

facts.label: What is the weather at Dix Park today?
facts.value: Use the live Today at this place panel for the National Weather Service forecast and active alerts at the park. Heat, lightning, heavy rain, and saturated ground matter here: water play pauses for nearby lightning, open lawns have limited shade, and troll and trail approaches can become muddy or slippery.

facts.label: What trails connect through Dix Park?
facts.value: Pine Loop Trail is the named quarter-mile natural-surface loop at Flowers Cottage. Rocky Branch Greenway is the paved Raleigh greenway connection along the park's east side, with access near the Grove and an accessible connection at Stone Houses. The Centennial Bikeway Connector enters near Blair Drive. Informal social paths around trolls are not maintained trails.

facts.label: Where are the hammocks at Dix Park?
facts.value: The official visitor map labels Hammock Grove along the Big Field side, and the Big Field and Sunflower Field descriptions also document hammocks or seasonal hammocks. They can be removed for weather, maintenance, events, or seasonal operations, so use the mapped area but do not assume an open hammock is guaranteed.

facts.label: Where are the swings at Dix Park?
facts.value: Swing Terrace at Gipson Play Plaza has the park's 91-foot mega swing and two accessible nest swings. Magnolia Room and Oak Room also list swings or sway benches, and the Big Field lists swings among its amenities. Use the exact subsite pin because these areas are far apart.

facts.label: How long does it take to find all five Dix Park trolls?
facts.value: The five trolls span the western Pine Loop/Flowers Field area, the Big Field pine grove, and the eastern Harvey Hill/Grove side. Plan a multi-mile outing or split the trek into west, central, and east stops. The route includes grass, natural paths, slopes, and stairs; save every exact pin and allow extra time with children or mobility needs.

facts.label: Is the new coffee and bar by Flowers Field open?
facts.value: Flowers Cottage at 2105 Umstead Drive is the planned home of Cottage Coffee and Park Bar. The official listing says Coming Soon and Opening Summer 2026, with coffee, tea, soft serve, baked goods, picnic provisions, craft beer, wine, and concessions planned. AuditMap will mark it open only after an official operational confirmation.

facts.label: Does the greenway at Dix Park go to Charlotte?
facts.value: No. Rocky Branch Greenway is part of Raleigh's Capital Area Greenway system and connects Dix Park to other Raleigh routes. It does not extend to Charlotte. Use Raleigh's current greenway map and closure notices when planning a longer ride beyond the park.

facts.label: Where should I park for Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: Downtown Cary has more than 2,000 free public parking spaces. Closest official options include the Academy Street Parking Deck at 206 S. Academy Street, the accessible deck behind Cary Regional Library, the Charlie Gaddy Lane lot, labeled street parking, and Town Hall Deck at 121 Wilkinson Avenue. A passenger and rideshare drop-off is on S. Walker Street near The Walker building.

facts.label: Which entrance should I use for Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: The park has accessible entries into each major area with ramps where needed. For The Nest, restrooms, lost and found, or accessibility services, use Guest Services on the bottom floor of Cary Regional Library near The Nest. Visitors with limited mobility can use the designated drop-off zone on Walker Street.

facts.label: Where are the restrooms at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: Downtown Cary Park has five restroom areas with 24 public toilets. A large bank of restrooms is inside Guest Services on the bottom floor of Cary Regional Library near The Nest. Wheelchair-accessible restrooms and water fountains are located throughout the park, and the family restroom in Guest Services has an adult changing table.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad at Cary park?
facts.value: Yes. Downtown Cary Park has a sprayground at Academy Plaza and a splash pad in The Nest. Both are currently open for the season from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily and close on the second Monday of each month for routine maintenance. Weather or repairs can also interrupt operation, so check same-day status.

facts.label: Is there a dog area at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: Yes. The Barkyard has separate off-leash areas for larger and smaller dogs, but entry requires an annual membership or day pass. It is generally accessible daily, with scheduled Wednesday maintenance closures.

facts.label: What are the standout areas inside Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: The park centers around Academy Plaza, The Nest play area, the Great Lawn and Pavilion, botanical gardens, Park Street Courts, and the Barkyard dog area. It is designed as a set of linked park rooms rather than one large open field.

facts.label: Are any Downtown Cary Park features closed today?
facts.value: The park is open daily from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m., but individual features have separate schedules. The splash pad and sprayground are currently open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. and close the second Monday each month for maintenance. The Barkyard closes the second Wednesday monthly and every fourth Wednesday from April through November, 7 a.m. to noon. Events or weather can affect specific areas, so check the park calendar and feature-status pages the day you visit.

facts.label: Are Downtown Cary Park paths stroller and wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Nearly all public routes through Downtown Cary Park are ADA accessible, with accessible entries and built-in ramps into each park area. Walkways include visual indicators, tactile paving, and stair treads. The exception is a maintenance path directly along the water's edge; visitors should remain on the main public paths for a continuous accessible route.

facts.label: What is in The Nest playground at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: The Nest is the park's main play area. It has two large cardinal-shaped climbing structures, multiple slides, a separate toddler area, and its own splash pad. Accessible slides, play zones for different ages and abilities, and a communication board are available. Children must be supervised, and some surfaces can become hot.

facts.label: Where can we have a picnic at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: Visitors may bring food and picnic on the Great Lawn. Accessible picnic tables are distributed around the park. For a shaded table beside The Nest, the Nest Pavilion has four picnic tables under a shade sail, but it is also a reservable space, so a rental can take priority. Outside alcohol is not permitted.

facts.label: Where is the best shade at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: Academy Plaza is shaded by mature oak trees, and the Nest Pavilion has a shade sail over picnic tables beside the playground. Willow Isle's L'ILE FOLIE artwork provides another shaded place to relax, while the Barkyard has natural shade for pass-holding dog visitors. The Great Lawn is comparatively open, so choose one of these named areas during hot weather.

facts.label: Where can I get food, coffee, beer, or wine at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: Market 317 inside Academy Pavilion is the dependable daily grab-and-go stop, normally 9 a.m.-6 p.m., with meals, snacks, pastries, coffee, beer, wine, and cold drinks. The weather-dependent Bark Bar serves beer, wine, nonalcoholic drinks, and light snacks on afternoon and evening hours beside Barkyard. Both are cashless.

facts.label: What events are coming up at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: AuditMap's Today section should be checked with the official park calendar before arrival. Downtown Cary Park hosts more than 750 annual programs, including CaryLIVE concerts, movies, markets, fitness, story times, art programs, and signature events that can change lawn access and parking.

facts.label: Can I pay with cash at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: No. Market 317, The Bark Bar, and Guest Services are card and contactless payment only. Bring a physical card or supported mobile wallet rather than relying on cash.

facts.label: How does weather affect Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: The splash pad, sprayground, Bark Bar, events, and some active areas can close for weather. Official group guidance says lightning within 10 miles suspends activities, with a 30-minute all-clear period after nearby lightning ends. Check the live NWS panel and park notices before relying on water play or outdoor programming.

facts.label: Where is Guest Services at Downtown Cary Park?
facts.value: Guest Services is on the bottom floor of Cary Regional Library near The Nest. It handles lost and found, dog-park passes, accessibility support, and visitor questions; the nearby family restroom includes an adult changing table. Call 919-653-7180 for same-day help.

facts.label: Where should I park at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Use the north parking lot at 8305 Camp Durant Road for the park office and the primary public visit. Park only in designated spaces. Campbell Lodge has a separate address at 3237 Spottswood Street and should not be used as a shortcut to the preserve's main lake, playground, restroom, or trail facilities.

facts.label: How do I reach the lake and playground at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: From the north parking lot, begin at the large orange gate and follow the dirt-and-gravel path approximately 200 yards. This walk leads toward the public restrooms and the area containing the 12-acre lake, playground, open field, picnic shelters, and trailheads. There is no general visitor vehicle access down that path.

facts.label: Where are the restrooms at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Public restrooms are about 200 yards down the dirt-and-gravel path that starts at the big orange gate in the north parking lot. They are not beside your parked vehicle or inside the office entrance, so allow time for the walk and handle urgent restroom needs before unloading extensive picnic or play gear.

facts.label: What time does Durant Nature Preserve close?
facts.value: The preserve opens daily at 7 a.m. Closing changes by month: 6 p.m. January, 6:30 February, 7 March, 8 April, 8:30 May, 9 June-July, 8:30 August, 8 September, 7 October, and 5:30 November-December. The office has much shorter hours: 8 a.m.-1 p.m. Monday-Thursday.

facts.label: Is Durant Nature Preserve free?
facts.value: Yes. General entry, parking, trails, playground use, gardens, and designated fishing access are free. Discovery Backpacks are loaned free during office hours. Registered programs and rentals such as shelters, Campbell Lodge, or the campfire circle may charge and require confirmation.

facts.label: Is Durant Nature Preserve stroller or wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Expect a meaningful surface challenge between the north lot and the main facilities: the City describes an approximately 200-yard dirt-and-gravel walk to the restrooms, lake, playground, and shelters. Natural trails add roots, grades, and weather effects. Contact the preserve before a visit that depends on a specific accessible route or program accommodation.

facts.label: What are the trails like at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Five miles of mostly natural-surface trails cross streams, hardwood and pine forest, wetlands, wildflowers, ferns, and the edges of two lakes. Maps are available at the office and posted at major intersections. Wear closed-toe footwear, choose a route before starting, and expect mud or roots after wet weather.

facts.label: Does construction affect Durant Nature Preserve trails?
facts.value: Yes. Stream and stormwater work closes a portion of Border Trail and can cause temporary single-lane traffic near Spottswood and Welborn streets. Other trails remain available unless separately posted. Follow onsite detours and check Raleigh Parks Alerts before relying on Border Trail for a loop.

facts.label: Can I fish at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Yes, in designated areas at the preserve's lakes under current North Carolina fishing rules. Personal boats and swimming are prohibited. Bring your own basic supplies unless you have confirmed a current loaner option, and supervise children closely around docks, banks, and changing water conditions.

facts.label: Can I mountain bike at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Only on designated bike trails and only when those surfaces are open and dry. Call the park office at 919-996-2271 for current bike-trail status. Do not ride hiking-only routes or use wet trails, and expect construction to alter part of the Border Trail area.

facts.label: What is the playground like at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: The nature-oriented playground serves ages 2-12 and uses a woodchip surface. It sits near the 12-acre lake, open playfield, public restrooms, picnic shelters, and trailheads, about a 200-yard walk from the north parking lot. It is not a drive-up playground, so pack gear you can comfortably carry.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Yes, but pets must remain restrained on a leash no longer than six feet. Stay on designated trails and remove waste. Dogs are not an exception to preserve rules protecting plants, wildlife, wetlands, and other visitors, and they should not enter the lakes.

facts.label: Can I borrow a Discovery Backpack at Durant Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Yes. The park office lends free backpacks focused on ponds, insects, birds, animal tracking, or nature art during office hours, currently 8 a.m.-1 p.m. Monday-Thursday. Availability is first-come, so call ahead when a backpack is central to your visit and return it before the office closes.

facts.label: Where should I park at Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: Use the main park entrance at 2100 Old North Carolina 98 Highway. The Welcome Center lot has two accessible spaces, while the playground and picnic-shelter area has four. Park near the facility that matches your visit rather than assuming every attraction begins at the same trailhead.

facts.label: What entrance should I use for Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: Navigate to the City's listed address, 2100 Old North Carolina 98 Highway in Wake Forest, and enter through the signed park drive. Start at the Welcome Center for current trail conditions, maps, programs, and loaner equipment; continue to the separate playground and shelter parking area for the shortest family route.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: Yes. Restrooms with accessible features are located at the Welcome Center and at the playground. Because this is a large 587-acre park, use them before starting a longer natural-surface trail or heading to a minimally developed fishing area.

facts.label: What time does Forest Ridge Park close?
facts.value: Hours change seasonally: 8 a.m.-6 p.m. November through February; 8 a.m.-7 p.m. in March and October; and 7 a.m.-8 p.m. April through September. Plan to be back at your vehicle before closing and check current alerts when weather may affect trails.

facts.label: Is Forest Ridge Park free?
facts.value: General entry, parking, playground use, the wildlife garden, trails, and designated bank-fishing access are free. Fishing equipment and other selected loaners are free with a RecLink account, while organized programs, meeting-room rentals, and reserved uses may charge.

facts.label: How accessible is Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: The park provides six accessible parking spaces: two at the Welcome Center and four at the playground/shelter area. The Welcome Center has push-button entry; accessible restrooms are at both primary facility areas; and shelters have accessible tables and grills. Natural trails and fishing banks vary considerably by surface and conditions.

facts.label: What is the playground like at Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: The adventure playground beside the picnic shelters is designed primarily for ages 5-12 and includes a zip line, slides, swings, climbing elements, and rubberized surfacing. Restrooms and accessible parking are in this area, making it the most convenient starting point for a family play visit.

facts.label: What trails are at Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: The City lists 3.25 miles of single-track mountain-bike trail, 1.85 miles of unpaved multi-use trail, 6.5 miles of natural-surface hiking trail, and a half-mile paved loop. Choose a route for your mobility and experience level, carry a map, and check status before using single-track after rain.

facts.label: Are the mountain-bike trails at Forest Ridge Park open?
facts.value: The City's current alert lists the mountain-bike trail as closed. These trails frequently close during or after rain to prevent erosion and may reopen as conditions improve, so check Raleigh Parks Alerts or call 919-996-5800 on the day of your ride rather than relying on an older status.

facts.label: Can I fish at Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: Yes, from designated bank-fishing areas during park hours and under current North Carolina fishing regulations. Infrastructure at the banks is minimal and bait is not sold at the office. Free loaner fishing equipment is available first-come, first-served with a RecLink account; call ahead when shoreline conditions matter.

facts.label: When is disc golf available at Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: The 18-hole course is seasonal, normally operating from October 15 through March 22 during regular park hours, with the first tee south of the main parking lot. It closes for the growing season so vegetation can recover. Loaner discs are available at the park office when the course is operating.

facts.label: Can I borrow equipment at Forest Ridge Park?
facts.value: Yes. First-come, first-served loaners at the Welcome Center include youth explorer and art backpacks, adult binoculars, a youth fort-building kit, balance bikes, fishing equipment, and seasonal disc-golf discs. facts.label: Where should I park at Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Navigate to 2900 Horseshoe Farm Road and use only the designated permeable-pavement parking spaces. The parking area provides dog-waste bags and access toward the restroom, meadow, farmhouse, picnic shelter, natural-surface loops, and paved Neuse River Greenway connector.

facts.label: Where should I start at Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Begin at the signed preserve parking area and restroom building. From there, choose the paved connector for the Neuse River Greenway, the roughly 0.9-mile Meadow Loop for an open-space circuit, or the approximately 0.6-mile River Walk for floodplain woods and river access. Photograph the posted map before leaving the developed area.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Yes. A composting restroom is located near the developed entrance and greenway connector. It was designed to function without connecting the preserve to public utilities. Use it before beginning the River Walk or a longer greenway trip because there are no additional facilities on the natural loops.

facts.label: What time does Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve close?
facts.value: The preserve opens daily at 7 a.m. Monthly closing times are 6 p.m. January, 6:30 February, 7 March, 8 April, 8:30 May, 9 June-July, 8:30 August, 8 September, 7 October, and 5:30 November-December. Leave enough daylight for the unlit natural-surface return.

facts.label: Is Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve free?
facts.value: Yes. General entry, parking, trails, greenway access, picnic use when available, and self-guided wildlife observation are free. Some scheduled nature programs may require RecLink registration and a fee, but there is no admission gate or routine trail charge.

facts.label: Is Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The developed area includes permeable parking, a composting restroom, an ADA-accessible picnic table, and a paved connector to the Neuse River Greenway. The Meadow Loop and River Walk are natural surface and may be soft, uneven, wet, or flooded. The paved greenway connection is the most predictable rolling route.

facts.label: Which trail should I take at Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Choose the approximately 0.9-mile Meadow Loop for open views along the wood line and lower meadow. Choose the roughly 0.6-mile River Walk for bottomland hardwood floodplain, natural levees, wetlands, and the Neuse River. Both are natural surface; combine them only when conditions and daylight support a longer walk.

facts.label: Can I reach the Neuse River Greenway from Horseshoe Farm?
facts.value: Yes. A paved connector runs from the preserve's restroom building to the Neuse River section of Raleigh's greenway. This makes Horseshoe Farm a useful trail access and rest stop, but it does not mean the preserve's Meadow and River Walk loops allow bicycles; those natural paths follow separate rules.

facts.label: Does Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve flood?
facts.value: It can. The River Walk enters bottomland hardwood floodplain within a Neuse River bend, so high water and recent storms can leave natural surfaces muddy, submerged, or impassable. Never cross posted closures or moving water; use the meadow or paved greenway connector when river conditions make the lower route unsafe.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Yes, on leash at all times. Stay on trails, pick up waste, and use the bags supplied near parking. The leash rule protects bottomland wildlife, native plants, nesting birds, other visitors, and pets themselves in meadow and floodplain habitat.

facts.label: Can I bike inside Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Bicycles may use the paved connector and Neuse River Greenway but are not allowed on the preserve's natural-surface trails. Dismount rather than taking a bike onto the Meadow Loop or River Walk. This protects soft soil, vegetation, and people using the narrow nature paths.

facts.label: Is drinking water available at Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve?
facts.value: Bring your own drinking water. The preserve's sustainable design avoids a public-utility connection and uses a composting restroom; historical state environmental-education guidance specifically notes that running water is not available. Carry enough for the meadow, river, or greenway distance you plan.

facts.label: Is Horseshoe Farm Nature Preserve good for birding?
facts.value: Yes. Open meadow, wetlands, bottomland forest, river edge, and protected native vegetation support a broad mix of resident and migratory birds. Wake Audubon reports more than 140 documented species. Walk quietly, remain on trail, avoid recorded-call disturbance, and bring binoculars and seasonal insect protection.

facts.label: Can I go inside the farmhouse at Horseshoe Farm?
facts.value: The renovated farmhouse supports nature education and interpretive use rather than daily drop-in museum hours. The City currently lists public opening on the second Sunday of each month from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Treat that schedule as program-dependent and confirm before making the building the purpose of your trip.

facts.value: For the Crabtree Creek-to-Glen Eden section, the City lists lots at 4121 Blue Ridge Road, 1510 Glen Eden Drive, and 3800 Blue Ridge Road. For the Glen Eden-to-Reedy Creek section, use the documented lot at 3501 Horton Street. facts.label: What is the best entrance to House Creek Greenway?
facts.value: Glen Eden is the most useful middle starting point: the official directory address is 1501 Glen Eden Drive and parking is listed at 1510 Glen Eden Drive. Start at Blue Ridge Road for the Crabtree Creek connection or Horton Street for the Reedy Creek side. There is no visitor center or single ceremonial entrance.

facts.label: Are there restrooms on House Creek Greenway?
facts.value: The City does not list a dedicated restroom on the House Creek trail page. Connected destinations may have facilities with separate hours, but they should not be treated as guaranteed trail restrooms. Use the Greenway Explorer before leaving and plan this short route without depending on an unlocked facility.

facts.label: What hours is House Creek Greenway open?
facts.value: The trail is open dawn to dusk daily. Parking lots, Marshall Memorial Park surroundings, Crabtree Valley destinations, and connected facilities may have different schedules. Finish before dusk and verify any gate or building you rely on.

facts.label: Is House Creek Greenway free?
facts.value: Yes. The public greenway is free to walk, run, or cycle. Private destinations and organized events reached from the trail can have separate fees or parking restrictions; free trail use does not create permission to use a private lot.

facts.label: Is House Creek Greenway wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The route is developed and paved, and many portions may work for wheelchairs and mobility devices. The full corridor is not guaranteed uniform: trailhead transitions, slopes, crossings, drainage, pavement condition, and temporary detours vary. Verify the exact start and segment in the City's map and alerts.

facts.label: How long is House Creek Greenway?
facts.value: The City lists House Creek Greenway as 2.8 miles. The Crabtree Creek-to-Glen Eden portion is about 1 mile, and Glen Eden-to-Reedy Creek is listed as 1.9 miles; rounded segment measurements can total slightly more than the corridor mileage. It follows House Creek beside the I-440 beltline.

facts.label: Is House Creek Greenway a loop?
facts.value: No. It is a linear connector. A full out-and-back is roughly 5.6 miles, while either named segment makes a shorter outing. For a one-way trip, arrange pickup or legal parking at both ends and do not assume convenient transit or rideshare service at the trailhead.

facts.label: What does House Creek Greenway connect to?
facts.value: The north end meets Crabtree Creek Trail near Crabtree Valley, and the south end meets Reedy Creek Trail at Wade Avenue. Those links open longer routes toward Umstead, NCMA, Meredith College, Kiwanis Park, Lassiter Mill, Anderson Point, and the Neuse River, but each extension should be planned separately.

facts.label: What is Marshall Memorial Park on House Creek Trail?
facts.value: Marshall Memorial Park is a small landscaped memorial area along about one-third of a mile near the Blue Ridge Road entrance, featuring a stone path and metal pergola. It is a brief trail-side place to pause, not a full-service community park with guaranteed restrooms or extensive recreation facilities.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed on House Creek Greenway?
facts.value: Yes. Dogs must remain controlled on a leash no longer than six feet, keep right, and owners must remove waste. Use extra care around bicycles, I-440 noise, crossings, narrow approaches, and busy connections near Crabtree Valley.

facts.label: Can I bike House Creek Greenway?
facts.value: Yes. The route is a useful bicycle connector between Crabtree Creek and Reedy Creek, but it is shared with walkers, runners, mobility devices, children, and dogs. Raleigh's greenway speed limit is 10 mph; keep right, yield, announce passes, and slow at trailheads and road interfaces.

facts.label: Does House Creek Greenway flood or close?
facts.value: Yes. Creek corridors can flood or collect debris, and maintenance or nearby road work can create detours. Check Raleigh Greenway Alerts before visiting, especially after storms. Never cross a barricade or moving water, and do not improvise a route onto I-440 ramps, private property, or unsafe roads.

facts.label: How do I reach and enter Jaycee Dog Run?
facts.value: Use the accessible sidewalk from the Wade Avenue parking lot to the dog run. facts.label: Does Jaycee Dog Run have a separate small-dog area?
facts.value: No. Raleigh specifically describes Jaycee as one shared enclosure with no dog-size restriction, unlike Oakwood, Millbrook, Buffaloe Road, and Carolina Pines. Small, shy, older, or mobility-limited dogs may be safer at a size-separated park or during a quiet period. Leave immediately if play becomes overwhelming.

facts.label: Is water available at Jaycee Dog Run?

Do not bring food, treats, or toys into the enclosure, and do not assume community-center access or an outdoor tap will be available.

facts.label: Is Jaycee Dog Run shaded or muddy?
facts.value: The City lists benches, natural shade, and a wood-chip surface. Wood chips can shift, conceal holes, or become wet and muddy after rain. Wear suitable shoes, inspect the enclosure, stop digging and fill holes, and bring towels or paw-cleaning supplies.

facts.label: What dogs are allowed at Jaycee Dog Run?
facts.value: Dogs must be healthy and fully vaccinated. Puppies under four months, females in season, and aggressive or uncontrollable dogs are prohibited. All breeds and sizes share the same enclosure when rules are met. A handler may supervise no more than three dogs and remains responsible for each one.

facts.label: Can I bring toys, treats, or a chair into Jaycee Dog Run?
facts.value: No. Raleigh prohibits food, treats, toys, and outside furniture inside dog parks because they can trigger guarding and conflict. Remove choke, prong, pinch, and spike collars; pick up waste; stop digging; fill holes; and watch your dog continuously.

facts.label: Can children enter Jaycee Dog Run?
facts.value: Children under 12 must be closely supervised. This matters especially at Jaycee because all dog sizes share one enclosure and the run sits near a playground. Children should not run, carry food or toys, approach unfamiliar dogs, or crowd the entry. Use the separate playground for child-centered activity.

facts.label: What should I do about a dog bite at Jaycee Dog Run?
facts.value: Remove dogs before conflict escalates. For an aggressive or uncontrollable dog, call Animal Control at 919-831-6311. After a bite, provide medical care, identify the dog and owner, and report the incident; call 911 for serious injury. Report fence, gate, waste, or surface maintenance issues at 919-996-4115.

facts.value: Jaycee Park has a community center, playground, two tennis courts, six sand-volleyball courts, athletic fields, a picnic shelter with nearby restrooms, gym, rooms, and weight room. Dogs must be leashed outside the dog run and are prohibited on athletic fields and courts, even if those areas are empty.

The approved park plan shows north and south parking areas with 166 total spaces and accessible spaces serving the community center and playground. Parking will be reconfigured during the aquatic-center project scheduled through 2029, so follow current construction signs and verify access before a major event.
facts.sourceLabel: John Chavis Memorial Park Approved Site Plan

facts.label: Which entrance should I use at John Chavis Memorial Park?
facts.value: Use 505 Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard for the community center, indoor restrooms, carousel tickets, and the main family amenities. The approved site plan also labels north and south playground entrances. Because aquatic-center construction will reconfigure parts of the site and parking, follow current signs rather than relying on an older internal route.
facts.sourceLabel: John Chavis Memorial Park Approved Site Plan

facts.label: Where are the restrooms at John Chavis Memorial Park?
facts.value: Reliable public restrooms are inside the community center at 505 Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard during center hours. The center includes a family restroom with a baby-changing table, and the locker rooms have accessible showers, restrooms, lockers, and baby-changing tables. Splash-pad visitors must dry off and change into dry clothing before entering.

facts.label: What accessibility details should visitors know at John Chavis Memorial Park?
facts.value: The approved plan includes accessible parking serving the community center. Inside, accessible showers and restrooms are available. The main playground uses rubber safety surfacing, while natural-play areas use mulch. For a program modification or route-specific help, Raleigh Parks Inclusion Services is available at 919-996-2147.

facts.label: Is construction or anything else affecting John Chavis Memorial Park?
facts.value: A new aquatic center and Heritage Plaza improvements are planned through 2029, and the project will reconfigure park parking. Carousel hours vary by season and it may close early during inclement weather; the splash pad is also disabled during inclement weather. Check the City park page before relying on a specific feature or internal driving route.
facts.sourceLabel: John Chavis Memorial Park Aquatic Center Project

facts.label: How can I reach John Chavis Memorial Park by bus?
facts.value: GoRaleigh Route 19 runs along Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard. The City lists a Route 19 stop directly in front of the Top Greene Cultural Center at 401 Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd., approximately one block west of John Chavis Memorial Park.
facts.sourceLabel: Top Greene Cultural Center Know Before You Go

facts.label: Is there a splash pad at John Chavis Memorial Park?
facts.value: Yes. The free splash pad is scheduled daily from 9:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., weather permitting. There is no lifeguard, children must be supervised, and children who are not toilet trained must wear swim diapers. No pets, food, drinks, or glass are allowed in the water-feature area.

facts.label: What is good for kids at John Chavis Memorial Park?
facts.value: The park's family draw centers on the playground, splash pad, track, and carousel, so it works well for active visits where children want a mix of play structures and open movement.

facts.label: What are the hours for John Chavis Memorial Park attractions?
facts.value: The community center is open Monday-Friday 10 a.m.-9 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m.-3 p.m., and Sunday 1-6 p.m. The splash pad is scheduled daily 9 a.m.-9 p.m. but stops for inclement weather. The carousel is closed Monday, runs Tuesday-Saturday 11 a.m.-6 p.m., and Sunday 2-6 p.m.; seasonal or weather changes can shorten carousel service.

facts.label: Is John Chavis Memorial Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, playground, splash pad, track, outdoor exhibit, picnic shelters, and open recreation areas are free. Carousel rides cost $2 for riders age one and older; children 12 months and younger ride free with a paying adult. Classes, room rentals, organized field use, and private events can have separate fees.

facts.value: Use the small onsite lot entered from South East Street; it includes reserved accessible spaces. Additional parking may be available on nearby streets where signs permit. Because programs and rentals can fill the small lot, allow time to read neighborhood restrictions and never block residences, driveways, bus stops, or construction access.

facts.label: Where is the entrance to Top Greene Cultural Center?
facts.value: Navigate to 401 Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard, but enter the small park parking lot from South East Street. Follow onsite signs from the lot to the Cultural Center's public entrance. Construction phasing may alter the approach during the planned expansion, so obey temporary fencing and current staff directions.

facts.label: Are public restrooms available at Top Greene Cultural Center?
facts.value: The existing center hosts public programs and rentals, but its current visitor page does not separately document ordinary drop-in restroom access. Restrooms follow building hours and may be affected by programs or construction. Call 919-996-6580 before visiting if restroom availability or an accessible fixture is essential.

facts.label: What hours is Top Greene Cultural Center open?
facts.value: The current building schedule is Tuesday-Saturday 11 a.m.-7 p.m. and Sunday 1-4 p.m.; Monday is closed. Individual classes, exhibits, rentals, after-hours events, holidays, and the 2026-2028 construction project can use different times or affect access, so check the current City listing before leaving.

facts.label: Is Top Greene Cultural Center free to visit?
facts.value: Ordinary entry to view the public cultural exhibits is free unless a special event states otherwise. Classes may require RecLink registration and a fee. Private use is not free: the banquet room currently has a two-hour minimum, hourly charge, application fee, refundable damage deposit, and possible after-hours supervisor fee.

facts.label: Is Top Greene Cultural Center wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Yes. The City states that the Cultural Center building is accessible throughout by wheelchair, scooter, or Electric Conveyance Vehicle, and the onsite lot has reserved accessible spaces. Contact staff at 919-996-6580 for a construction-era route check or Raleigh Parks Inclusion Services for a program modification.

facts.label: What can I see at Top Greene Cultural Center?
facts.value: The center presents exhibits about African American culture and the East Raleigh-South Park Historic District. Its Centuries in the Making exhibit covers education, healthcare, businesses, and community contributions. Displays can rotate, so the exact objects and gallery availability may differ from online images.

facts.label: Does Top Greene Cultural Center have historic artifacts?
facts.value: Yes. The City's Top Greene collection preserves more than 2,000 artifacts documenting life in East Raleigh and South Park. Only a selection can be displayed at once; additional records can be explored through the Historic Resources and Museum Program's online collection database.

facts.label: Who was John P. "Top" Greene?
facts.value: John P. "Top" Greene was a community activist and South Park resident for whom the center and surrounding cultural park are named. The City formally adopted the expanded names in 2025 to reflect the site's mission and its relationship to Raleigh's largest historic African American neighborhood.

facts.label: What programs are offered at Top Greene Cultural Center?
facts.value: Programs change throughout the year and include history, culture, art, creativity, learning, and community gatherings. Browse Raleigh RecLink and the City event calendar for current dates, ages, registration, fees, capacity, and accessibility. A normal center-hours listing does not guarantee that a class has walk-in space.

facts.label: Can I take the bus to Top Greene Cultural Center?
facts.value: Yes. The City says GoRaleigh route 19, Martin Luther King/Sunnybrook, serves a stop in front of the center. Check the live route, direction, fare policy, and service alerts before traveling, especially during roadwork or construction around the campus.

facts.label: Is Top Greene Cultural Center under renovation?
facts.value: A major renovation and expansion is scheduled as a 2024-2028 Parks Bond project, with construction planned during 2026-2028. The current City place page still publishes open hours, but access may change as work advances. Check the project and status pages for closures rather than assuming every future feature is already built.

facts.label: Does the South Park Heritage Trail start at Top Greene?
facts.value: The renovated center is planned as the trailhead for a new roughly two-mile South Park Heritage Trail linking downtown, greenway and park spaces, and the historic neighborhood through African American interpretation. It is a future project, not a reason to assume a completed signed loop exists today; check the project page before planning a trail visit.

facts.label: Can I rent a room at Top Greene Cultural Center?
facts.value: Yes, subject to staff approval. The current banquet room holds up to 99 people and includes use of a warming kitchen, where food may be warmed but not cooked from scratch. A request is not final until staff approve it and payment is confirmed; deposits, application charges, minimum hours, and after-hours staffing apply.
