facts.label: Are there restrooms at Kiwanis Park?
facts.value: Plan around the neighborhood center rather than assuming a separate restroom stays open with the outdoor park. The center is open Monday-Friday 9 a.m.-8 p.m. and Saturday 9 a.m.-3 p.m., and is closed Sunday. Call 919-996-3135 before a restroom-dependent visit because building access can change for programs, rentals, holidays, or maintenance.

facts.label: Does Kiwanis Park have basketball courts and fields?
facts.value: Yes. Kiwanis has one full outdoor concrete basketball court, a lighted 185-foot baseball field, and two unlighted multipurpose fields. Courts are typically first come when not reserved. Field use and organized practices can require a reservation through Raleigh Athletics, so an empty-looking field may still be scheduled.

facts.label: Can I reserve the picnic shelter at Kiwanis Park?
facts.value: Yes. The shelter holds about 60 people and has 10 tables, but no electricity or water. The City lists it at $15 per hour and requires approval and payment before a reservation is final. Unreserved casual use may be available, but a posted or confirmed reservation has priority.

facts.label: Does Kiwanis Park have an off-leash dog park?
facts.value: Kiwanis has a fenced dog run with benches, wood chips, and a waste-bag dispenser. Unlike Raleigh dog parks that advertise separate small- and large-dog sections, the City does not list size-separated areas or a water source here. Dogs must be leashed outside the run, and toys, food, treats, and outside furniture are prohibited inside Raleigh off-leash areas.

facts.label: Can I access the Raleigh greenway from Kiwanis Park?
facts.value: Yes. Kiwanis Park is a trailhead on Crabtree Creek Trail, one of the major paved corridors in Raleigh's Capital Area Greenway. The citywide system has more than 100 miles across 28 trails and is open dawn to dusk. Check the Greenway Explorer and current alerts before leaving because floods, construction, fallen trees, or maintenance can close an individual segment while the park remains open.

facts.label: Is Kiwanis Park accessible for wheelchairs and strollers?
facts.value: The renovated playground uses a rubber surface, and developed paths connect the main recreation facilities. Conditions and grades can differ at the fields and greenway connection. For a route-specific accommodation, contact Kiwanis Park at 919-996-3135 or Raleigh Parks Inclusion Services before visiting.

facts.label: What time does Kiwanis Park close?
facts.value: Use outdoor park amenities from dawn to dusk. The neighborhood center follows a separate schedule: Monday-Friday 9 a.m.-8 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m.-3 p.m., and closed Sunday. A lit baseball field does not mean the whole park or building remains available at night; reserved activities follow their confirmed schedule.

facts.label: Is Kiwanis Park free?
facts.value: General entry, marked parking, playground use, the basketball court when available, dog run, and greenway access are free. Room rentals, the picnic shelter, organized field use, classes, and private programs can require reservations and fees. Non-Raleigh residents pay a 25 percent surcharge on eligible indoor rental rates.

facts.label: Where can I find shade at Kiwanis Park?
facts.value: The picnic shelter provides reliable open-air shade, and trees provide changing shade around portions of the 24-acre park. The basketball court, baseball and multipurpose fields, playground areas, and greenway approaches can be exposed. The shelter has no water or electricity and is not safe severe-weather protection; during lightning or dangerous wind, use an open substantial building or enclosed vehicle.

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Open dawn to dusk daily under Raleigh's dog-park directory. Kiwanis Neighborhood Center hours are separate.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: Free to the public. Programs, rooms, fields, courts, and rentals may have separate schedules or charges.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: The dog run is within a developed neighborhood park, but the City does not document an enclosure-specific accessible route. Wood chips, gates, mud, and crowding can affect access; contact Kiwanis staff for current conditions.

facts.label: Where should I park for Kiwanis Park Dog Run?
facts.value: Navigate to Kiwanis Park at 2525 Noble Road and use marked park parking. The same campus serves the neighborhood center, playground, fields, courts, and Crabtree Creek Greenway trailhead, so spaces may be busier during programs or games. Do not park in nearby private lots or block neighborhood streets.

facts.label: How do I enter Kiwanis Park Dog Run safely?
facts.value: Follow park signs from the Noble Road campus to the fenced dog run. Keep your dog leashed across the parking lot and park, wait if dogs crowd the gate, remove choke, prong, pinch, or spike collars, secure the outside gate, and unleash before entering the play enclosure. Leash again before opening the exit gate.

facts.label: Is there a restroom near Kiwanis Park Dog Run?
facts.value: Kiwanis Neighborhood Center is on the same park campus, but indoor restroom access follows building hours: 9 a.m.-8 p.m. Monday-Friday, 9 a.m.-3 p.m. Saturday, and closed Sunday. The City does not list a dedicated dog-run restroom. Confirm building access and never leave a dog unattended in the enclosure.

facts.label: What hours is Kiwanis Park Dog Run open?
facts.value: Raleigh lists its public dog parks as open dawn to dusk daily. The neighborhood center's later weekday hours do not extend dog-run hours. Posted closures for weather, mud, maintenance, or safety take priority, so check Raleigh Parks Status after heavy rain.

facts.label: Is Kiwanis Park Dog Run free?
facts.value: Yes. Ordinary use of the dog run and public park is free. Neighborhood-center programs, room or field reservations, leagues, and other organized activities may charge separately.

facts.label: Is Kiwanis Park Dog Run wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The enclosure is in a developed public park, but the City does not publish a dog-run-specific accessible route. Wood chips, gate force, mud, slope, and crowding may create barriers. Contact Kiwanis Neighborhood Center at 919-996-6833 before visiting for current parking-to-gate and surface details.

facts.label: Does Kiwanis Dog Run separate small and large dogs?
facts.value: The official Kiwanis page describes one dog run and does not list separate small- and large-dog sections. Treat it as a shared enclosure unless current gate signs say otherwise. Small, shy, older, or mobility-limited dogs may be safer during a quiet period or at a size-separated Raleigh dog park.

facts.label: Is water available at Kiwanis Park Dog Run?
facts.value: The City's dog-run amenity list does not include a dog or human water source. Bring enough water and a clean portable bowl, especially during warm weather. Do not assume the neighborhood center is open or that an outdoor tap is potable.

facts.label: Is Kiwanis Dog Run shaded or muddy?
facts.value: The City confirms a wood-chip surface and benches but does not list shade as an enclosure amenity. Wood chips can shift, hide holes, and become wet or muddy after rain. Plan sun protection, wear suitable shoes, and bring towels or paw-cleaning supplies.

facts.label: What dogs are allowed at Kiwanis Park Dog Run?
facts.value: Dogs must be healthy and fully vaccinated. Puppies under four months, females in season, and aggressive or uncontrollable dogs are prohibited. A handler may supervise no more than three dogs and remains responsible for each dog's behavior.

facts.label: Can I bring toys, treats, or a chair into Kiwanis Dog Run?
facts.value: No. Raleigh prohibits food, treats, toys, and outside furniture in dog parks because they can trigger guarding and conflict. Remove choke, prong, pinch, and spike collars; use the supplied waste bags; stop digging; fill holes; and actively supervise your dog.

facts.label: Can children enter Kiwanis Park Dog Run?
facts.value: Children under 12 must be closely supervised. The dog run is not a playground: children should not run, carry food or toys, approach unfamiliar dogs, or crowd the gates. Kiwanis Park has a separate playground with a rubber surface for ages 2-12.

facts.label: What should I do about a bite or maintenance issue at Kiwanis Dog Run?
facts.value: Remove dogs before a conflict escalates. Call Animal Control at 919-831-6311 for an aggressive or uncontrollable dog; after a bite, get medical care, identify the dog and owner, and call 911 for serious injury. Report fence, gate, waste, or surface problems to Raleigh Parks maintenance at 919-996-4115.

facts.label: What else is near Kiwanis Park Dog Run?
facts.value: Kiwanis Park includes a neighborhood center, playground for ages 2-12, athletic fields, courts, and a Crabtree Creek Greenway trailhead. Dogs must be leashed outside the enclosure and kept off playgrounds, athletic fields, and courts. The greenway can extend the outing, but it is shared and follows separate trail rules.

facts.value: Navigate to the mapped park location at 810. Parking layout and overflow rules are not yet fully catalogued in this Basic record, so follow official signs and do not block neighborhood streets or service entrances.

places.name: Lake Johnson Loop Trails
places.type: Paved lakeside greenway and natural-surface trail network

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Park trails and bathrooms are open sunrise to sunset. The Waterfront Center, Crowder Woodland Center, pool, rentals, and programs follow separate schedules.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: Trail and general park access are free. Boat rentals, pool admission, programs, facility rentals, and some activities may charge; fishing requires the applicable North Carolina license.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: The paved East Loop and Waterfront Center provide the most predictable access, with accessible parking, restrooms, deck, overlook, and fishing dock. West-side natural trails have changing grades and surfaces and are not equivalent accessible routes.

facts.label: Amenities
facts.value: 2.8-mile paved East Loop, West-side natural-surface trails, Lake overlooks, Boardwalk and dam views, Walnut Creek Greenway connection, Waterfront Center, Accessible restrooms and fishing dock, QR fitness stations, Interpretive Poetry Trail, Hammock posts, Fishing access, Wildlife viewing, Four documented parking areas

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 4601 Avent Ferry Road, Raleigh, NC

facts.label: Where should I park for the Lake Johnson loop trails?
facts.value: For the East Loop and services, use the Waterfront Center at 4601 Avent Ferry Road, the south lot at 5051 Avent Ferry Road, or the dam lot at 1320 Lake Dam Road. For west-side natural trails, the clearest start is Thomas G. Crowder Woodland Center at 5611 Jaguar Park Drive; the south lot also links both sides. Use only marked park spaces.

facts.label: Which Lake Johnson trail entrance is best for a first visit?
facts.value: Start at the Waterfront Center, 4601 Avent Ferry Road, for the paved East Loop, accessible restrooms, covered lake overlook, accessible fishing dock, staff-area orientation, and direct trail access. Start at Crowder Woodland Center for the wooded west-side trails, QR fitness route, and Interpretive Poetry Trail.

facts.label: Are there restrooms on the Lake Johnson loops?
facts.value: Accessible restrooms are available at the Waterfront Center and Thomas G. Crowder Woodland Center, and the City says park bathrooms are open sunrise to sunset. Other buildings and seasonal facilities have separate hours. Choose the starting center that matches your route rather than assuming a restroom appears midway around the lake.

facts.label: What hours are the Lake Johnson trails open?
facts.value: The park trails and bathrooms are open sunrise to sunset. The Waterfront Center, Crowder Woodland Center, pool, boat rentals, and programs follow their own schedules. Begin early enough to complete the chosen loop and return before sunset.

facts.label: Are the Lake Johnson loop trails free?
facts.value: Yes. Walking, running, and general trail access are free. Boat rentals, paddling programs, pool admission, reserved facilities, and other programs may charge. Fishing from approved locations requires a current North Carolina fishing license.

facts.label: Which Lake Johnson loop is most accessible?
facts.value: Choose the paved East Loop and Waterfront Center. That lot has three accessible spaces, an entrance ramp, accessible restrooms, covered deck and lake overlook, and an accessible fishing dock. The natural-surface west side has roots, changing grades, and variable conditions and should not be treated as an equivalent accessible loop.

facts.label: What is the difference between Lake Johnson's East and West loops?
facts.value: The East Loop is the 2.8-mile paved greenway around the east side and is part of Walnut Creek Greenway. The current park page describes about 1.5 miles of unpaved natural-surface trail on the west side, while the system trail list labels a 2.1-mile West Loop. Use the park map for the exact west-side route rather than assuming every west path forms one paved loop.

facts.label: Can I walk all the way around Lake Johnson?
facts.value: The East Loop is a documented 2.8-mile paved loop, while west-side natural trails can be combined using the park map. Roads, the lake crossing, and trail junctions can make an all-lake route less obvious than a single circle. For a predictable first trip, complete the East Loop or choose a mapped west-side out-and-back from Crowder Woodland Center.

facts.label: Can I bike the Lake Johnson loops?
facts.value: Biking is allowed only on greenway trails. The paved East Loop supports bicycles under Raleigh's shared-trail rules and 10 mph speed limit. Bikes are not permitted on the south half of the west-side natural trail section. Check the park map at junctions and do not ride onto hiking-only paths.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed on the Lake Johnson trails?
facts.value: Yes. Dogs must be under control on a leash no longer than six feet, and owners must remove waste. Keep dogs out of the water, yield on narrow natural trails, and use extra care around bicycles, wildlife, fishing lines, and crowded boardwalk areas.

facts.label: Where is the QR fitness trail at Lake Johnson?
facts.value: Six QR fitness stations cover roughly a one-mile loop on the west side, accessible from Thomas G. Crowder Woodland Center at 5611 Jaguar Park Drive. A phone with cellular data is needed to open the exercise videos. The stations cover upper body, core, flexibility, and lower-body exercises.

facts.label: Where is the Lake Johnson Interpretive Poetry Trail?
facts.value: The one-mile Interpretive Poetry Trail is on the wooded west side and features work by ten local poets on signs along natural-surface trails. Start from the Crowder Woodland Center side and use the City's interactive poetry map; it is a quieter nature-and-art walk, not the paved East Loop.

facts.label: Can I swim or wade from the Lake Johnson trails?
facts.value: No. Swimming and wading are prohibited. Fishing is allowed only from the boardwalk, fishing pier, designated bank area, or personal paddlecraft under applicable regulations. Use designated water access and never enter the lake from a trail edge.

facts.label: Do the Lake Johnson trails close after storms?
facts.value: Trail conditions can change because of storms, fallen trees, flooding, erosion, prescribed burns, maintenance, or events. Check Lake Johnson park alerts and Raleigh greenway alerts before visiting. Natural-surface west trails are especially sensitive to wet conditions; avoid muddy paths rather than widening them.

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Park, trails, and park restrooms are open sunrise to sunset; centers and pool have separate schedules.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General park and trail access are free. Boat rentals, pool admission, programs, shelters, and facility rentals may charge.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessible parking is distributed among the Waterfront Center, Woodland Center, south lot, and Lake Dam Road lot. The Waterfront Center has a ramp, accessible restrooms, overlook, and accessible fishing dock.

facts.label: Amenities
facts.value: Paved lake loops, Natural-surface trails, Fishing, Paddling, Waterfront Center, Woodland Center, Seasonal pool and spray ground, Picnic shelters

facts.value: 4601 Avent Ferry Road, Raleigh, NC

facts.label: Where should I park at Lake Johnson Park?
facts.value: Use 4601 Avent Ferry Road for the Waterfront Center, boardwalk, accessible fishing dock, and paddling. Use 5611 Jaguar Park Drive for the Thomas G. Crowder Woodland Center and west-side natural trails. Additional smaller lots sit along Avent Ferry Road and Lake Dam Road; choose the lot nearest your activity rather than assuming the park has one entrance.

facts.label: Which Lake Johnson entrance should I use?
facts.value: Use the Waterfront Center entrance at 4601 Avent Ferry Road for the lake overlook, fishing dock, boardwalk, paddling, and east loop. Use the Woodland Center at 5611 Jaguar Park Drive for the park office, west-side forest, programs, and Interpretive Poetry Trail. The pool has its own entrance at 5623 Jaguar Park Drive.

facts.label: Where are restrooms at Lake Johnson Park?
facts.value: Accessible restrooms are available at both the Waterfront Center and Thomas G. Crowder Woodland Center, and the City states park trail bathrooms are open sunrise to sunset. Use a restroom before a long loop because facilities are concentrated at developed areas rather than continuously along the trail.

facts.label: What time does Lake Johnson Park close?
facts.value: The park, trails, and park bathrooms are open from sunrise to sunset. The Waterfront Center, Woodland Center, boat service, programs, and seasonal pool use separate operating schedules, so daylight park access does not guarantee that a building or rental service is open.

facts.label: Is Lake Johnson Park free?
facts.value: Walking, running, ordinary park entry, and marked parking are free. Boat rentals, registered programs, the seasonal pool, shelters, and indoor facility rentals may charge. Fishing requires a current North Carolina fishing license even though the park itself has no general admission fee.

facts.label: Is Lake Johnson Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The Waterfront Center has three accessible spaces, a ramped entrance, accessible restrooms and overlook, plus a ramped fishing dock. The Woodland Center has four accessible spaces and accessible restrooms. Other lots include additional accessible spaces, but natural trails have roots, grades, and uneven surfaces; call 919-996-3141 for route-specific help.

facts.label: How long is the walk around Lake Johnson?
facts.value: The paved east loop is 2.8 miles and the paved west loop is 2.1 miles. The west side also has natural-surface routes, including a one-mile wooded Interpretive Poetry Trail. Use the park map before combining loops, and expect hills, roots, mud, and weather closures away from paved greenway sections.

facts.label: Can I rent a kayak at Lake Johnson?
facts.value: Yes. Third-party lockers near the Waterfront Center offer kayak and stand-up paddleboard rentals, and Raleigh also schedules paddling programs. Availability, price, age rules, and weather limits belong to the current rental or program booking; do not assume equipment is staffed or available just because the park is open.

facts.label: Where can I fish at Lake Johnson?
facts.value: Fishing is permitted from the boardwalk, accessible fishing pier, designated bank-fishing area, and personal paddle craft. A current North Carolina fishing license is required. The Waterfront Center offers free cane-pole and children's tackle-box loans when available, but visitors provide their own bait.

facts.label: Can I swim in Lake Johnson?
facts.value: No. Swimming and wading in the lake are prohibited. Lake Johnson Pool is a separate seasonal facility at 5623 Jaguar Park Drive with a spray ground, baby pool, and lap and recreation pool; it follows its own hours, admission rules, and operating status.

facts.value: The outdoor trail and park are generally open dawn to dusk daily. Lake Lynn Community Center and its restrooms follow separate building hours.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: The loop and general park access are free. Community-center programs, rentals, reservations, and organized activities may charge; fishing requires the applicable North Carolina license.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: The named loop is paved, with developed park and neighborhood connections, but slopes, boardwalk and bridge transitions, drainage, construction, and pavement conditions vary. West-side rehabilitation is planned to improve width, grading, drainage, bridges, and access.

facts.label: Where should I park for Lake Lynn Loop Trail?
facts.value: The City lists lots at Lake Lynn Park, 7921 Ray Road, and 3210 Lynn Road, plus neighborhood street access at 7609 Glenharden Drive. A fourth greenway lot at 6499 West Millbrook Road serves Wooten Meadow and Hare Snipe Creek rather than the simplest lake-loop start. Use 7921 Ray Road when community-center facilities matter.

facts.label: What is the best entrance to Lake Lynn Loop?
facts.value: Start at Lake Lynn Park and Community Center, 7921 Ray Road, for the clearest combination of parking, orientation, restrooms during building hours, playgrounds, fields, and the loop. Use 3210 Lynn Road for the opposite side. Glenharden Drive is neighborhood access and should not be treated as a full-service trailhead.

facts.label: Are there restrooms on Lake Lynn Loop?
facts.value: Restrooms are available inside Lake Lynn Community Center during its building hours, not automatically for every dawn-to-dusk trail visit. The City does not promise a separate always-open loop restroom. Use the center before starting when it is open and plan without guaranteed facilities after it closes.

facts.label: What hours is Lake Lynn Loop open?
facts.value: Outdoor park space and the loop are generally open dawn to dusk daily. Community Center hours are Monday-Friday 7 a.m.-9 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m.-3 p.m., and Sunday 1-6 p.m., subject to updates and closures. Trail access does not guarantee that the building or restrooms are open.

facts.label: Is Lake Lynn Loop free?
facts.value: Yes. Walking, running, cycling, public-art viewing, playground use, and general park access are free. Community-center programs, classes, leagues, rentals, and shelter reservations may charge. Fishing requires a current North Carolina fishing license.

facts.label: Is Lake Lynn Loop wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The named loop is paved and developed access points can support wheelchairs and mobility devices, but the entire circuit is not perfectly uniform. Slopes, boardwalk and bridge approaches, drainage, pavement wear, and project work vary. Planned west-side rehabilitation includes trail widening, grading, drainage, bridge replacement, and improved neighborhood access.

facts.label: How long is Lake Lynn Loop?
facts.value: Raleigh's dedicated trail page and current system list define the named paved Lake Lynn Loop as 1.2 miles. The broader park page currently mentions 2.8 miles, but that conflicts with the trail-specific record. Connected Hare Snipe Creek segments or alternate paths can create longer trips, so use the City trail map when distance matters.

facts.label: Is Lake Lynn Trail a complete loop?
facts.value: Yes. The named route is a paved circuit around Lake Lynn. Watch signs near the Hare Snipe Creek junction so you remain on the lake loop; continuing south changes the outing into a longer linear greenway trip toward Wooten Meadow. Start and finish at the same documented parking area.

facts.label: Where does Lake Lynn Loop connect?
facts.value: The loop connects with Hare Snipe Creek Greenway, a 2.3-mile route between Wooten Meadow Park and Lake Lynn Park. That extension offers a longer outing but is not part of the 1.2-mile named lake circuit. Plan the added distance and return before leaving the loop.

facts.label: Can I bike Lake Lynn Loop?
facts.value: Yes. The paved loop is a shared Raleigh greenway with centerline and safety markings. The speed limit is 10 mph. Keep right, yield to pedestrians, announce passes on the left, and slow on boardwalks, bridges, near public art, and around children, dogs, anglers, and trailheads.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed on Lake Lynn Loop?
facts.value: Yes, under Raleigh's shared-trail rules. Dogs must remain controlled on a leash no longer than six feet, keep right with their handler, and owners must remove waste. Do not allow pets to disturb wildlife, anglers, children, or people using narrow boardwalks and bridges.

facts.label: Where can I fish at Lake Lynn?
facts.value: Fishing is allowed from the docks and pedestrian bridge with a current fishing license and live bait. Bank fishing is prohibited, and personal watercraft are not allowed on the lake. Keep hooks, lines, and equipment out of the shared trail and boardwalk travel path.

facts.label: What public art is on Lake Lynn Loop?
facts.value: Twenty stainless-steel, origami-inspired sculptures by artist team A Gang of Three were installed around the loop in 2026. They create trail-side points of interest without requiring museum admission. View them from the path and avoid climbing, moving, or attaching items to the artwork.

facts.label: Will Lake Lynn Loop construction affect my visit?
facts.value: It may. West-side rehabilitation is planned on a 2025-2027 project timeline and includes new pavement, widening, grading, drainage, access work, markings, and bridge replacement. Check the project page and greenway alerts immediately before visiting; do not enter closed work zones or improvise through neighborhoods.

facts.label: What time does Lake Lynn Park close?

facts.label: Is Lake Lynn Park free?

Classes, indoor gym use under certain programs, field reservations, room rentals, and the picnic shelter charge. facts.label: Is the Lake Lynn loop accessible for wheelchairs and strollers?

Bridges, slopes, surface wear, and temporary closures still vary around the 2.8-mile circuit. Contact Lake Lynn Community Center at 919-996-2911 for a route-specific accommodation or current condition.

facts.label: How long is the Lake Lynn walking loop?
facts.value: The paved greenway loop around Lake Lynn is 2.8 miles. It includes pedestrian bridges and connects into Raleigh's greenway network, so watch signs at trail junctions if you want the lake-only circuit. Allow extra time with children, wheels, fishing stops, or crowded bridge sections.

facts.label: What ages are the Lake Lynn playgrounds for?
facts.value: Lake Lynn has separate woodchip-surface playground areas for ages 2-5 and ages 5-12, with toddler swings listed by the City. Restrooms are inside the community center and follow building hours, so a dawn, dusk, or holiday playground visit may not have restroom access.

facts.label: What courts are available at Lake Lynn Park?
facts.value: The park has four outdoor tennis courts with backboards and push-button lighting from dusk to 10 p.m., plus two first-come bocce courts. The community center has two indoor full gym courts lined for basketball, volleyball, and pickleball; indoor availability follows programs, open play, rentals, and fees.

facts.label: Where can I fish at Lake Lynn?
facts.value: Fishing is allowed from the docks and pedestrian bridge. Anglers need a current fishing license and must use live bait. Bank fishing is prohibited, and personal watercraft are not allowed, so do not plan to fish from the shoreline or launch a kayak.

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Seasonal daily hours range from 8 a.m.-6 p.m. in midwinter to 6 a.m.-8 p.m. May-August.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: Park entry and fishing access are free, but a fishing license is required. Personal boat launching, equipment rentals, programs, courts, shelters, and facilities may charge.

facts.label: Accessibility

facts.label: Where should I park at Lake Wheeler Park?
facts.value: Route to 6404 Lake Wheeler Road and follow signs for your activity. The upper Waterfront Center lot serves shelters, the accessible fishing dock, and overlook; additional accessible spaces sit down the road toward the boat ramps. Trailer users should follow launch-area circulation rather than occupying ordinary visitor spaces.

facts.label: Which entrance should I use at Lake Wheeler Park?
facts.value: Use the signed main entrance at 6404 Lake Wheeler Road. Continue toward the Waterfront Center for the office, restrooms, overlook, shelters, and accessible fishing dock, or follow boat-ramp signs for launching. Check the current lake alert before towing a boat because low water can change launch availability.

facts.label: Are restrooms available at Lake Wheeler Park?
facts.value: Yes. Restrooms with accessible features are at the Waterfront Center, beside the deck and veranda overlooking the lake. Trail and shoreline areas do not have continuous facilities, so use the Waterfront Center before heading onto a natural trail or out on the water.

facts.label: What time does Lake Wheeler Park close?
facts.value: Hours change seasonally: 8 a.m.-6 p.m. in December-January; 7 a.m.-6 p.m. in November and February; 7 a.m.-7 p.m. in October and March; 7 a.m.-8 p.m. in September and April; and 6 a.m.-8 p.m. May-August. Boats must leave the water 30 minutes before sunset or closing.

facts.label: Is Lake Wheeler Park free?
facts.value: General park entry and fishing access are free, although anglers need a current North Carolina fishing license. Personal boat launches cost $5 per day for Raleigh residents, $7 for nonresidents, or $3 for ages 55 and older; annual passes are available. Rentals, programs, shelters, and courts may charge separately.

facts.label: Is Lake Wheeler Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The upper lot has four accessible spaces, including spaces near Magnolia Shelter and the sidewalk to the accessible fishing dock. Two more accessible spaces are near the boat-ramp road. A ramp reaches the Waterfront Center, accessible restrooms, deck, and veranda; natural trails remain uneven with roots, rocks, and changing surfaces.

facts.label: Can I launch a motorboat at Lake Wheeler?
facts.value: Yes. Motorized and nonmotorized boats may launch with a daily or annual pass, but personal watercraft such as Jet Skis are prohibited. Travel counter-clockwise, observe the 40 mph limit and no-wake markers, and note lake-wide no-wake hours Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday until 11 a.m.

facts.label: Where can I fish at Lake Wheeler?
facts.value: Fish from the two designated piers or the shoreline of Simpkins Pond; bank fishing along the main Lake Wheeler shoreline is prohibited. No separate City fishing permit fee is charged, but every angler needs a current North Carolina fishing license. A rod-and-reel loaner program may be available at the office.

facts.label: Does Lake Wheeler Park have a playground?
facts.value: Yes. The woodchip-surface playground serves ages 2-12 and includes swings intended for ages 5 and older. It is near other developed park amenities, but shade and restroom distance vary; use the park map and Waterfront Center as the reliable restroom reference point.

facts.label: Can visitors swim at Lake Wheeler?
facts.value: No. Swimming and wading are prohibited because Lake Wheeler is an active drinking-water reservoir. Waterskiing and tubing from permitted boats may occur, but entering the water to swim is not allowed, including from a private boat.

facts.label: Where should I park for Lassiter Mill Park?
facts.value: Use the City-listed greenway lot at 3300 Lassiter Mill Road and the park approach at Lassiter Falls Circle. Parking is limited, so arrive early and use only marked spaces; nearby residential, business, and no-parking areas are not overflow. Construction staging beginning in 2026 may change the practical entrance or available spaces.

facts.label: Which entrance should I use for Lassiter Mill Park?
facts.value: Use 3300 Lassiter Falls Circle for the historic dam, mill-remnant overlook, plaque, lawn, and picnic area. The City also identifies 3300 Lassiter Mill Road as the greenway parking point. Trail construction can change crossings near the road and bridge, so follow current signs rather than an older saved route.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Lassiter Mill Park?
facts.value: Do not plan on a public restroom at this small historic and greenway access site. Raleigh's official parking and project pages do not list one, and there is no community center. Use a restroom before arriving, especially before a longer Crabtree Creek Trail ride or walk.

facts.label: What time does Lassiter Mill Park close?
facts.value: Use the park and Crabtree Creek Greenway from dawn to dusk under Raleigh's general operating rule. The site has no staffed visitor center or lit recreation facility, and the dam and creek bank become harder to navigate safely in low light.

facts.label: Is Lassiter Mill Park free?
facts.value: Yes. General entry, the historic overlook, picnic area, and greenway access are free. Fishing requires the appropriate current North Carolina license and compliance with posted rules, but the City does not list a separate park admission or parking fee.

facts.label: Is Lassiter Mill Park wheelchair and stroller accessible?
facts.value: The parking approach and paved Crabtree Creek Trail are the most predictable routes. The current corridor also includes an unpaved section, steps, and changing bank conditions near Lassiter Mill Road, while the dam overlook has grass, rocks, and uneven edges. Construction is intended to improve this connection but will temporarily change access.

facts.label: Can I access Crabtree Creek Greenway at Lassiter Mill?
facts.value: Yes. Lassiter Mill is a City-listed parking and access point on the paved 18-mile Crabtree Creek corridor, which connects west toward Kiwanis Park, Crabtree Valley and Umstead and east toward Anderson Point and the Neuse River Trail. The local road crossing and unpaved segment are entering a major improvement project.

facts.label: Will construction affect Lassiter Mill Park and the greenway?
facts.value: Yes. Raleigh plans construction from August 2026 through fall 2028 on the Crabtree Creek corridor between Hartford Street and Lassiter Mill Road, including the unpaved segment, stream bank, boardwalk and steps, and the road bridge area. Expect signed detours, closures, or altered parking and check the project and greenway alerts before visiting.

facts.label: What remains of the historic Lassiter Mill?
facts.value: Visitors can see the dam, remnants of the former mill across Crabtree Creek, and an interpretive plaque describing the site. The mill itself is not a restored building open for tours. View the remains from established public areas and do not treat private property, the dam structure, or the opposite bank as an invitation to enter.
facts.sourceLabel: Visit Raleigh and Yates Mill Associates

facts.label: Can I fish at Lassiter Mill Park?
facts.value: Fishing takes place along Crabtree Creek where signs and conditions permit. Carry a current North Carolina fishing license and follow posted water and harvest rules. Banks and rocks near the dam can be steep, slippery, flooded, or unstable; choose an established safe position and never enter a closed construction area.

Ask staff or check onsite signs for the shortest accessible route from the playground because the shelter, building, and play area are distinct parts of the campus.

facts.label: What hours is Laurel Hills Park open?
facts.value: The Community Center is open 10 a.m.-9 p.m. Monday-Friday, 9 a.m.-3 p.m. Saturday, and 1-6 p.m. Sunday. Outdoor park areas are generally used dawn to dusk. Restrooms, staff help, indoor gym access, and programs depend on the Center or facility schedule rather than daylight alone.

facts.label: Is Sassafras Playground free?
facts.value: Yes. General park admission and use of Sassafras All Children's Playground are free. Programs, indoor sports, room rentals, shelter reservations, and reserved fields or basketball courts may charge. A submitted reservation is not final until City approval and payment confirmation.

facts.label: How accessible is Sassafras All Children's Playground?
facts.value: The playground was designed so children with different abilities can play together and includes a wheelchair-accessible play structure. That verified feature does not guarantee every component fits every sensory, transfer, or mobility need. Use the developed route from parking and contact the Center for specific equipment or accommodation questions.

facts.label: What makes Sassafras an inclusive playground?
facts.value: Sassafras is an all-children's playground intentionally designed for children of different abilities to share the same play environment, including a wheelchair-accessible structure. Families seeking a particular swing, transfer platform, quiet space, fencing condition, or surfacing detail should verify that specific need with the Center before traveling.

facts.label: Are there nature trails at Laurel Hills Park?
facts.value: The park has a small pond and nature area with an overlook, instructional benches, walking paths, and a boardwalk documented in City materials. Conditions and surfaces can change near water and woods, so use the paved developed park routes for the most predictable accessibility and supervise children at the pond edge.

facts.label: Can I fish in the pond at Laurel Hills Park?
facts.value: No. The pond is an observation and nature-education feature, and the City explicitly prohibits fishing. Use the overlook and boardwalk to watch wildlife and leave plants and animals undisturbed; choose a City lake or designated fishing park for angling.

facts.label: Can I play basketball at Laurel Hills Park?
facts.value: Yes. Two outdoor courts sit directly beside the baseball area and can be reserved through the Community Center; scheduled use has priority. The Center also has a large indoor gym with two full-size courts that can operate together or separately for programs, open play, and paid rentals.

facts.label: What fields are at Laurel Hills Park?
facts.value: The park has two youth baseball fields, each listed at 300 feet to the fence, plus a 150-by-150-foot multipurpose field beside Field 2. Scheduled leagues and approved rentals have priority over informal play, and field conditions can change with weather or maintenance.

facts.label: Can I reserve the picnic shelter at Laurel Hills Park?
facts.value: Yes. The shelter has capacity around 75, ten tables, two charcoal grills, nearby restrooms, and no electricity. The current rate is listed at $20 per hour. Submit through RecLink or contact the Center, but do not announce a gathering until staff has approved the request and confirmed payment.

facts.value: Use 5105 Country Trail for the park's primary visitor approach. facts.label: Are there restrooms at Leesville Community Park?
facts.value: Yes. The 2026 park improvements added a permanent restroom building near the renewed playground and picnic area. Availability can still depend on posted hours, maintenance, or temporary closures, so do not assume the restroom remains unlocked after normal daylight park use.

facts.label: What hours is Leesville Community Park open?
facts.value: The outdoor park is generally used dawn to dusk. The City does not publish separate daily building hours on the park page, so restroom access, maintenance work, special events, and nearby library or school schedules should not be inferred from outdoor park availability. facts.label: Is Leesville Community Park free?
facts.value: Yes. General park admission, playground use, the paved trail, picnic area, reading nook, and Heritage Garden are free. A special program or organized event may have separate registration requirements, but ordinary self-guided visits do not require a ticket.

facts.label: Is Leesville Community Park accessible for wheelchairs and strollers?
facts.value: The renewed park has a paved trailhead, a 10-foot-wide asphalt multipurpose trail, permanent restroom, expanded playground with safety surfacing, picnic area, and EV charging. These developed areas offer the most predictable access. The historic cemetery and chimney setting may include less-even natural ground.

facts.label: What is the new playground at Leesville Community Park like?
facts.value: The expanded playground has areas designed for ages 2-5 and 5-12, with slides, cargo nets, climbing structures, swings, fencing, and renewed rubberized safety surfacing. The 2026 improvements also placed a permanent restroom, picnic area, and reading nook in the renewed visitor area.

facts.label: How long is the trail at Leesville Community Park?
facts.value: The documented park trail is approximately 1,400 linear feet and 10 feet wide with paved asphalt surfacing. It is a short multipurpose connector rather than a long destination greenway and provides an alternate route toward Country Trail and the Leesville School Complex.

facts.label: Can families picnic at Leesville Community Park?
facts.value: Yes. The 2026 project added a new picnic area alongside the playground improvements and reading nook. The City does not list it as a reservable shelter on the current park page, so treat ordinary seating as shared, first-come park space unless onsite signs or RecLink indicate otherwise.

facts.label: What are the chimney and cemetery at Leesville Community Park?
facts.value: The Heritage Garden preserves remnants of a yeoman family farm from the late 1800s and early 1900s, including the home's stone chimney and a family cemetery. Treat both as protected historic features: stay on appropriate paths, supervise children, and do not climb, move stones, or disturb gravesites.

facts.label: Is there EV charging at Leesville Community Park?
facts.value: Yes. An electric-vehicle charging station was included in the completed 2026 improvements. Charging availability, connector condition, time limits, and any payment terms can change, so check the charger itself and avoid treating an EV space as ordinary park parking.

facts.label: Where is the main entrance to Lions Park?

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Lions Park?

facts.label: What hours is Lions Park open?

facts.label: How accessible is Lions Park?

facts.label: What playgrounds are at Lions Park?
facts.value: Lions Park has separate playground areas designed for ages 2-5 and 5-12, both with rubber safety surfacing. The City's newer photos show climbing and sliding structures, swings, and outdoor play instruments. Use the age-appropriate area and supervise children because the surrounding campus also has active courts, roads, fields, and BMX activity.

facts.label: Can visitors ride the BMX track at Lions Park?
facts.value: Lions Park is home to Capital City BMX, a purpose-built dirt racing track. It is not an ordinary paved bicycle loop: riding, practice, races, equipment rules, waivers, fees, and weather closures are managed through Capital City BMX. Check the current racing information before bringing a bike or promising track access.

facts.label: How many tennis courts are at Lions Park?
facts.value: There are eight outdoor tennis courts and a practice backboard. Courts are typically first-come, first-served unless scheduled use has priority. Timer-controlled lighting operates from dusk to 10 p.m. from March through November, so winter evening availability is more limited.

facts.label: Are there basketball courts at Lions Park?
facts.value: Yes. Lions Park has two concrete outdoor basketball courts with lighting. The Community Center also has an air-conditioned wood-floor gym with six sets of bleachers, capacity listed around 100-250, and a current rental rate of $85 per hour. Indoor play depends on programs, open-play schedules, or reservations.

facts.label: What ballfields are at Lions Park?
facts.value: The park has four lighted fields: two softball fields at approximately 300 and 317 feet, a 264-foot youth baseball field that can also support softball, and a 350-foot regulation baseball field. Approved rentals and leagues have priority, and weather can close fields independently of the rest of the park.

facts.label: Can I reserve the picnic shelter at Lions Park?
facts.value: Yes. The shelter is listed for about 60-100 people with six tables, two grills, no electricity, and a current rate of $20 per hour. Requests require staff approval and payment confirmation, and a 25 percent nonresident surcharge may apply to the hourly rental rate.

facts.label: Does Lions Park Community Center have a fitness room?
facts.value: Yes. The adults-only fitness room includes a treadmill, elliptical, stationary bike, universal weight machine, and a set of free weights. The City currently lists membership at $12 per month for adults 18 and older. Ask the front desk about orientation, supervision, and current access hours.

facts.label: Is there public art at Lions Park?

facts.label: Hours

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 201 East Hargett Street, Raleigh, NC

facts.label: Where should I park for Marbles Kids Museum?
facts.value: The museum recommends the city-owned Wilmington Street Station Deck directly across the street, entered at 117 South Wilmington Street or 122 South Blount Street. It currently offers two free weekday hours and is free most weekends until 5 p.m., but Marbles does not own the deck and rates or event rules can change. Moore Square Deck at 233 South Wilmington Street is another nearby city option.

facts.label: Where is the entrance to Marbles Kids Museum?
facts.value: The main museum entrance is at 201 East Hargett Street, at Hargett and Blount streets across from Moore Square. Automatic doors serve the main entrance. Have each guest's QR ticket ready on a phone or printout, or purchase admission at the Welcome Desk. IMAX has a distinct entrance and ticketing flow on the same campus.

facts.label: Where are the restrooms and changing areas at Marbles?
facts.value: Accessible stalls are in every public restroom, with one public restroom per museum floor and additional facilities in IMAX. A single-occupant family restroom is on the first floor inside Splash. Baby-changing stations are in all public and single-occupant restrooms. A first-floor nursing room and second-floor Mamava pod provide private feeding spaces.

facts.label: What hours is Marbles Kids Museum open?
facts.value: The current official schedule is 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Monday through Sunday, with extended museum hours until 7 p.m. Thursday. Members may enter at 9 a.m. Special events, holidays, maintenance, and IMAX showtimes can follow different schedules, so check the live calendar before leaving.

facts.label: How much does Marbles Kids Museum cost?
facts.value: Current advance admission is $9.50 and day-of admission is $12.50 for adults, children, and seniors. Children under age one and Marbles members are free. Military admission is $8.50 advance or $11.50 day-of. Monday-Thursday after 3 p.m., Play Late for Less is $4.75 advance or $6.25 day-of. IMAX and special-event tickets are separate.

facts.label: Is Marbles Kids Museum wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Yes. The museum documents automatic entrance doors, an elevator between both exhibit floors, accessible stalls in all public restrooms, accessible IMAX seating, and free manual wheelchairs available first-come at the Welcome Desk or IMAX concessions with ID as a deposit. Personal care attendants accompanying guests with disabilities receive complimentary admission.

facts.label: Do I need advance tickets for Marbles?
facts.value: Advance tickets are recommended but not required. Buying ahead currently saves $3 per paid museum admission. Online buyers receive a confirmation and a separate email with QR codes for each guest; show the codes on a phone or printed page. Walk-up tickets may be purchased at the Welcome Desk when capacity allows.

facts.label: What ages is Marbles Kids Museum best for?
facts.value: Marbles officially recommends museum play for children age 10 and under. Babies and toddlers have dedicated experiences such as Toddlers Hollow, while older children can engage with active, imaginative, money, engineering, art, nature, water, and role-play exhibits. IMAX films vary by title and may suit older children and adults as well.

facts.label: When is Marbles Kids Museum least crowded?
facts.value: Marbles says weekends and holidays are busiest and weekday afternoons are typically quieter. During summer, Monday is designated as a no-groups day; during the school year, Tuesday is the no-groups day. These patterns do not guarantee low attendance, especially during camps, breaks, weather events, or special programs.

facts.label: What sensory accommodations does Marbles offer?
facts.value: Marbles is a KultureCity Certified Sensory Inclusive Venue. Free noise-reducing headphones, weighted blankets, fidget tools, picture schedules, and picture maps are available at the Welcome Desk. A social story supports advance preparation, and free registered Sensory Friendly Playtime events provide a calmer museum and reduced-volume, lights-up IMAX documentary experience monthly.

facts.label: Can we eat at Marbles Kids Museum?
facts.value: Bean Sprouts Cafe is on the Marbles campus and works to accommodate many food allergies; the first-floor PlayStore also sells packaged allergy-friendly snacks and drinks. Courtyard picnic tables are available first-come, first-served. Food rules differ for ordinary visits, parties, and groups, so confirm current outside-food policy before packing a full meal.

facts.label: Can I leave and re-enter Marbles Kids Museum?
facts.value: Yes. Keep the admission sticker issued at check-in for same-day reentry. Once checked in, visitors may stay until closing, and late arrivals can check in at the Welcome Desk after their timed entry. Tickets are non-refundable but may be rescheduled or credited when requested at least 24 hours before entry time.

facts.label: Can I take transit to Marbles Kids Museum?
facts.value: Yes. GoRaleigh Station is one block away between South Wilmington and South Blount streets and serves local and regional buses. Raleigh Union Station at 510 West Martin Street is about eight blocks away, which Marbles estimates as a 15-minute walk. Check current routes, fares, elevator access, and service alerts before traveling.

facts.label: Is IMAX included with Marbles museum admission?
facts.value: No. Museum admission and Marbles IMAX tickets are sold separately online or at the Welcome Desk, though combination or group options may be offered. Check the specific film, age fit, format, showtime, captioning, sensory screening, and arrival deadline. Movies begin on schedule and cannot wait for late guests.

facts.label: What can we combine with a Marbles visit?
facts.value: Moore Square is directly across Blount Street and provides lawn, seating, public space, and nearby food options. The City of Raleigh Museum, North Carolina State Capitol, North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences, and downtown restaurants are walkable for families able to extend the day, but each has separate hours, admission, and parking considerations.

facts.label: Where is the main entrance to Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: Use the Community Center at 3050 North New Hope Road as the staffed starting point. It provides the clearest orientation toward the skatepark, inline rink, lower deck, shelter, playgrounds, fields, garden, and indoor recreation spaces spread around the large campus.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: Yes. Indoor visitor facilities are available in the Community Center during posted building hours. Outdoor facilities may remain active on different schedules, so families using the skatepark, rink, shelter, fields, or playgrounds should plan around Center hours and check onsite signs for any event-day facilities.

facts.label: What hours is Marsh Creek Park open?
facts.value: The Community Center is open 10 a.m.-9 p.m. Monday-Friday, 9 a.m.-3 p.m. Saturday, and 1-6 p.m. Sunday. Outdoor park areas are generally used dawn to dusk, while classes, open gym, field reservations, skate activities, and private rentals can follow separate schedules.

facts.label: Is Marsh Creek Park free?
facts.value: General park admission, the playgrounds, skatepark, garden viewing, first-come picnic shelter, and available casual outdoor use are free. Programs and indoor activities may charge. The inline rink is currently listed at $30 per hour, while room, gym, and covered-deck rentals have separate rates and approval requirements.

facts.label: How accessible is Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: The two playgrounds have rubber surfacing and wheelchair-accessible play structures. The developed Community Center, paved parking, indoor gym and restrooms, inline rink, and lower deck provide other firm-surface options. The skatepark is specialized terrain, and exact field or garden routes should be confirmed when mobility access is essential.

facts.label: What is Marsh Creek Skate Park like?
facts.value: Built in 2009, Marsh Creek is Raleigh's only permanent skatepark and includes street, flow, and bowl elements. The City requires a helmet, elbow pads, and knee pads. Bring correctly fitted safety gear and inspect wetness, debris, crowding, and surface conditions before riding; never promise a beginner that every feature will be appropriate.

facts.label: Is there an inline hockey rink at Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: Yes. The outdoor rink measures approximately 185 by 85 feet and uses a Plexiflor inline-skating surface. The City lists a $30-per-hour rental rate. Scheduled rentals have priority, so check availability before organizing hockey, practice, or a group skate even if the rink appears empty.

facts.label: What playgrounds are at Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: Separate playgrounds serve ages 2-5 and 5-12. Both have rubber safety surfacing and a wheelchair-accessible play structure. Choose the age-appropriate area and supervise closely because the surrounding destination includes a skatepark, inline rink, parking, fields, and other active recreation uses.

facts.label: What fields are at Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: The park has a lighted 254-foot youth baseball field that can also support softball and a roughly 240-by-200-foot multipurpose field. Leagues and approved rentals have priority, and weather can close athletic fields while other park facilities remain open. Confirm field status before organized play.

facts.label: Can I reserve the picnic shelter at Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: No reservation is needed or accepted for the standalone picnic shelter. It is first-come, first-served, holds about 45 people, has eight tables and charcoal grills, no electricity, and sits near the skatepark and inline rink. For guaranteed event space, consider the separately rentable covered lower deck or indoor rooms.

facts.label: What indoor recreation is available at Marsh Creek Community Center?
facts.value: The Center has an air-conditioned hardwood gym lined for full and small basketball courts plus volleyball, and a fitness room with treadmills, elliptical machines, a recumbent bike, universal machine, stability ball, and stretching station. Access depends on programs, open play, membership rules, or rentals rather than ordinary park admission.

facts.label: Can visitors see the garden and urban farm at Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: Yes. The park's agricultural area includes raised beds, pollinator gardens, edible landscaping, a teaching garden, and a 1.5-acre urban-farm partnership with Raleigh City Farm. Self-guided viewing should not interfere with crops or classes; register through the Center for hands-on gardening and orchard programs.

facts.label: Does the Marsh Creek Trail connect to Marsh Creek Park?
facts.value: Do not assume it does. The City-listed Marsh Creek Trail is a separate 0.3-mile greenway segment through Brentwood Park between Glenraven Drive and Ingram Drive, with parking near Vinson Court. This Marsh Creek Park listing refers to the recreation campus at 3050 North New Hope Road.

facts.label: How many pickleball courts are at Method Community Park?

facts.label: Can I play basketball at Method Community Park?

facts.label: What fields are at Method Community Park?

facts.label: Can I reserve the picnic shelter at Method Community Park?

facts.label: Why is Method Community Park historically important?
facts.value: The park occupies the former Berry O'Kelly Training School grounds. Its Community Center honors educator and community leader Berry O'Kelly and Harveleigh Monte Rivera White. facts.label: Can visitors see the Berry O'Kelly School exhibit?
facts.value: Yes, when the Pioneers Building exhibit room is open or a history tour is arranged. The building was the old Agricultural Building of Berry O'Kelly High School, described by the City as North Carolina's first fully accredited and largest rural high school for African Americans. facts.label: When will Method Community Park renovations happen?
facts.value: The current City schedule places design, permitting, and bidding in 2025-2027 and construction in 2027-2028. facts.label: How do I enter Millbrook Dog Park safely?
facts.value: Follow signs within Millbrook Exchange Park to the dog-park gates and choose the posted small- or large-dog section. Keep your dog leashed until inside the gated vestibule, wait if the entry is crowded, remove choke, prong, pinch, or spike collars, close the outside gate, then unleash. Reverse that sequence when leaving.

facts.label: Are there restrooms near Millbrook Dog Park?
facts.value: Restrooms are available in Millbrook Exchange Community Center during building hours: 10 a.m.-9 p.m. Monday-Friday, 9 a.m.-3 p.m. Saturday, and 1-6 p.m. Sunday. Pool and tennis facilities follow separate access rules. Do not depend on an indoor restroom during the dog park's early or late hours, and never leave a dog unattended.

facts.label: What hours is Millbrook Dog Park open?
facts.value: The dedicated City page lists 7 a.m.-10 p.m. every day. Lights are provided at night, making this different from Raleigh's dawn-to-dusk dog runs. Posted closures for maintenance, weather, mud, or safety still take priority; do not assume other park buildings remain open until 10 p.m.

facts.label: Is Millbrook Dog Park free?
facts.value: Yes. The City explicitly lists the dog park as free to the public. Pool admission, tennis programs, classes, rentals, leagues, and reserved shelters or rooms may have separate fees.

facts.label: Is Millbrook Dog Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The dog park is on a developed recreation campus with parking and night lighting, but the City does not publish an enclosure-specific accessible route. Wood chips, mud, gate force, grade, and crowding may create barriers. Call Millbrook Exchange Community Center at 919-996-4156 for current parking-to-gate details and accommodations.

facts.label: Does Millbrook Dog Park separate small and large dogs?
facts.value: Yes. The City lists fenced areas for both small and large dogs, and the City of Oaks Foundation also describes two spacious sections. Follow the size designation posted at the gate rather than choosing only by crowd level. Size separation reduces mismatch but does not replace active supervision.

facts.label: Is water available at Millbrook Dog Park?
facts.value: Yes. Drinking fountains are provided for both dogs and humans. Fountains can be shut off for freezing weather, repair, or maintenance, so bring backup water and a portable bowl during heat. Food, treats, and toys are prohibited in the enclosure even though water is available.

facts.label: Is Millbrook Dog Park shaded or muddy?
facts.value: The official amenity list includes a shade structure, picnic tables, benches, and a wood-chip base. Wood chips can shift, conceal holes, and become wet or muddy after rain. Inspect the play area, wear suitable shoes, and bring towels or paw-cleaning supplies.

facts.label: Does Millbrook Dog Park have agility equipment?
facts.value: Yes. Raleigh lists agility equipment as a feature. Introduce equipment calmly, keep the landing area clear, and do not force or lift an unwilling dog onto a feature. The equipment is shared enrichment, not a reserved training course, and handlers remain responsible for avoiding collisions.

facts.label: What dogs are allowed at Millbrook Dog Park?
facts.value: Dogs must be healthy and fully vaccinated. Puppies under four months, females in season, and aggressive or uncontrollable dogs are prohibited. A handler may supervise no more than three dogs and remains responsible for each dog's conduct.

facts.label: Can I bring toys, treats, or a chair into Millbrook Dog Park?
facts.value: No. Raleigh prohibits food, treats, toys, and outside furniture in dog parks because they can trigger guarding and conflict. Remove choke, prong, pinch, and spike collars; collect waste; stop digging and fill holes; and watch your dog continuously rather than relying on the fence.

facts.label: Can children enter Millbrook Dog Park?
facts.value: Children under 12 must be closely supervised. Children should not run, carry food or toys, approach unfamiliar dogs, climb agility equipment, or crowd gates. Millbrook Exchange Park has separate playgrounds for child-centered activity.

facts.label: What should I do about a bite or maintenance problem at Millbrook Dog Park?
facts.value: Remove dogs before conflict escalates. Call Animal Control at 919-831-6311 for an aggressive or uncontrollable dog; after a bite, seek care, identify the dog and owner, and call 911 for serious injury. Report damaged gates, fencing, lights, fountains, waste, or surfaces to Raleigh Parks maintenance at 919-996-4115.

facts.label: What else is near Millbrook Dog Park?
facts.value: The wider park includes a year-round main pool, seasonal wading pool, community center, playgrounds, Millbrook Tennis Center, ball fields, shelters, greenway paths, and the Immigrant Gate II artwork. Dogs must remain leashed outside the dog park and are prohibited on playgrounds, courts, athletic fields, and pool decks.

facts.label: Where should I park for Moore Square?

facts.label: Which entrance should I use for Moore Square?
facts.value: The park paths have zero-entry access at all four corners and along the Martin Street, Hargett Street, and Blount Street sides. The historic Visitor Center's front entrance is stair-only, so visitors needing step-free access should ask on-site staff for the appropriate accessible route.

facts.label: Where are the restrooms at Moore Square?
facts.value: Public restrooms are at the park's Restrooms and Information Kiosk. The City currently lists them as open every day from 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.; the square itself remains open later, until 11:00 p.m.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad at Moore Square?
facts.value: Yes. The free Moore Square splash pad is at 225 E. Martin Street and is scheduled daily from 9:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. from April through October, weather permitting. There is no lifeguard; children must be supervised, and children who are not toilet trained must wear swim diapers.

facts.label: Is Moore Square easy to reach without driving?
facts.value: Yes. GoRaleigh Station is directly across Blount Street from Moore Square, with a signed walkway to the park and connections to numerous GoRaleigh and GoTriangle routes.

facts.label: Is anything closed at Moore Square right now?
facts.value: The square, splash pad, restrooms, and Visitor Center are operating on their listed schedules, but the Moore Square dog park remains temporarily closed for construction. The City lists the current dog-park closure through August 15, 2026. Large events can also change access to the lawn or plazas, so check the Moore Square calendar before a time-sensitive visit.

facts.label: Are the paths through Moore Square paved and accessible?
facts.value: Yes. The City describes paved sidewalks throughout the square as accessible to wheelchairs, scooters, and ECVs, with zero-entry path access at every corner and along Martin, Hargett, and Blount streets. The natural play area is a different surface and may not be accessible to every visitor.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Moore Square?
facts.value: Moore Square has a natural play area rather than a conventional fixed-equipment playground. The park also schedules Imagination Playground and Game On programs with loose play pieces, giant lawn games, board games, ping pong, and shuffleboard. These programmed materials are not guaranteed to be out all day, so check the daily calendar.

facts.label: Is the Moore Square dog park open?
facts.value: Not yet. The former temporary pop-up dog park closed in August 2025, and the replacement permanent dog park is still under construction. The City's current status alert lists the closure through August 15, 2026; verify the alert before bringing a dog specifically for off-leash play.

facts.label: Can I have a picnic at Moore Square?
facts.value: Yes. For a casual picnic, visitors can bring a blanket or chair to the central lawn when it is not reserved for an event. The Grove Rooms under the oak trees include community seating, and the Central Plaza has tables. The square does not list a traditional covered picnic shelter or public grill, so check the event calendar before relying on a particular lawn or plaza.

facts.label: Where is the best shade at Moore Square?
facts.value: The most reliable shade is around the bordering grove of mature oak trees and the Grove Rooms beneath them. The central event lawn is much more open, so choose the tree-framed edges for a hot-weather stop and expect shade position to move during the day.

facts.label: What public art or landmarks are in Moore Square?
facts.value: Look for Brad Goldberg's Grove Rooms, public-art gathering spaces integrated beneath the historic oak grove. The Visitor Center's Square Roots exhibit explains Moore Square's history since 1792, and the splash pad, central lawn, and granite-framed park edge are the easiest orientation landmarks.
facts.sourceLabel: City of Raleigh Percent for Public Art

facts.label: What hours is Moore Square open?
facts.value: Moore Square is open daily from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m., with possible extended access for approved special events. The Visitor Center and Square Roots history exhibit use shorter hours, Tuesday-Sunday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Event setup can temporarily occupy lawns or paths while the broader square remains open.

facts.label: Is Moore Square free?
facts.value: General entry, lawn use, natural play, the Visitor Center history exhibit, and many City programs are free. Food vendors, markets, private rentals, and selected festivals or partner events can charge separately. Nearby parking follows City deck, lot, or curb rules rather than being included with park access.

facts.label: Is Moore Square wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Paved sidewalks throughout the square support wheelchairs, scooters, and ECVs, with zero-entry path access at every corner and along Martin, Hargett, and Blount streets. The historic Visitor Center's front entrance requires stairs, and the natural play area may not suit every visitor. Call 919-996-6486 for the best alternate building route or site-specific assistance.

facts.label: Where should I park for Mordecai Historic Park?
facts.value: Parking is available at the park's 1 Mimosa Street address, with additional street parking along Cedar Street and Mordecai Drive. Accessible spaces are available in the Mimosa Street lot and beside the Visitor Center at 1101 Wake Forest Road. Orange signs guide the short walk from the Mimosa lot to the Visitor Center.

facts.label: Where should I start my visit to Mordecai Historic Park?
facts.value: Begin at the Visitor Center at 1101 Wake Forest Road, on the corner of Wake Forest Road and Cedar Street. This is where visitors buy guided-tour tickets, pick up a free self-guided grounds map, find exhibits, restrooms, the gift shop, and current tour information. The park's mailing and navigation address is 1 Mimosa Street.

facts.label: Where are the restrooms at Mordecai Historic Park?
facts.value: Outdoor comfort stations are in the red buildings on the Cedar Street side. Indoor restrooms and a water fountain are in the Visitor Center. The City lists these facilities as open Tuesday-Saturday 9 a.m.-4 p.m. and Sunday 1-4 p.m., even though the Visitor Center's published public hours begin at 10 a.m. Tuesday-Saturday.

facts.label: What hours is Mordecai Historic Park open?
facts.value: The outdoor park grounds are open dawn to dusk daily. The Visitor Center and regular tour operation are open Tuesday-Saturday 10 a.m.-4 p.m. and Sunday 1-4 p.m.; Monday is closed. Tours, restrooms, programs, rentals, and trolley service have narrower schedules than the grounds.

facts.label: Is Mordecai Historic Park free?
facts.value: Walking the grounds, viewing building exteriors, using a self-guided map, and visiting the Visitor Center's permanent and rotating exhibits are free. Guided building tours currently cost $8 for adults and $5 for youth; children age six and under are free. Trolley rides, private tours, programs, and rentals are separate.

facts.label: Is Mordecai Historic Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Accessible spaces are available in the Mimosa Street lot and next to the Visitor Center. Ramps serve the Visitor Center, its restrooms, and the first floor of Mordecai House. Other historic buildings and some program areas have uneven surfaces or steps; guides provide outdoor interpretation and interior photographs when a room cannot be entered.

facts.label: When do Mordecai Historic Park tours leave?
facts.value: One-hour guided tours leave the Visitor Center at the top of the hour, beginning at 10 a.m.; the last tour leaves at 3 p.m. Public tours are not offered while school groups are onsite, so call 919-996-4364 before making a special trip. Groups of ten or more may request a private tour.

facts.label: Can I explore Mordecai Historic Park without taking a tour?
facts.value: Yes. Building exteriors and park grounds are available for self-guided visits whenever the park is open, and the Visitor Center supplies a map during its operating hours. Historic building interiors may only be entered on a guided tour, so a self-guided visit is an outdoor and exterior experience.

facts.label: What historic buildings can I see at Mordecai Historic Park?
facts.value: The campus includes Mordecai House, a smokehouse, plantation office, Allen Kitchen, Andrew Johnson Birthplace, Federal Building, Badger-Iredell Law Office, St. Mark's Chapel, and Bouchall-Danielson House. Several structures were moved to the park, while Mordecai House is Raleigh's oldest house still standing in its original location.

facts.label: Does Mordecai Historic Park discuss slavery and plantation history?
facts.value: Yes. The City identifies the property as the former site of Wake County's largest plantation and describes the Lane and Mordecai families alongside the enslaved and freed African Americans who lived and worked there from 1785 into the 1960s. Guided interpretation, exhibits, artifacts, and digital resources provide the fullest context.

facts.label: Is Andrew Johnson's birthplace at Mordecai Historic Park?
facts.value: Yes. The small Andrew Johnson Birthplace building is one of the historic structures preserved on the campus. It was moved from its original downtown location, so visitors should understand it as a relocated historic building rather than the original surrounding site. Interior access follows guided-tour rules.

facts.label: What garden is at Mordecai Historic Park?
facts.value: The recreated Ellen Mordecai Garden interprets an 1830s kitchen garden using documentation from Ellen Mordecai's memoir and letters. It is part of the outdoor historic landscape and can be viewed on a self-guided grounds visit; planting appearance varies by season and maintenance cycle.

facts.label: Do Historic Raleigh Trolley tours leave from Mordecai Park?
facts.value: Yes. Historic Raleigh Trolley tours begin and end at Mordecai Historic Park, but they are a separate experience with separate tickets and a seasonal schedule. The general season runs on selected Saturdays from March through December; check the current trolley page before traveling because times, themes, capacity, and special tours change.

facts.label: How long should I plan for Mordecai Historic Park?
facts.value: Allow about one hour for the guided tour itself. Add time before departure to park, walk to the Visitor Center, buy tickets, and use the restroom, plus additional time for exhibits, the garden, and exterior exploration. A free grounds-only visit can be shorter and flexible, but it will not include historic interiors.

facts.label: Is the NCMA Museum Park open when the museum is closed?
facts.value: Yes. The outdoor Museum Park is open daily, including holidays, from dawn to dusk. The indoor galleries normally operate Wednesday through Sunday, so park hours and building hours are different.

facts.label: Is the NCMA Museum Park free?

facts.label: Where are restrooms in the NCMA Museum Park?

facts.label: What outdoor art should I see first at NCMA?
facts.value: For a first visit, begin with the iconic earth-cast rings of Gyre, the camera-obscura experience inside Cloud Chamber for the Trees and Sky, and Wind Sculpture II near Lowe's Pavilion. The official park map identifies more than 30 works across the campus.

facts.label: Which NCMA Museum Park trail is best for wheelchairs or strollers?
facts.value: Start at the Welcome Center and use the shorter all-access Eco Trail route to the Ellipse. NCMA describes it as about one-quarter mile on paved, mostly level pathways. The longer option runs about three-quarters of a mile one way to the pond and includes more varied conditions.

facts.label: Can I bring a dog to the NCMA Museum Park?
facts.value: Leashed dogs are permitted in the outdoor Museum Park. Keep pets away from artworks, planted areas, and wildlife, clean up after them, and check current park rules before visiting.

facts.label: Can I take a bus to the North Carolina Museum of Art?
facts.value: Yes. GoRaleigh Route 27L Blue Ridge provides public transportation to NCMA. Check the current schedule and choose the stop closest to your intended park entrance.

facts.label: Are any NCMA Museum Park trails or facilities closed?
facts.value: The outdoor park is normally open daily from dawn to dusk, but trail construction, storm damage, wet conditions, art installation work, concerts, and maintenance can close individual routes, lawns, parking areas, or artworks. The Welcome Center, Park Theater restrooms, food, galleries, and programs have separate schedules. Check the Trail Closures section on NCMA's Museum Park page before a route-specific visit.

facts.label: Which entrance should I use for the NCMA Museum Park?
facts.value: Use Museum Drive from Blue Ridge Road for West and East Buildings, the main galleries, and the north-side parking lots. Use District Drive for the Welcome Center, accessible restrooms, smokestack, Musical Swings, Ellipse, Eco Trail, and south-side parking. Walkers and cyclists can also enter from Reedy Creek Road and the Capital Area Greenway.

facts.label: Which NCMA Museum Park trail is wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Begin at the Welcome Center for the All-Access Eco Trail. Its shorter route follows three signs to the Ellipse and is approximately one-quarter mile on paved, mostly level paths. The longer route is about three-quarters of a mile one way to the pond. Other paved park trails follow the natural terrain and can exceed recommended ADA grades, while unpaved trails are not wheelchair routes. Free accessible parking and drop-off are available near the museum buildings.

Trailhead transitions, slopes, bridge approaches, flooding, construction, and pavement conditions vary. Check the exact segment in the City's Explorer and alerts.

facts.label: How long is the Neuse River Greenway and is it paved?
facts.value: Raleigh's official route is 27.5 miles and paved, running from Falls Lake Dam to the Wake-Johnston County line. City distances assume a start at Falls Lake Dam. Neighboring continuations can make a longer outing but are outside Raleigh's stated mileage.

facts.label: Is the Neuse River Greenway a loop?
facts.value: No. It is a long linear trail. For a short visit, plan an out-and-back and turn around after half your desired total distance. For a one-way trip, arrange a legal shuttle or pickup and confirm both parking areas and closing times; do not assume transit, rideshare, food, water, or repairs will be available at a remote turnaround.

facts.label: Where does the Neuse River Greenway connect?
facts.value: It connects with Abbotts Creek Trail, Buffaloe Road Athletic Park, Anderson Point Park, Milburnie Dam, Crabtree Creek Trail, Walnut Creek Trail, and routes toward Wake Forest, Knightdale, and Johnston County. It is part of the Mountains-to-Sea Trail, but it is not a continuous Raleigh-to-Charlotte greenway.

facts.label: Can I canoe, kayak, or fish from the Neuse River Greenway?
facts.value: Yes, at designated access locations rather than every trail point. Raleigh provides six launches for non-motorized paddlecraft along 17 miles of the Neuse beginning at Falls Lake Dam, and the corridor offers fishing. Check launch and river conditions, use proper flotation equipment, and never assume a trail parking point is a boat launch.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed on the Neuse River Greenway?
facts.value: Yes. Dogs must be controlled on a leash no longer than six feet, stay to the right, and owners must remove waste. A short non-retractable leash is safest around bicycles, wildlife, children, bridges, and narrow boardwalk approaches.

facts.label: Can I bike the Neuse River Greenway?
facts.value: Yes. The paved route is shared with walkers, runners, mobility devices, and other users. Raleigh's greenway speed limit is 10 mph: keep right, yield to pedestrians, announce passes on the left, and slow at curves, bridges, boardwalks, trailheads, children, and dogs.

facts.label: Does the Neuse River Greenway flood or close?
facts.value: Yes. High water, debris, bridge work, maintenance, or construction can affect this river and wetland corridor. Check Greenway Alerts immediately before a longer trip. Never cross a barricade, enter moving water, or detour across private property or a high-speed road.

facts.label: Is there food or water on the Neuse River Greenway?
facts.value: The City lists a food-vendor location near 12098 Old Falls of Neuse Road, but vendor attendance is not guaranteed. Treat most of the 27.5-mile corridor as a bring-your-own-water and snacks trip, and never plan a long ride around an unconfirmed vendor.
