places.name: Ruffner Mountain

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: The preserve, pavilion, and trails are open Tuesday through Sunday from 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. November through February and 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. March through October; closed Mondays. The Nature Center is generally open Thursday through Sunday from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: Nonmembers must purchase a $5 visitor parking permit; member parking is included with a current permit. Programs, memberships, rentals, and events may charge separately.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 1214 81st Street South, Birmingham, AL 35206

facts.label: What hours is Ruffner Mountain open?
facts.value: Trails, preserve, and pavilion are open Tuesday–Sunday 7 a.m.–5 p.m. November–February and 7 a.m.–7 p.m. March–October; closed Mondays. The Nature Center is generally open Thursday–Sunday 9 a.m.–5 p.m., staffing permitting.

facts.label: What address should I use for Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: Use 1214 81st Street South, Birmingham, AL 35206. This routes to the designated preserve parking area and Nature Center; do not follow unofficial neighborhood approaches to trails.

facts.label: How does parking work at Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: Nonmembers must buy a $5 visitor parking permit through ParkMobile or the pavilion vending machine; members display their permit. When the lot is full, the preserve is full, and parking along 81st Street is prohibited.

facts.label: Does Ruffner Mountain charge admission?
facts.value: The required visitor charge is structured as a $5 nonmember parking permit. Member parking is included with a valid permit; programs, events, memberships, and rentals may have separate costs.

facts.label: Are restrooms available at Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: Plan around the Nature Center and pavilion area for developed visitor facilities. Nature Center access is limited to its Thursday–Sunday schedule and staff capacity, so confirm before relying on indoor restrooms.

facts.label: What are the trails like at Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: Ruffner's preserve trails cross wooded, rocky ridge terrain and old quarry landscapes, with roots, uneven natural surfaces, slopes, and variable distances. Download the official preserve map before leaving the Nature Center area.

facts.label: Are Ruffner Mountain trails shaded?
facts.value: Much of the trail system runs through forest and receives substantial tree cover, but quarry openings, overlooks, and disturbed mining areas can be exposed. Carry water and use sun protection in warm weather.

facts.label: Why might Ruffner Mountain stop admitting visitors?
facts.value: The preserve closes Mondays, outside seasonal hours, and whenever its designated lot reaches capacity. Severe weather, trail damage, prescribed work, staffing, or special operations can also close trails or the Nature Center.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed on Ruffner Mountain trails?
facts.value: Yes. Ruffner Mountain welcomes dogs on its trails, but they must remain leashed. Leashes protect pets from wildlife, cliffs, quarry hazards, other dogs, and sensitive habitat, and owners must carry out waste.

facts.label: Can I picnic at Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: The pavilion and Nature Center area provide the most practical developed gathering base, but Ruffner is primarily a protected trail preserve rather than a general picnic park. Facility rentals and organized gatherings require advance arrangements, and all visitors still depend on limited designated parking.

facts.label: What can visitors with limited mobility access at Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: The Nature Center and pavilion are the most developed visitor facilities. Preserve trails are natural-surface routes with roots, rocks, grades, quarry terrain, and weather-related mud, so review the official map and contact staff for a route matched to specific mobility needs.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: Jefferson County Greenways does not list conventional playground equipment at Ruffner Mountain. Family visits center on the Nature Center's Wildlife Ambassadors, seasonal encounters and programs, pollinator gardens, the pavilion, and age-appropriate forest trails. Choose another Birmingham park for swings or slides. At Ruffner, keep children on marked routes and away from closed mine openings, quarry edges, wildlife, and rough terrain; bicycles are not permitted on the trails.

facts.label: Is there swimming or a splash pad at Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: No pool, splash pad, or designated swimming area is listed at Ruffner Mountain. It is a forested nature preserve and former mining landscape centered on hiking, wildlife, overlooks, quarry and mining history, and Nature Center programs. Ponds, quarry water, creeks, drainage areas, and stormwater are habitat or landscape features rather than inspected water play. Stay on marked trails, carry drinking water, and use a separately listed Birmingham aquatic facility for swimming.

facts.label: Can I reach Ruffner Mountain without a car?
facts.value: Yes. MAX On-Demand lists Ruffner Mountain as a destination in its Eastside service area and can connect with Woodlawn Transit Center and other neighborhood points. This is not a traditional fixed-route stop: book through the MAX Connect service, confirm the exact trailhead and pickup time, and do not assume the Nature Center entrance and eastern trailhead are interchangeable. Carry enough water and retain a backup return plan where cellular coverage may be weak.

facts.label: What are the main landmarks at Ruffner Mountain?
facts.value: The Nature Center at 1214 81st Street South is the best staffed starting point, with an exhibit hall of native wildlife ambassadors, pavilion, maps, restrooms, and access to the trail network. The signature hike follows Quarry and Quarry Overlook trails toward historic mining remnants, the limestone quarry, Cambrian Overlook, and broad Birmingham views. Ruffner has about 14 miles of mountainous trails and more than one access point, so download the preserve map and do not follow unmarked routes into old mining terrain.

facts.label: Ruffner Mountain Quarry
facts.value: Ruffner Mountain Quarry is the exposed limestone destination reached from the preserve's Quarry Trail network, where visitors can see rock faces and look for fossil evidence of ancient sea life.

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: LeFleur's Bluff State Park is open daily from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Campground access, Mississippi Museum of Natural Science, playground complex, golf, and special facilities use separate schedules.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: Day-use entrance is $2 per person; children age five and under enter free. Camping, museum admission, pavilion rentals, golf, disc rentals, and other facilities charge separately.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.value: 3315 Lakeland Terrace, Jackson, MS 39216

facts.label: What address should I use for LeFleur's Bluff State Park?
facts.value: Use 3315 Lakeland Terrace, Jackson, MS 39216 for the state park. Mississippi Museum of Natural Science uses 2148 Riverside Drive, so navigate to the exact entrance for camping, Mayes Lake, museum, playground, or golf.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: What hours is LeFleur's Bluff State Park open?
facts.value: General day-use hours are 8 a.m.-5 p.m. daily. The museum, campground, playground complex, golf course, and reserved facilities maintain separate schedules and holiday closures.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: How much does LeFleur's Bluff State Park cost?
facts.value: General entrance is $2 per person, with children age five and under free. The museum, camping, pavilions, golf, disc rental, and special activities charge separately.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Where are the playgrounds at LeFleur's Bluff?
facts.value: The state park has two playground units between the pavilions in the Mayes Lake section. The larger LeFleur's Bluff playground complex near the museums is a separate destination with its own hours and holiday closures.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Can I reserve a pavilion at LeFleur's Bluff?
facts.value: Yes. Five picnic pavilions can be reserved for gatherings. The shaded Riverside day-use area also has picnic tables, some charcoal grills, and views toward a large playground.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: What trails are at LeFleur's Bluff State Park?
facts.value: The park offers nature trails and an 18-hole disc golf course within its wooded urban landscape. Trail conditions change with rain and river or lake weather; use the interactive park map for current routing.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Can I launch a boat on Mayes Lake?
facts.value: Yes. Visitors may launch their own boat, kayak, or paddleboard. Only electric trolling motors are allowed; jet boats are prohibited. Anglers ages 16-65 need a Mississippi fishing license.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Is LeFleur's Bluff golf course open?
facts.value: No. The official park page currently says the golf course is closed for maintenance until further notice. Confirm the status before traveling for golf; the rest of the state park may remain open.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Where should I park at LeFleur's Bluff?
facts.value: Use 3315 Lakeland Terrace for the Mayes Lake state-park side, camping, pavilions, lake, disc golf, and two park playgrounds. The Museum District playground and museums use the separate Museum Boulevard and Riverside Drive campus with parking at both museums.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Where are restrooms at LeFleur's Bluff?
facts.value: Day-use facilities and the Museum District have destination-specific restrooms, while overnight guests use a campground bathhouse with hot showers. Current renovation projects can affect bathhouse or concession facilities, so confirm with the park before relying on one location.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Is the LeFleur's Bluff Playground the same as the state park playgrounds?
facts.value: No. The inclusive LeFleur's Bluff Playground links the Natural Science and Children's museums on the Museum District campus and has its own hours and holiday closures. The Mayes Lake state-park section separately has two playground units between its pavilions.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather shelter at LeFleur's Bluff State Park?
facts.value: The Riverside day-use area has a spacious shaded picnic section, and five reservable pavilions serve the park; wooded nature trails and campground areas also provide tree cover. Mayes Lake, playgrounds, disc golf, golf, boat launch, and open recreation areas can be exposed. The Museum of Natural Science and other complex buildings have separate admission and hours, and pavilions are not severe-weather shelters; during lightning, flooding, high wind, or dangerous heat, use a confirmed-open substantial building or enclosed vehicle.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at LeFleur's Bluff State Park?
facts.value: Yes, but only in designated pet areas and on an adequate leash no longer than six feet. Pick up and dispose of waste, and remove any pet that disturbs other guests. Pets are prohibited in and around swimming-pool and lake-beach areas; museums, playgrounds, golf, events, lodging, and other separately managed facilities may apply additional restrictions.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.label: Can you swim or use a splash pad at LeFleur's Bluff State Park?
facts.value: No operating pool, splash pad, or designated swimming beach is listed for LeFleur's Bluff. Mayes Lake is presented for fishing, boat launching, kayaking, and paddleboarding with electric trolling motors only, not swimming. Use the lake only for the listed activities and choose another currently operating Jackson-area aquatic facility when swimming or water play is the goal.
facts.sourceLabel: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks

facts.value: Mayes Lake is the fishing, non-motorized paddling, and electric-trolling-motor water destination inside LeFleur's Bluff State Park.

facts.label: Is there parking at Parham Bridges Park?

facts.label: How long is the Parham Bridges walking trail?

facts.value: Sunset Canopy is the park's largest dependable covered outdoor area, and trees in Visionary Grove, the hammock area, and newer plantings provide growing patches of shade. Much of the river lawn, overlooks, playground, and paths remains exposed to sun, wind, and Mississippi River weather; canopy spaces may also be occupied by programs or private events. During lightning, dangerous wind, flooding, or extreme heat, use an open substantial building such as Beale Street Landing or return to a vehicle.

facts.label: Can dogs go to Tom Lee Park?
facts.value: Yes. Dogs are welcome in Memphis River Parks, including Tom Lee Park, but must remain on a leash unless inside a specifically designated dog park; Tom Lee Park itself is not an off-leash dog park. Memphis limits ordinary park leashes to under six feet, and owners must collect and dispose of all pet waste. Keep dogs out of the playground, misting fountain, food-service areas, and any event zone that posts a stricter animal policy.

facts.label: Where can I have a picnic at Tom Lee Park?
facts.value: For a simple visit, bring a blanket or use available seating near the river lawns, hammock grove, playground, or Sunset Canopy without blocking programs or event setups. The Sunset Canopy is a multiuse civic space, not a private first-come pavilion. Any gathering over 25 people requires both a Memphis Parks reservation certificate and a City special-event or public-assembly permit; exclusive areas, vendors, amplified sound, tents, furniture, or catered setups should be coordinated with Memphis River Parks before arrival.

facts.label: Is there water play at Tom Lee Park?
facts.value: Tom Lee Park has a misting fountain along its riverfront paths, useful for cooling off, but it is not a swimming pool or full splash pad. The Life on the River playground is dry play, and visitors must not enter the Mississippi River from the park. Fountain availability can change with temperature, maintenance, events, or winterization, so ask a park ranger at the Hanover Welcome Center if the misting feature is important to the visit.

facts.label: How do I reach Tom Lee Park without a car?
facts.value: Use MATA's live trip planner with Tom Lee Park or the Beale Street Landing side as the destination, then walk downhill from downtown to the riverfront. The park is long: target Beale Street Landing for the north end and welcome center, or use an address nearer Vance Avenue for southern lawns and play areas. Confirm the return route before descending, especially at night or during festivals when Riverside Drive and nearby stops may be closed or rerouted.

facts.label: Tom Lee Memorial
facts.value: Tom Lee Memorial marks the Mississippi River rescue story for which the park is named and sits within the long riverfront landscape.

facts.value: Cherokee Park is open daily from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. Restrooms, sprayground, golf, shelters, and organized facilities can use shorter or seasonal schedules.

facts.label: What address should I use for Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Use 745 Cochran Hill Road, Louisville, KY 40206 for a general arrival. Big Rock, Hogan's Fountain, Baringer Hill, dog run, golf, and trailheads are spread across the park, so route to the named feature when possible.

facts.label: Where should I park at Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Use designated roadside and activity-area parking near your destination, such as Big Rock, Hogan's Fountain, Baringer Hill, or Cochran Hill. The one-way Scenic Loop can make missed turns time-consuming; keep left to stay in the park and right to leave.

facts.label: How does Cherokee Park's Scenic Loop work?
facts.value: The Scenic Loop is 2.3 miles with a one-way vehicle lane and a separate lane for walkers, runners, and cyclists. Natural hiking and mountain-bike trails branch into wooded, rolling terrain with roots, rocks, mud, and steeper grades.

facts.label: Where are the playground and sprayground at Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Cherokee Park lists both playground and sprayground amenities, with the Big Rock area serving as a well-known family destination near Beargrass Creek. Sprayground operation is seasonal and can pause for maintenance or water restrictions.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Yes. Louisville lists restrooms among the park amenities, serving major areas rather than every trail. Use the official map to plan around facilities near developed destinations and do not expect restrooms within wooded trail sections.

facts.label: Is there an off-leash dog area at Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Yes. Cherokee Park has a designated dog run near Cochran Hill. Dogs must remain controlled outside the enclosure, and Louisville dog-run access may require current membership or key credentials.

facts.label: Is Cherokee Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, Scenic Loop, trails, playground, sprayground, picnic areas, fields, and open space are free. Golf, shelter reservations, dog-run membership, permits, and organized programs can charge separately.

facts.label: Is Cherokee Park's Scenic Loop fully open?
facts.value: Louisville's newsroom reported a tree blocking part of the Scenic Loop on June 26, 2026. Check the current Metro Parks alert before driving the loop; storms, flooding, fallen trees, maintenance, and events can change access quickly.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Woodlands and mature trees shade much of the Scenic Loop, Beargrass Creek valley, and many picnic areas. Reservable shelters are available at Baringer Hill, Big Rock, and the Stegner Pavilion near Hogan's Fountain; the former Hogan's Fountain teepee pavilion was demolished and should not be expected. During lightning, flooding, or dangerous wind, leave creek bottoms and large trees and use a substantial building or vehicle rather than a picnic shelter.

facts.label: Which picnic shelters can I reserve at Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Louisville lists reservable shelters at Baringer Hill, Big Rock, and the Hogan's Fountain area. A reservation guarantees exclusive use; an unreserved shelter is free first come, first served when no reservation notice is posted. The historic Hogan's Fountain teepee pavilion was demolished, so confirm the exact current shelter name and map pin when booking. Weddings, alcohol, amplified sound, tents, vendors, inflatables, or groups of 250 or more require additional approval or permits.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad at Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Yes. Louisville lists a traditional spraypad at 745 Cochran Hill Road. It is a converted wading-pool style feature with a single spray obelisk rather than a large modern aquatic playground, and the City describes a roughly 20-to-25-week seasonal operating period from dawn to dusk. Water can be shut off for maintenance, weather, or system conditions, so check Louisville Parks aquatics notices before making it the sole reason for a visit.

facts.label: Which TARC bus reaches Cherokee Park?
facts.value: TARC Route 29 stops at Cherokee Parkway and Willow Avenue, a useful western entrance near the Scenic Loop. Cherokee Park is large and hilly, so that stop is not equally close to Cochran Hill, the spraypad, Hogan's Fountain, trails, or athletic areas. Enter the exact feature in TARC's current planner, allow for a walk into the park, and check service changes because Louisville is transitioning to a redesigned network.

facts.label: Where are the major landmarks and public art in Cherokee Park?
facts.value: Look for two works by Louisville sculptor Enid Yandell. The Daniel Boone statue marks the Eastern Parkway entrance, while Hogan's Fountain stands beside the Scenic Loop and its surrounding gathering area. The fountain was created in 1903-1904 as a watering fountain for horses and dogs and was restored in 2023. Use the Eastern Parkway entrance for Boone or navigate toward Hogan's Fountain rather than expecting both landmarks at one central plaza.

facts.label: What hours is Louisville Waterfront Park open?

facts.label: Which address should I use for Waterfront Park?
facts.value: Use 401 River Road for the original Children's Play Area, 1101 River Road for Adventure Playground, Splash Park, and Big Four Bridge, or 1105 Rowan Street for PlayPort. Route to the feature, not the park's central pin.

facts.label: Where should I park at Louisville Waterfront Park?
facts.value: Use the color-coded lot closest to your destination: Orange for the original Children's Play Area, Silver for Adventure Playground, Splash Park, and Big Four Bridge, or Aqua for PlayPort. Event restrictions and paid rates can vary.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Waterfront Park?
facts.value: Yes. Restrooms are distributed through the park and generally operate 9 a.m.–9 p.m. from mid-April through mid-November. PlayPort has a dedicated restroom building; off-season availability is more limited.

facts.label: Which Waterfront Park playground should I choose?
facts.value: The original Children's Play Area is near Orange lot; Adventure Playground is by Silver lot and the Big Four Bridge; PlayPort is a 3.5-acre all-abilities STEM-focused play and learning landscape by Aqua lot. Each is a separate destination.

facts.label: When is Waterfront Park's Splash Park open?
facts.value: The Splash Park beside Adventure Playground is scheduled daily from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. from May through October. Weather, maintenance, water conditions, and events can interrupt operation.

facts.label: Can I walk or bike across the Big Four Bridge?
facts.value: Yes. Paved accessible paths connect the waterfront to the converted Big Four pedestrian and bicycle bridge, which crosses the Ohio River to Jeffersonville, Indiana. Expect a substantial ramp climb and an exposed bridge deck.

facts.label: Is Waterfront Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Yes. Park paths were designed to ADA standards, with ramp alternatives where stairs occur. PlayPort includes all-abilities play and a nearby restroom building; confirm event-specific routes when lawns or paths are fenced.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Waterfront Park?
facts.value: Leashed pets are welcome in general park areas but are prohibited on the Big Four Bridge, playgrounds, fountains, and Splash Park. There is no general off-leash area within Waterfront Park.

facts.label: What can be closed or unavailable at Louisville Waterfront Park?
facts.value: The park is generally open daily from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m., but restrooms normally keep seasonal hours from mid-April through mid-November. Concerts, festivals, races, Thunder Over Louisville, flood conditions, riverfront construction, and event setup can close lawns, paths, River Road, parking areas, or bridge approaches. Check the Waterfront Park calendar and Louisville street-closure notices before a time-sensitive visit.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather cover at Louisville Waterfront Park?
facts.value: Festival Plaza has a shady tree grove and is partly covered by the expressway, and the Under the Bridges area has picnic tables with overhead rain and sun cover. Additional trees shade portions of the paths and playground picnic areas, while the Great Lawn, wharf, bridge approaches, splash areas, and river edge are exposed. Expressway cover is not a severe-weather shelter; leave the river and use an open substantial building or vehicle during lightning, flooding, or high wind.

facts.label: Where can I have a picnic at Louisville Waterfront Park?
facts.value: Five picnic areas offer tables and river views, including areas beside the original Children's Play Area and Adventure Playground. Casual groups may bring food, but alcohol, glass, personal grills, fires, anchored tents, and inflatables are prohibited; use only the park grills beside the playground picnic areas. Gatherings over 50 people must use the event-planning process.

facts.label: Can I reach Louisville Waterfront Park by bus?
facts.value: Yes, but choose the stop for the exact section of this long riverfront park. Downtown TARC routes place visitors within walking distance of the Great Lawn and western park, while cross-river and east-downtown service can be more practical for the Big Four Bridge area. TARC launches a redesigned network on August 2, 2026, so use its live trip planner with 401 River Road, 1101 River Road, or 1105 Rowan Street rather than relying on an older route number; events and riverfront road closures can move stops.

facts.label: What are the must-see landmarks in Louisville Waterfront Park?
facts.value: The Big Four pedestrian and bicycle bridge is the signature landmark, reached from its looping ramp beside Big Four Lawn, the Swing Garden, Lincoln Memorial, and Vietnam Memorial. Farther west, major anchors include the TurfMutt Great Lawn, Wharf and Festival Plaza, Belle of Louisville docks, Tetra sculpture, Overlook, playgrounds and splash park, Brown-Forman Amphitheater, and PlayPort. The park stretches for many blocks, so use its numbered visitor map and route to the feature closest to your plans.

facts.label: What address should I use for Iroquois Park?

facts.label: Where should I park at Iroquois Park?
facts.value: General parking is distributed near recreation and trail areas. For amphitheater events, premier parking is sold closest to the venue, while free event parking is available on Rundill Road south of Frisbee Way and at DeSales High School when designated.

facts.label: What are the walking trails like at Iroquois Park?
facts.value: The park has a roughly five-kilometer paved walking loop plus natural hiking and horse trails through steep forested hills. Natural routes can be rocky, rooted, muddy, and much more strenuous than the paved loop.

facts.label: Is the Iroquois Park playground wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Louisville specifically lists a wheelchair-accessible playground, along with a seasonal sprayground. Use the official park map to distinguish the family recreation area from the amphitheater and hill trails.

facts.label: Is there a sprayground at Iroquois Park?

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Iroquois Park?
facts.value: Yes. Restrooms serve developed park areas, and the amphitheater has family restrooms with changing stations in its concession tunnel during venue operations. Do not assume trail or overlook restrooms are open at all hours.

facts.label: Is Iroquois Park free?
facts.value: General entry, trails, playground, sprayground, picnic areas, courts, and overlook access are free. Ticketed amphitheater events, golf, premium event parking, permits, and rentals charge separately.

facts.label: Can I drive to the Iroquois Park North Overlook every day?
facts.value: No. Vehicle access through the Uppill Road gate is limited to published open-gate dates, while overlook improvements and road projects may add restrictions. Pedestrian access and conditions should be confirmed on the current project page.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Iroquois Park?
facts.value: The forested hills and many trail sections provide extensive natural shade, and Louisville lists picnic shelters in developed areas. The North Overlook, athletic fields, golf areas, and portions of the paved loop are exposed; the amphitheater opens for scheduled operations rather than as a general refuge. Trees and open shelters are not safe in lightning or dangerous wind, so use an open substantial building or vehicle during severe weather.

facts.label: Where can dogs go at Iroquois Park, and what rules apply?
facts.value: Dogs may accompany visitors on Iroquois Park's ordinary paths and permitted trails, but Louisville requires pets to remain on leash and owners to pick up waste. Iroquois does not list a designated dog run, so it should not be treated as an off-leash park. Use extra care on narrow natural trails shared with faster mountain-bike traffic and obey any event, golf-course, playground, or facility restrictions.

facts.label: Which picnic shelter can I reserve at Iroquois Park?
facts.value: Louisville lists the Sunnyhill shelter as Iroquois Park's reservable picnic shelter. A reservation guarantees exclusive use; if no reservation notice is posted, an otherwise available shelter may be used first come, first served at no charge. Shelters are offered daily from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. year-round. Weddings, alcohol, amplified sound, tents, vendors, inflatables, or large organized events can require additional permits, so contact Metro Parks rather than treating a shelter booking as approval for every activity.

facts.label: Which bus goes to Iroquois Park?
facts.value: TARC Routes 4 and 6 serve Iroquois Park from downtown Louisville, and both list the amphitheater as a park-and-ride location. Route 4 approaches through the University of Louisville and New Cut Road corridor, while Route 6 serves the Sixth Street and Auburndale corridor. Use the live planner for the amphitheater, overlook, golf course, playground, or Sunnyhill shelter because the park's hills and loop roads make some destinations a long walk from another stop.

facts.label: What landmarks should I see in Iroquois Park?
facts.value: The panoramic North Overlook and the restored 1938 WPA-era Iroquois Amphitheater are the park's two signature destinations. A stair-and-trail route from the lot near Uppill and Rundill Roads connects toward Corbly Trail and the overlook, while the amphitheater uses 1080 Amphitheater Road and its own event access. The old-growth forest, scenic loop, other overlooks, golf and disc-golf areas, playground, sprayground, and shelters fill separate districts across the hilly park, so choose the exact destination before arriving.

facts.label: Where should I park for Riverfront Park?

facts.label: Where are the playgrounds in Riverfront Park?

facts.label: When are Riverfront Park splash pads open?

facts.label: Can I walk or bike along the river at Riverfront Park?
facts.value: Yes. Paved paths and plazas run through the long downtown park and connect to Junction Bridge, downtown destinations, and the broader Arkansas River Trail system. Expect street crossings and event detours in some sections.

facts.label: Where is the sculpture garden in Riverfront Park?
facts.value: Vogel Schwartz Sculpture Garden is a free riverfront landscape of public art within the park. Riverfront Park also preserves La Petite Roche and Quapaw Line interpretation connected to Little Rock's name and settlement history.

facts.label: Is Little Rock Riverfront Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, playgrounds, seasonal splash pads, sculpture garden, paths, plazas, and history features are free. Parking, pavilion rental, ticketed events, food, museums, and nearby attractions may charge.

facts.label: Is the toddler splash pad at Riverfront Park open?
facts.value: The City reported a temporary mechanical closure at the start of the 2026 season and expected reopening after repair. Check the live splash-pad page because the toddler and Peabody systems can have different operating status.

facts.label: Can I reserve a pavilion in Little Rock Riverfront Park?
facts.value: Yes. The Belvedere, History, and Ozark pavilions, Vogel Schwartz Sculpture Garden, and Forever-a-Rose Garden are reservable. Standard Riverfront reservation hours are 10:00 a.m.-9:00 p.m.; prices and capacity depend on the exact space.

facts.label: Where can families find restrooms at Riverfront Park?
facts.value: Restroom availability is concentrated near developed River Market, playground, pavilion, and event areas rather than continuously across all 11 blocks. Locate the nearest open facility before beginning a long river walk, especially outside event hours.

facts.label: Is Little Rock Riverfront Park accessible?
facts.value: The principal riverfront promenades, plazas, pavilion areas, and approaches to major playground and public-art destinations use paved surfaces. Grade, distance, bridge approaches, crowds, and temporary event barriers can affect the easiest route.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather shelter at Riverfront Park?
facts.value: Trees and landscaped sitting areas provide pockets of shade, while the History Pavilion and amphitheater offer limited open-air cover. The river edge, bridges, playground areas, plazas, fountains, sculpture zones, and lawns remain exposed, and the park does not have a dependable general-purpose indoor visitor building. During lightning, flooding, high wind, or dangerous heat, leave the Arkansas River corridor and use a confirmed-open substantial building or enclosed vehicle rather than an open pavilion.

facts.label: Can I bring a dog to Little Rock Riverfront Park?
facts.value: Yes, if the dog remains effectively controlled by a leash or another supervised restraint from which it cannot escape. Riverfront Park is not a designated fenced dog run, so keep pets restrained on the Arkansas River Trail, lawns, plazas, bridges, and sculpture areas; remove waste and stay out of playgrounds, splash features, food areas, and events where pets are restricted.

facts.label: What are the trails like at Two Rivers Park?

facts.label: Is there a playground at Two Rivers Park?

facts.label: Is Two Rivers Park suitable for wheelchairs or strollers?

facts.label: Is Two Rivers Park free?

facts.label: What can close Two Rivers Park trails?
facts.value: River flooding, saturated natural trails, storm damage, bridge or pavement repairs, and construction can close individual routes while the main park remains open. Check Little Rock Parks notices after high water or severe weather.

facts.label: Can I reserve the pavilion at Two Rivers Park?
facts.value: Two Rivers Park includes a pavilion, picnic tables, restrooms, and parking. Little Rock pavilion reservations generally require advance notice, so contact Parks and Recreation to confirm whether the pavilion is reservable, current fees, and any event requirements.

facts.label: How large is the Two Rivers Park trail system?
facts.value: The regional recreation plan inventories roughly 1.7 miles of multi-use paved trail, 3.7 miles of narrower paved walking routes, 0.6 mile of mountain biking, and 2.6 miles of hiking within Two Rivers Park. Conditions and open segments change with flooding and repairs.

facts.label: How does Two Rivers Park connect to the Arkansas River Trail?
facts.value: The 1,162-foot pedestrian bridge connects the park to River Mountain and the broader Arkansas River Trail toward Big Dam Bridge. This makes the park a practical walking and cycling destination, but bridge or riverfront work can interrupt through travel.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather shelter at Two Rivers Park?
facts.value: A pavilion and scattered tree cover serve the picnic area near the confluence, but the pedestrian bridge, open fields, river edges, community garden, and long paved trails are exposed. The park does not have a dependable staffed indoor visitor building, and its low river setting can close during or after flooding. A picnic pavilion is not safe for lightning or high wind; leave the river corridor and use an open substantial building or vehicle.

facts.label: Can I bring a dog to Two Rivers Park?
facts.value: Yes. Two Rivers is used as a dog-friendly walking destination, but it is not a fenced dog park: keep pets leashed and under control on the paved trail, bridge, natural paths, fields, and river edges, and remove all waste. Wildlife and shared bicycle traffic make an attached leash especially important even in the broad open fields.

facts.label: Can children swim or use a splash pad at Two Rivers Park?
facts.value: No splash pad, pool, or designated swimming beach is listed at Two Rivers Park. The Arkansas and Little Maumelle river edges are natural waterways with currents, changing levels, steep or muddy banks, debris, and no lifeguards. Keep children back from the shoreline, follow flood closures, and use a separately operated Little Rock aquatic facility for water play.

facts.label: What are the main landmarks at Two Rivers Park?
facts.value: Two Rivers Bridge is the primary eastern gateway, carrying the Arkansas River Trail over the Little Maumelle River into the park. From there, paved and natural trails cross wetlands and open fields toward the confluence of the Arkansas and Little Maumelle rivers. Other practical anchors include the community garden, inclusive playground, pavilion, restrooms, picnic area, equestrian trail, and boat access. The park is low-lying and can flood, so never cross water covering a trail or ignore a closure.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather shelter at Trinity Park?

The Trinity River, ponds, floodplain, and drainage areas should not be treated as designated swimming locations. Use a separately listed Fort Worth pool or sprayground and confirm its current seasonal hours before making a water-play trip.

facts.label: What are the main destinations in Gateway Park?
facts.value: Gateway Park is a large natural and recreation landscape rather than a completed public-art destination. Its clearest anchors are Fort Woof, the City's five-acre off-leash dog park; the mountain-bike trail network and trailheads; disc golf; athletic fields; playground; shelters; bridges; and an observation deck near the Trinity River corridor. A City public-art project and major master-plan improvements are still in design or development, so do not treat proposed artwork, splash pad, skate park, or destination playground as open until Fort Worth announces completion.

facts.value: The Water Gardens are open daily from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. Water features, lighting, rentals, and individual areas can be interrupted by maintenance, freezing weather, events, or safety operations.

facts.label: Where is the main entrance to the Water Gardens?
facts.value: Use 1502 Commerce Street, Fort Worth, TX 76102. The main entrance is at the northwest corner, where cascading water leads toward the central pools and square.

facts.label: Where should I park for the Fort Worth Water Gardens?
facts.value: The park does not advertise a dedicated free visitor lot. Use a signed downtown garage, paid lot, or legal metered space near Commerce Street, or arrive via Fort Worth Central or T&P transit stations and walk.

facts.label: Can I reach the Water Gardens by transit?
facts.value: Yes. The downtown location is walkable from Fort Worth Central Station and T&P Station, making TEXRail, Trinity Railway Express, and local transit useful alternatives to paid downtown parking.

facts.label: Is the Fort Worth Water Gardens accessible?
facts.value: Level plaza areas provide views of several features, and the City offers accessibility accommodations on request. The Active Pool's descent uses steep table-topped stairs and is not an appropriate route for every visitor; enjoy it from upper viewpoints when needed.

facts.label: Can children play in the water at Fort Worth Water Gardens?
facts.value: No. Swimming and wading are strictly prohibited in every pool and water feature. The Water Gardens is an architectural viewing and quiet-meditation space, not a splash pad or interactive water-play park.

facts.label: Are the Fort Worth Water Gardens free?
facts.value: Yes. General admission is free. Downtown parking, private events, professional permits, and nearby attractions can have separate charges.

facts.label: Why might a Water Gardens feature be off?
facts.value: Freezing temperatures, mechanical service, water conservation, cleaning, private rentals, weather, and safety work can shut down one or more pools while the surrounding park remains accessible. Obey all barriers and posted notices.

facts.label: Are public restrooms available at the Fort Worth Water Gardens?
facts.value: Do not assume restrooms are open for an ordinary walk-in visit. The City lists restroom access as an added amenity for approved reservations, so use a nearby public facility before entering if restroom access is essential.

facts.label: What should I see at the Fort Worth Water Gardens?
facts.value: The main features are the 38-foot-deep Active Pool, misting Aerated Pool, reflective Quiet Pool, Wet Wall, entry cascades, Central Square, Mountain, stage, and lawn. View every water feature from designated paths and never enter the water.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at the Fort Worth Water Gardens?
facts.value: Trees around Central Square and the Quiet Pool provide intermittent shade, but most of the 5.4-acre site is exposed concrete, steps, plazas, and water-feature edges. The City lists no general visitor center or always-open pavilion, and reservable restrooms are event amenities rather than public shelter. In extreme heat or severe weather, leave the garden and use a nearby open downtown building or vehicle; never enter a water feature to cool off.

facts.label: Which parts of the Fort Worth Water Gardens require stairs?
facts.value: The garden is primarily concrete plaza, ramps, terraces, and many steps. Central Square and perimeter viewpoints provide the most manageable developed surfaces, while the Active Pool descends 38 feet on table-topped stairs and the Mountain rises about 20 feet through tiered concrete; neither should be treated as the accessible route. Wet spray, algae, heat, crowds, and worn edges can make surfaces slippery, so remain on designated dry walkways and never enter or wade in any pool.

facts.label: Is there a playground or splash area at the Fort Worth Water Gardens?
facts.value: The City does not list a playground at the Water Gardens, and its fountains are architectural water features rather than a splash pad. Swimming and wading are prohibited in every pool. Families may view the cascades, Aerated Pool, Quiet Pool, central plaza, lawn, and nighttime lighting, but children need continuous close supervision around deep water, spray, ledges, and the Active Pool's steep 38-foot stair descent. Choose another Fort Worth park for equipment or water play and remain on designated dry walkways here.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at the Fort Worth Water Gardens?
facts.value: Fort Worth requires a dog away from its owner's property to remain accompanied and on a leash. The Water Gardens is not a dog park, and its deep pools, spray, narrow ledges, and steep Active Pool stairs make close control essential. Keep pets on designated dry walkways, never allow them into any fountain or pool, remove waste, and follow event or lawn restrictions.
facts.sourceLabel: City of Fort Worth Animal Care and Control

facts.label: Can I have a picnic at the Fort Worth Water Gardens?
facts.value: A short carried meal is possible on an available dry seat or at the Stage and Lawn, the complex's only grassy area, but this 5.4-acre architectural site is not a conventional picnic park and the City lists no public picnic tables, shelters, or grills. Keep all food and belongings well away from pool edges, supervise children continuously, and never enter the water. Reserve the Amphitheatre/Lawn or another named zone for an organized gathering; private events require at least two weeks' notice and departmental approval.

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Scissortail Park is open daily from 6:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. The children's playground is open from dawn to dusk; sprayground, boating, restaurants, sports, events, and offices use separate schedules.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General park admission, playground, sprayground, dog park, gardens, lawns, paths, and most open recreation are free. Metered or garage parking, boat rentals, food, private events, reserved sports facilities, and occasional ticketed programming charge separately.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 300 SW 7th Street, Oklahoma City, OK 73109

facts.label: What address should I use for Scissortail Park?
facts.value: Use 300 SW 7th Street, Oklahoma City, OK 73109 for the general Upper Park. Route to 650 S. Hudson Avenue for the Boathouse, 655 S. Robinson Avenue for the playground, or 403 SW 10th Street for Lower Park's Sports Pavilion.

facts.label: Where should I park for Scissortail Park?
facts.value: Metered two-hour street spaces line S. Hudson, Oklahoma City Boulevard, and S. Robinson. Nearby Convention Center, Sheridan Walker, Arts District, and Century Center garages are listed at $2 per hour or $10 per day; event pricing can vary.

facts.label: Does the OKC Streetcar stop at Scissortail Park?
facts.value: Yes. The Scissortail Park stop is at Oklahoma City Boulevard and S. Robinson Avenue on the northeast corner. EMBARK buses and downtown circulation also connect the park, making transit useful during events when nearby parking fills.

facts.label: Are there public bathrooms at Scissortail Park?
facts.value: Yes. Public restrooms are available near major destinations, including the playground and Scissortail Boathouse. The Boathouse also has a shaded patio and cafe; Lower Park facilities may follow sports or event operations.

facts.label: What are the playground hours at Scissortail Park?
facts.value: The children's playground is open from dawn to dusk. It includes climbing walls, geometric dome climbers, children's gardens, a large fort with tower and slides, shade, nearby public restrooms, and adjacent interactive fountains.

facts.label: Is the Scissortail Sprayground open?
facts.value: The sprayground opened for the 2026 season on May 22 and is listed for daily operation from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. Jets can shut down for wind, lightning within eight miles, weather, water-quality work, or maintenance; water shoes are recommended.

facts.label: Where is the dog park at Scissortail Park?
facts.value: The park has a half-acre fenced dog park with separate areas for large and small dogs, drinking fountains, and boulders. Dogs must remain leashed everywhere outside the enclosure and are not permitted in the sprayground water.

facts.label: Is Scissortail Park accessible?
facts.value: The park provides accessible perimeter parking, restrooms, ground-level paths, ramps to the stage and boathouse, accessible playground and workout equipment, Braille entry and restroom signs, an accessible pedal boat, and Silver Flyer mobility tours.

facts.label: Is Scissortail Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, playground, sprayground, dog park, paths, gardens, lawns, and open recreation are free. Parking, boat rentals, food, reserved courts or fields, private events, and occasional ticketed programs charge separately.

facts.label: What Scissortail Park features are weather dependent?
facts.value: Sprayground jets stop for high wind or lightning, boating is seasonal and weather dependent, the playground closes after dusk, and large events can change lawn, road, parking, or bag access. Follow current park notices before a feature-specific visit.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather shelter at Scissortail Park?
facts.value: Useful shade is available at the playground and Play Pavilion, Boathouse patio, Picnic Grove trellises, Event Pavilion, Sports Pavilion patio, and wooded lakeside areas. The great lawns, lake bridge, sprayground, sports fields, courts, promenade, and much of the Lower Park remain exposed. These covered outdoor structures are not severe-weather shelters; when lightning, high wind, or dangerous heat develops, follow Park Ambassador directions and use a confirmed-open substantial building or enclosed vehicle.

facts.label: What are the walking surfaces and accessible routes at Scissortail Park?
facts.value: Multiple paved walking and jogging paths connect the Upper and Lower Park, lake, gardens, playground, sprayground, lawns, sports areas, and Skydance Bridge. The park and visitor bureau describe ADA-accessible pathways and facilities, but lawns, native prairie plantings, play surfacing, bridge approaches, and event layouts differ from the primary hard-surface loops. Use the paved paths for a stroller or mobility device, and watch for fountain overspray, Oklahoma heat, ice, construction, and festival barriers.

facts.label: Where can I picnic at Scissortail Park?
facts.value: Use an available table, lawn area, or the covered picnic area at the 6,400-square-foot Event Pavilion in the southeast Upper Park. Food is also sold at SPARK, the Perch, and scheduled food trucks. Personal grills are not allowed anywhere in Scissortail Park. The pavilion and major lawns may be programmed, private, or ticketed for events, so check the calendar and contact the events team before planning a group gathering that needs guaranteed space.

facts.label: What are the main landmarks at Scissortail Park?
facts.value: In the Upper Park, the main anchors are Scissortail Lake and Boathouse, the 240-foot Lake Bridge, Love's Travel Stops Stage and Great Lawn, playground and fountains, gardens, and Promenade. The Lake Bridge frames views of the Oklahoma City skyline, Skydance Bridge, and historic Union Station. Lower Park contains a separate sports and recreation district, so use the official map and route to the named feature rather than the general park address.

facts.label: Skydance Bridge
facts.value: Skydance Bridge is a 380-foot pedestrian bridge and illuminated landmark inspired by Oklahoma's state bird; it links Scissortail Park's Upper and Lower parks across Interstate 40.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: The 15-acre outdoor grounds, gardens, Children's Garden, playground, water features, dog park, paths, and public art are free. Crystal Bridge admission is ticketed; carousel, ice rink, classes, food, parking, events, and rentals can charge separately.

facts.label: What address should I use for Myriad Botanical Gardens?
facts.value: Use 301 W. Reno Avenue, Oklahoma City, OK 73102 for the main gardens and Crystal Bridge Conservatory. The grounds fill a downtown block, so approach from the side closest to the Children's Garden, dog park, carousel, or event destination.

facts.label: Where should I park for Myriad Botanical Gardens?
facts.value: Use legal metered street parking around the gardens or a nearby downtown garage. Myriad's parking guidance notes that vehicles with a valid disability placard or plate may use downtown meters free for the posted time limit; event demand can fill nearby spaces.

facts.label: Are there public restrooms at Myriad Botanical Gardens?
facts.value: Yes. Visitor restrooms are available in developed garden facilities around the Crystal Bridge and public-use areas. Conservatory access, events, and late-evening grounds hours can affect which indoor facilities are open, so use restrooms before facilities close.

facts.label: Is there a children's playground at Myriad Gardens?
facts.value: Yes. The Children's Garden includes a playground with adaptive equipment, nature and story areas, and nearby seasonal water play. Pets are not permitted inside the Children's Garden, though service animals are allowed.

facts.label: Is the Thunder Fountain open at Myriad Gardens?
facts.value: The outdoor water features, including the family-favorite Thunder Fountain area, are listed daily through Labor Day from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Weather, water quality, maintenance, and seasonal changes can interrupt operation.

facts.label: Where is the dog park at Myriad Botanical Gardens?
facts.value: The fenced off-leash dog park is east of the Crystal Bridge Conservatory. Leashed pets are welcome on most exterior grounds but not inside the conservatory, Children's Garden, or water features; only service animals may enter the conservatory.

facts.label: Is Myriad Botanical Gardens wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The renovated Crystal Bridge includes an elevator, and a complimentary wheelchair is available first come with a driver's license held by guest services. Outdoor paths and adaptive playground features support accessible visits, though event layouts can alter routes.

facts.label: What art can I see at Myriad Botanical Gardens?
facts.value: Outdoor works include Hans Van de Bovenkamp's red Gateway sculpture, Kendall Howerton's limestone Goldfish, Don Narcomey's Storyteller's Chair, and Nancy Schön's Friendship prairie-dog sculpture. These pieces are on the free exterior grounds.

facts.label: Is Myriad Botanical Gardens free?
facts.value: The outdoor grounds, ornamental gardens, Children's Garden, playground, water features, dog park, paths, and public art are free. Crystal Bridge Conservatory requires admission; carousel, ice rink, classes, food, parking, and some events have separate costs.

facts.label: What has separate hours at Myriad Gardens?
facts.value: The outdoor grounds stay open 6 a.m.-11 p.m., but Crystal Bridge, water features, carousel, ice rink, shops, classes, and events use separate or seasonal schedules. Crystal Bridge closes on Thanksgiving and Christmas, and water features are seasonal through Labor Day.

facts.label: Where can I cool off or find shade at Myriad Botanical Gardens?
facts.value: Tanenbaum Reflection Garden is the most clearly designated shady outdoor respite, and the Children's Garden has a covered pavilion. Crystal Bridge Conservatory is climate controlled but ticketed and only available during its posted hours. Devon Lawn, Seasonal Plaza, and other event spaces can be exposed; in severe weather use an open substantial building rather than relying on a garden pavilion.

facts.label: What are the walking surfaces and slopes at Myriad Botanical Gardens?
facts.value: The 15-acre outdoor garden combines paved accessible perimeter routes with winding stone paths, meandering children's-garden walks, terraces, lawns, bridges, and stairways around the lake. Accessible paths reach the water's edge without using the stair fountain, while Meinders Terrace and planted slopes can involve grades and less direct routes. Seasonal ice-rink construction, fountains, wet stone, events, and dense plantings can narrow circulation; use the official map and select the accessible perimeter route when avoiding stairs.

facts.label: Where can I picnic at Myriad Botanical Gardens?
facts.value: Sheridan Lawn is the most practical casual picnic area, and visitors may bring a blanket, chairs, and prepared food for open-lawn programs; glass is prohibited. Keep all food and drinks out of Thunder Fountain and the seasonal splash plaza, and do not take food into the Crystal Bridge Conservatory. Tables can be limited or added only for events, so bring a blanket. Reserve a Gardens venue or the Children's Garden Pavilion for a birthday, guaranteed seating, or organized group setup.

facts.label: How do I reach Myriad Botanical Gardens without a car?
facts.value: The Gardens sit in the walkable downtown transit area between Reno Avenue, Hudson Avenue, Sheridan Avenue, and Robinson Avenue. Use EMBARK's live planner for the nearest bus or OKC Streetcar stop to your starting point, then walk to the garden entrance that best matches the Crystal Bridge, Children's Garden, or event lawn. Downtown construction and event closures can shift stops, so verify the final block before leaving.

facts.label: Cost and fees

facts.label: Where should I start at Lake Hefner?
facts.value: Choose a destination before routing: Stars and Stripes Park for south-side recreation and views, Lions Children's Park for the playground, East Wharf for restaurants, the north lot off Hefner Road for north trail access, or a named marina, fishing dock, or golf facility.

facts.label: Where can I park for the Lake Hefner trail?
facts.value: Official trail parking is available at Stars and Stripes Park, Lions Children's Park, East Wharf off Britton Road, and the north lot off Hefner Road. Use only lake roads and designated lots; do not park on grass, trail shoulders, or service roads.

facts.label: How long is the trail around Lake Hefner?
facts.value: The Bert Cooper Trail loop is about 9.8 miles of asphalt and concrete for walking, running, and cycling. A portion crosses the dam road shared with vehicles, and the route connects toward the Hefner-Overholser Trail.

facts.label: Are there restrooms around Lake Hefner?
facts.value: Yes. The lake has restrooms, and portable toilets and water fountains are distributed around the trail near developed recreation areas. They are not present at every mile or informal viewpoint, so plan around a named park or trailhead.

facts.label: Where are playgrounds at Lake Hefner?
facts.value: Lions Children's Park and Stars and Stripes Park are the primary family destinations along the lake, and the City lists multiple playgrounds among Lake Hefner amenities. Route to the named park rather than the lake center.

facts.label: Can I picnic at Lake Hefner?
facts.value: Yes. Picnic areas, grills, and group shelters are available around the lake. Open picnic areas are generally first come, while group shelters and organized events may require reservations or permits.

facts.label: Is Lake Hefner Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, designated parking, the paved loop, playgrounds, picnic areas, and shoreline viewing are free. Fishing, boating, storage, golf, shelter reservations, organized sports, and food require permits or separate payment.

facts.label: What accessible facilities are at Lake Hefner?
facts.value: The paved multi-use loop and developed parks provide step-free recreation options, with parking and restrooms at major areas. Conditions vary around the full 9.8-mile route, especially where it shares the dam road, so select a shorter named segment when needed.

facts.label: What can close the Lake Hefner trail or lake areas?
facts.value: Trail resurfacing, severe weather, high wind, ice, maintenance, water operations, races, and permitted events can affect individual segments or lots. The City directs trail-closure questions to OKC Parks, and all posted gates or barriers should be followed.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Lake Hefner Park?
facts.value: The Bob Hope Pavilion at Stars and Stripes Park is the main covered gathering space, with seating for more than 100, lights, picnic tables, nearby restrooms, and lake views. Smaller trees provide intermittent shade elsewhere, but the shoreline, trails, docks, fields, and open water are highly exposed to Oklahoma sun and wind. Leave the lake during lightning or dangerous wind and use a substantial building or vehicle rather than the pavilion or a tree.

facts.label: Where can dogs go at Lake Hefner Park, and what rules apply?
facts.value: Pets are welcome in Lake Hefner's public lake areas, including paths and picnic areas, but they must remain on a leash at all times. Dogs may not swim or wade in the reservoir, and Lake Hefner does not function as an off-leash dog park. Keep pets away from the waterline where necessary and remove their waste.

facts.label: Can I take EMBARK to Lake Hefner?
facts.value: EMBARK's NW Rapid connects downtown Oklahoma City with the Lake Hefner area along Northwest Expressway, but it does not circle the reservoir or deliver visitors to every trailhead, marina, golf course, restaurant, or Stars and Stripes Park. Enter the exact destination in the live planner and inspect the final walking route before leaving; several lake edges are separated from transit by wide roads and long distances.

facts.label: Can visitors swim or use a splash pad at Lake Hefner?
facts.value: No. Oklahoma City prohibits swimming in Lake Hefner, and the lake district does not list a splash pad. The reservoir supports permitted boating and fishing, but people and pets may not swim or wade. For family water play, choose a separately listed Oklahoma City aquatic center or sprayground rather than entering the reservoir from a trail, picnic area, dock, or boat ramp.

facts.label: What are the main landmarks around Lake Hefner?
facts.value: Lake Hefner has no single central arrival point. Stars and Stripes Park on the south side is a strong family landmark with the Bob Hope Pavilion, Eisenhower Plaza, a patriotic flag-and-five-star design, and a modern rocket slide. facts.value: The main park entrance is on W. 13th Street near the Wichita-Valley Center Floodway. Use the official map to route to Sunrise Boundless Playscape, Tom Scott Lake, a numbered shelter, sports complex, Environmental Art Park, or a specific fishing dock.

facts.label: Where should I park at Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: Parking areas are distributed around the lakes, playgrounds, shelters, sports complex, courts, and open recreation areas. Drive only on designated roads and choose the lot nearest your activity because the park is too large for one central parking point.

facts.label: How long are the paths at Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: The official map lists about 4.33 miles of bike paths, including a 3.46-mile perimeter loop and shorter 1.86- and 1.93-mile north and south loops. The paths can be used outside regular park hours under County rules.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: Yes. Multiple restrooms are marked around the park near developed recreation, playground, shelter, and lake areas. They are not at every dock or path segment, so use the official map before a long loop.

facts.label: What playgrounds are at Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: The park has multiple playgrounds, including Sunrise Boundless Playscape, plus play areas near shelter and lake destinations. Use the map to select the play area closest to restrooms and your planned parking.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: Leashed pets are allowed, with a maximum leash length of eight feet. Owners must remove waste. The park rules do not identify an off-leash enclosure, so dogs should remain leashed throughout the park.

facts.label: Can I reserve a shelter at Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: Yes. The park offers four enclosed shelters and one open shelter for online reservation, plus three small open shelters available first come. Events of 500 or more require contact with the park office at least 180 days ahead.

facts.label: Is Sedgwick County Park free?
facts.value: General entry, parking, paved paths, playgrounds, lakeside recreation, shore fishing access, courts, and open areas are free. Shelter reservations, large events, organized sports, and permits can have separate charges.

facts.label: What activities are not allowed at Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: Swimming, wading, boating, camping, hunting, off-road driving, and glass containers are prohibited. Special events or superintendent orders can alter normal hours or access, and fishing must remain from shore or provided docks under Kansas rules.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather shelter at Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: Cottonwood, Horseshoe, Plum, and Sunflower are enclosed reservable shelters, while several additional shelters are open-sided; confirm the exact facility on the shelter map before arriving. Trees provide intermittent shade, but lakes, fishing docks, fields, courts, playgrounds, and long paths are exposed. Enclosed rental buildings are not guaranteed public storm shelters, so follow county weather guidance and use an open substantial building or vehicle during severe weather.

facts.label: Can visitors swim at Sedgwick County Park in Wichita?
facts.value: No designated swimming area, pool, or splash pad is listed at Sedgwick County Park. Its four small lakes are associated with fishing, docks, scenery, and model boats, not public swimming. Do not confuse this Wichita park with Lake Afton Park, a separate Sedgwick County facility southwest of the city that has three designated swimming areas and requires compliance with its own permits and rules. At Sedgwick County Park, keep people out of the lakes and use the Boundless Playscape and other land amenities.

facts.label: Can I take Wichita Transit to Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: Wichita Transit Route 17 Park is the relevant fixed route for the park area. Use the live InfoPoint planner with your exact destination and confirm the nearest stop and return trip: the Boundless Playscape, lakes, shelters, dog park, sports areas, and zoo-side destinations are distributed across a large campus, so a perimeter stop may still require a long walk.

facts.label: What are the main landmarks in Sedgwick County Park?
facts.value: Sunrise Boundless Playscape is the primary family landmark, a 1.5-acre inclusive play area with equipment for toddlers through elementary-age children and multiple adaptive features. The 400-acre park also contains four small lakes, a sledding hill, trails, tennis, dog areas, and five reservable shelters distributed across the property. Memories Park provides oversized photo-backdrop features. Choose the playscape, a numbered shelter, lake, or trail access before arriving.

facts.label: Which Riverside Park should I visit in Wichita?
facts.value: Use Central Riverside Park at 720 Nims for the wildlife exhibit, playground, splash pad, restrooms, gazebo, walking loop, and public art. North Riverside is at 900 N. Bitting and South Riverside at 551 W. Central, with different recreation facilities.

facts.label: Is there parking at Central Riverside Park?

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Riverside Park?

facts.value: Yes. Central Riverside has a playground with sand safety surfacing near the splash pad, picnic areas, parking, restrooms, and Kansas Wildlife Exhibit.

facts.label: When is the Riverside Park splash pad open?
facts.value: Celebration Plaza Splash Pad at Central Riverside is free and normally operates May through September, daily from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It can close unexpectedly for safety or mechanical issues, so check Wichita's live splash-pad status before leaving.

facts.label: Is there a walking path at Central Riverside Park?
facts.value: Yes. A half-mile oval walking path follows the historic park layout and includes twelve interpretive markers with archival images and local history. Sidewalks also connect the major Central Riverside amenities.

facts.label: What can I see at Central Riverside Park?
facts.value: Highlights include the free Kansas Wildlife Exhibit with more than 25 species, The Hiker bronze, Solar Calendar stone installation, Spanish-American War memorial cannon, gazebo and lily-pad sculptures, and twelve historical markers along the loop.

facts.label: Is Riverside Park shaded?
facts.value: Yes. The Riverside parks are known for mature shade and ornamental trees, with picnic areas and paths beneath the canopy. Splash-pad and playground exposure still varies by time of day, so summer visitors should bring sun protection.

facts.label: Is Riverside Park in Wichita free?
facts.value: General park entry, parking, playground, seasonal splash pad, Kansas Wildlife Exhibit, walking loop, public art, picnic areas, and gazebo are free. Equipment rentals, reserved venues, events, and nearby attractions may charge.

facts.label: How can I check the Riverside splash pad before visiting?
facts.value: Use Wichita's splash-pad status page on the day of your visit. The City updates unexpected safety or mechanical closures there; weather, special events, wildlife care, and maintenance can also affect individual park features.

facts.label: Can I bring a dog to Riverside Park in Wichita?
facts.value: Yes, if the dog remains leashed, monitored, and under control and you remove all waste. Riverside Park is not on Wichita's official list of designated off-leash dog parks, so open lawns and paths are not off-leash areas. Keep pets away from the Kansas Wildlife Exhibit, splash pad, playground equipment, and any signed restricted space; use one of the City's named dog parks for off-leash exercise.

facts.label: Where can I picnic at Riverside Park in Wichita?
facts.value: Central Riverside Park is the most practical family picnic destination, with picnic tables, restrooms, parking, playground, splash pad, gazebo, and extensive shade near 720 Nims. Most open shelters are first come, first served; Riverside Stage is one of the locations that can be rented for guaranteed group use. The Riverside system includes separate North, Central, and South sections, so route to Central Riverside when the wildlife exhibit, splash pad, and family amenities are the priority.

facts.label: Which Wichita bus serves Riverside Park?
facts.value: Wichita Transit Route 17, the Park Line, serves Central Riverside Park with stops on Central Avenue at Nims and on Nims near Franklin. Use the Central-and-Nims stops for the south and central park or the Nims-and-Franklin stops for the north side, then walk to the wildlife exhibit, playground, splash pad, or river path. Check InfoPoint for live departures and direction before boarding.

facts.label: How accessible is Central Riverside Park in Wichita?
facts.value: Convenient sidewalks reach the park's major areas, and the City lists parking and restrooms among its facilities. Individual historic structures, lawn routes, the sand-surface playground, wildlife exhibit, splash pad, bridge approaches, and event setups can differ, so use the closest destination entrance and follow posted accessible routes.

facts.label: Where should I park for The RiverFront?

facts.value: Yes. The parks are served by Omaha Metro and ORBT routes, downtown walking routes, bike share, and rideshare drop-offs. Gene Leahy Mall sits between Old Market and north downtown, making it the easiest central transit destination.

facts.label: Where are restrooms at The RiverFront?
facts.value: Each park has permanent accessible restrooms: beside Arches Playground near 11th and Farnam in Gene Leahy Mall, at the Skate Kiosk near 8th and Farnam in Heartland of America Park, and east of Discovery Playground at Lewis & Clark Landing.

facts.label: Where are The RiverFront playgrounds?
facts.value: Arches Playground is in Gene Leahy Mall near 11th and Farnam, while the larger Discovery Playground is at Lewis & Clark Landing beside Kiewit Luminarium. Both include accessible and lower-impact play features.

facts.label: Is there water play at The RiverFront?
facts.value: Yes. Gene Leahy Mall includes the Cascades interactive water feature, and Lewis & Clark Landing includes an urban beach area. Operation is weather and maintenance dependent, and the beach is an designed play landscape rather than Missouri River swimming access.

facts.label: Where is The RiverFront dog park?
facts.value: The fenced dog park is in Gene Leahy Mall near 8th and Douglas, with separate small- and large-dog sides, artificial turf, tunnels, and hills. Dogs must remain leashed elsewhere in the three parks.

facts.label: Is The RiverFront wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Yes. All three parks use gently sloping routes, accessible wayfinding, companion seating, accessible playground transfer systems, and wheelchair-accessible public and family restrooms. Identifiable routes connect the major amenities.

facts.label: Is The RiverFront free?
facts.value: General park admission, playgrounds, dog park, paths, lawns, sculpture garden, and most public activities are free. Parking, skating or recreation rentals, food, reserved venues, and selected events may charge.

facts.label: What RiverFront features can close independently?
facts.value: Cascades, Skate Ribbon, playground elements, kiosks, lawns, roads, and event spaces can close for weather, maintenance, private rentals, or major programming while the larger park remains open. Follow same-day signs and staff directions.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather shelter at The RiverFront?
facts.value: Gene Leahy Mall has a mixed canopy of birch, locust, oak, maple, elm, serviceberry, and hawthorn, plus a performance pavilion and developed play areas. Shade is less dependable across Heartland of America Park's broad lawns, lake, pier, and amphitheater and Lewis & Clark Landing's river edge, beach, prairie garden, and playground. Permanent restrooms are available in each park, but kiosks and pavilions are not guaranteed storm refuge; leave exposed riverfront areas during lightning, high wind, flooding, or dangerous heat.

facts.label: What are the walking surfaces and accessible routes at The RiverFront?
facts.value: The three-park district uses gradually or gently sloping hard-surface paths, promenades, plazas, crosswalks, and pedestrian bridges, with signs identifying accessible routes to major attractions and restrooms. A designated trailway links Gene Leahy Mall, Heartland of America Park, and Lewis & Clark Landing; lawns, sandy beach, prairie planting, play surfacing, and water-feature edges differ from that route. Wheelchairs and mobility devices are supported throughout, while bicycles and scooters may be ridden only on identified trails rather than interior pedestrian paths.

facts.label: Where can I picnic at The RiverFront in Omaha?

Choose the specific park nearest the playground, lake, river, or activity you want rather than using one general pin. Keep food out of water features, leave paths and play areas clear, and check the daily event schedule before relying on a lawn or pavilion for a group. facts.label: Which part of Omaha's RiverFront should I visit?

facts.label: Are there playgrounds at Zorinsky Lake Park?
facts.value: Yes. Multiple playgrounds serve family areas around the lake, including accessible play features near parking and shelters. Route to the mapped playground because the lake loop is too large to treat every lot as equivalent.

facts.label: Can I reserve a shelter at Zorinsky Lake Park?
facts.value: Yes. Numbered shelters are available through Omaha's reservation system; amenities vary by shelter. For example, shelter 4 lists four tables, a nearby restroom, and a playground roughly 500 yards away.

facts.label: Is Zorinsky Lake Park accessible?
facts.value: The paved lake path and developed family areas provide step-free recreation, and newer playground facilities include accessible elements. Distances between lots, restrooms, and destinations are substantial, so select the exact access point before arriving.

facts.label: Is Zorinsky Lake Park free?
facts.value: General entry, designated parking, paved trails, playgrounds, open picnic areas, fishing access, and public recreation are free. Shelter reservations, fishing licenses, boating requirements, organized sports, and events may charge.

facts.label: What can affect Zorinsky Lake Park access?
facts.value: Trail work, lake operations, storms, ice, flooding, sports events, shelter reservations, and restroom winterization can affect individual amenities. Obey posted water advisories and closures before boating, fishing, or using remote trail segments.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Zorinsky Lake Park?
facts.value: Numbered picnic shelters provide covered space near several family and recreation areas, and wooded sections offer intermittent trail shade. The reservoir loop, boat and fishing access, sports fields, and open shoreline remain exposed to sun, wind, lightning, and winter weather; shelters may also be reserved. During severe weather, leave the lake edge and use a substantial building or vehicle rather than a picnic shelter or tree.
facts.sourceLabel: City of Omaha Parks and Recreation

facts.label: Where can dogs go at Zorinsky Lake Park, and what rules apply?
facts.value: Dogs may accompany visitors on Zorinsky's trails and ordinary park grounds when they are controlled and not running at large. Omaha park law also prohibits dogs and other animals from entering park lakes, ponds, fountains, or streams, so do not let a dog swim or wade in Zorinsky Lake. This is not a designated off-leash park; keep the dog leashed and remove waste throughout the visit.
facts.sourceLabel: City of Omaha Code of Ordinances

facts.label: Can visitors swim or use a splash pad at Zorinsky Lake Park?
facts.value: The lake recreation area has no designated swimming beach or splash pad; its listed water activities center on fishing and no-wake boating. Zorinsky Pool at 3808 S. 156th Street is a separate staffed City of Omaha aquatic facility near the park and follows seasonal hours, admission, and capacity rules. Navigate to the pool specifically and confirm it is open rather than entering the lake for family swimming.
facts.sourceLabel: City of Omaha Parks, Recreation and Public Property

facts.label: Does public transit go directly to Zorinsky Lake Park?
facts.value: Do not assume a Metro bus stops at a park entrance. Zorinsky is a large west-Omaha lake with access points around 156th Street, F Street, and nearby neighborhoods, and the final distance can be substantial. Check Metro's live planner for your exact trailhead or pool address; if it does not return a practical walk, plan a bicycle, rideshare, or car connection for the final leg.

facts.label: Where should I start at Zorinsky Lake Park?
facts.value: Zorinsky Lake is the park's central landmark, but trails, fishing access, sports fields, playgrounds, shelters, and the aquatic center use different sides and entrances around the large west-Omaha reservoir. Choose the exact trailhead, shelter, pool, or lake access before driving rather than following a pin to the middle of the water. Allow extra time for the loop and check City notices for trail, water-quality, construction, or seasonal facility changes.
facts.sourceLabel: City of Omaha Parks, Recreation and Public Property

facts.value: Gray's Lake Park generally uses extended hours: 5:00 a.m. to midnight April through October and 6:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. during the rest of the year. Beach, concessions, rentals, and water play use seasonal schedules.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General park, parking, trail, accessible playground, seasonal sprayground, beach, bridge, terrace, and open space are free. Boat and bike rentals, concessions, reserved facilities, and organized trail events charge separately.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.
