facts.label: What address should I use for Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: Use 2101 Fleur Drive, Des Moines, IA 50321. The park has multiple parking lots serving the beach and playground side and the terrace and trail side, so follow signs for the feature you plan to use.

facts.label: Is parking free at Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: Yes. The City lists public parking lots at the park, with access on different sides of the lake. Summer weekends and organized runs can fill the closest lots, so use the alternate lot rather than parking illegally on nearby roads.

facts.label: Can I walk or bike around Gray's Lake?
facts.value: Yes. A paved shared walking and bike trail loops the lake and crosses the signature pedestrian bridge, with connections toward downtown and Water Works Park. It is heavily used, so keep right and expect congestion near family areas.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: Yes. Public restrooms serve the developed beach, terrace, parking, and recreation areas. Seasonal winterization and concession schedules can affect nearby indoor services, so do not assume every building is open year-round.

facts.label: Is there an accessible playground at Gray's Lake?
facts.value: Yes. The park's accessible playground includes two toddler bucket swings and is beside the newer sprayground near the beach-side parking area.

facts.label: Is there a sprayground at Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: Yes. A new sprayground opened beside the accessible playground near the beach parking lot in May 2026. Water operation is seasonal and can pause for weather, maintenance, or water-system issues.

facts.label: What is accessible at Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: The park lists an accessible playground, paved trail and bridge, parking, restrooms, terrace, and developed beach facilities. Watercraft and concession operations have separate accessibility and seasonal conditions.

facts.label: Is Gray's Lake Park free?
facts.value: General entry, parking, trail, bridge, playground, sprayground, beach, and open space are free. Boat and bike rentals, concessions, private reservations, and organized trail events charge separately.

facts.label: How do I check if the Gray's Lake beach is safe?
facts.value: From Memorial Day through Labor Day, Des Moines conducts weekly beach water-quality monitoring. Advisories appear on the official park page, at the beach, and on City social channels; the Iowa DNR hotline is 515-725-3434.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: The Christine Hensley Terrace includes a purpose-built shade structure beside the concessions and restroom building, and scattered trees shade portions of the grounds. The beach, bridge, lake loop, sprayground, and broad lawns are mostly exposed. The terrace cover is useful for sun or ordinary rain but not lightning or dangerous wind; leave the waterfront and use an open substantial building or vehicle during severe weather.

facts.label: Where can dogs go at Gray's Lake Park, and what rules apply?
facts.value: Leashed pets may use the lake loop and ordinary park grounds, and owners must clean up and remove waste. Dogs are not allowed on the beach or on watercraft rented from the City, and Gray's Lake has no designated off-leash area. Keep the leash attached for the entire park visit and use another facility for off-leash exercise.

facts.label: Can I reserve a gathering space at Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: Yes. The park's named reservable gathering space is Christine Hensley Terrace and its Terrace building; the City also rents designated open-space areas. For a casual picnic, use available park seating or lawn without claiming an event area, obstructing the lake loop, or bringing an organized setup. Reserve the Terrace for guaranteed use, and obtain the required permit for alcohol, large groups, trail activities, equipment, or a structured event; the beach, boat-rental area, bridges, and playground are separate public amenities.

facts.label: Can I take a bus to Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: Yes, with a short final walk. DART Route 8 travels between DART Central Station and the south side along Thomas Beck Road and Fleur Drive, passing the east side of Gray's Lake. Use the live planner for 2101 Fleur Drive or Christine Hensley Terrace and confirm the closest active stop, because DART replaced its network and moved many stops in June 2026. The park loop and beach lie beyond Fleur Drive, so allow time to reach the exact amenity.
facts.sourceLabel: Des Moines Area Regional Transit Authority

facts.label: What is the signature landmark at Gray's Lake Park?
facts.value: The pedestrian bridge across Gray's Lake is the park's signature visual anchor and part of the illuminated paved loop used by walkers and cyclists. For family amenities, use the beach-side area with the accessible playground and seasonal sprayground. For gatherings and concessions, navigate to Christine Hensley Terrace. The trail network also connects toward downtown, Gray's Station, and Water Works Park, so the bridge is a useful orientation point rather than the only destination.

facts.label: Kruidenier Trail Bridge
facts.value: Kruidenier Trail Bridge is the illuminated pedestrian and bicycle bridge crossing Gray's Lake and the park's signature after-dark landmark.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General park, trails, natural play area, picnic areas, public parking, and open landscape access are free. Concerts, reserved event parking, food, shelter rentals, bike share, private events, and selected programs charge separately.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: What address should I use for Water Works Park?
facts.value: Use 2201 George Flagg Parkway, Des Moines, IA 50321. For concerts, route to Lauridsen Amphitheater or the event instructions because temporary entrances, traffic control, and parking reservations can differ from normal park access.

facts.label: Where should I park at Water Works Park?
facts.value: Multiple on-site lots serve the park, with paved and accessible parking near Lauridsen Amphitheater, Killinger Family Stage, and the Biergarten. Concert parking can be reserved and lots may open only two hours before showtime.

facts.label: Can I bike through Water Works Park?
facts.value: Yes. Paved regional trails cross the park and connect toward Gray's Lake and central Des Moines. Stay on trails after normal park hours, and expect event detours, river flooding, or maintenance to affect individual segments.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Water Works Park?
facts.value: Yes. The park has two enclosed restroom facilities serving developed recreation and event areas. They are not distributed across all 1,500 acres, and event or winter operations may affect access.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Water Works Park?
facts.value: The Reichardt Family Natural Play Area offers nature-based family play rather than a conventional neighborhood playground. It sits within the broader park near developed visitor amenities and trail connections.

facts.label: Can I picnic at Water Works Park?
facts.value: Yes. Picnic tables and a shelter are available, with the shelter also offered for private rentals. Tailgating and camping are prohibited, and concert events may restrict outside food, alcohol, or access to reserved areas.

facts.label: What accessible facilities are at Water Works Park?
facts.value: Paved lots with accessible spaces serve the amphitheater, stage, and Biergarten, and paved trails link major developed areas. The vast natural landscape includes longer distances and variable surfaces away from those hubs.

facts.label: Is Water Works Park free?
facts.value: General entry, normal public parking, trails, natural play area, picnic areas, and open landscape access are free. Concerts, event parking, food, shelter rentals, bike share, and private programs can charge.

facts.label: What can close roads or trails at Water Works Park?
facts.value: Concerts, festivals, reserved parking, Raccoon River flooding, storms, utility operations, and trail work can change access. Event lots may open two hours before a show and close one hour afterward, so normal parking guidance may not apply.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Water Works Park?
facts.value: Wooded sections and mature trees provide seasonal shade, and a picnic shelter serves the developed family area. The Lauridsen Amphitheater and Killinger Family Stage are event structures with separate schedules and should not be assumed available as general shelter. Broad lawns, play areas, trails, and river edges remain exposed; during flooding, lightning, or dangerous wind, leave low areas and use a substantial building or vehicle rather than a picnic roof or tree.

facts.label: Where can dogs go at Water Works Park, and what rules apply?
facts.value: Dogs may use Water Works Park when controlled on a leash no longer than 6 feet; animals may not run at large except in an area specifically designated for off-leash use. No off-leash area is identified for this park, so keep the leash attached throughout the visit and remove waste. Ticketed concerts prohibit pets inside the concert venue except service animals, even though the surrounding public park ordinarily allows leashed dogs.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad or swimming at Des Moines Water Works Park?
facts.value: No splash pad, public pool, or designated swimming beach is listed at Des Moines Water Works Park. The 1,500-acre park is designed around trails, woodland, natural play, events, picnics, and the Raccoon River; the river is not a staffed family swimming area and can rise or flood rapidly. Do not confuse this park with Waterworks Park Splash Pad in Grimes, which is a different city and destination.

facts.label: Can I take DART to Water Works Park?
facts.value: Do not assume special-event buses are regular daily service. DART has provided dedicated Water Works Park shuttles for events such as RAGBRAI, but those trips operate only when announced. Use DART's current trip planner with 2201 George Flagg Parkway and verify whether a normal route and safe final walk are available for your date; otherwise arrange a ride, and confirm event-specific transit separately when attending a concert or festival.
facts.sourceLabel: Des Moines Area Regional Transit Authority

facts.label: What landmarks should I find in Water Works Park?
facts.value: The Lauridsen Amphitheater, Manatt Great Lawn, and Killinger Family Stage form the main event core, with the Des Moines Biergarten under trees to the east and the Reichardt Family Natural Play Area nearby. River Constellation is the park's defining public artwork: 45 illuminated poles create a walk-through light-and-sound sculpture near the amphitheater. The wider 1,500-acre riverside park has trails and natural areas, so route to the amphitheater or play area for developed amenities.
facts.sourceLabel: Des Moines Water Works Park Foundation

places.name: Pappajohn Sculpture Park

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Pappajohn Sculpture Park is open during Des Moines city park hours, daily from sunrise to midnight. Events, maintenance, conservation work, and severe weather can restrict individual lawns or sculptures.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General admission to the sculpture park and mobile or virtual visitor guides is free. Metered parking, organized events, commercial activity, and nearby downtown services may charge separately.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: Where is Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: The park is at 1330 Grand Avenue in downtown Des Moines, within Western Gateway Park. It is an open landscape with access from Grand Avenue and surrounding streets rather than a ticketed building entrance.

facts.label: Where should I park for Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: Ample metered street parking surrounds the park. Read current space signs and payment hours; downtown events can remove spaces or change rates, so use a nearby public garage if curb parking is full.

facts.label: Can I reach Pappajohn Sculpture Park by transit or bike?
facts.value: Yes. Grand Avenue bike lanes serve the park, and DART routes connect Western Gateway with downtown. The park is also walkable from central downtown hotels, offices, library, and nearby cultural destinations.

facts.label: How do I walk through Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: Pedestrian paths and surrounding sidewalks cross the compact 4.4-acre landscape, while broad lawns provide additional viewing space. Use the Art Center's mobile visitor guide to identify works and artists without a fixed tour route.

facts.label: Is Pappajohn Sculpture Park accessible?
facts.value: Yes. The Art Center describes it as an accessible, pedestrian-friendly setting. Street crossings, lawn conditions, temporary events, and winter weather can still affect the easiest route between individual works.

facts.label: Can I touch the sculptures at Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: No. Touching, climbing, or sitting on sculptures is prohibited because it damages the work, except for Scott Burton's Seating for Eight, which is designed for use. Photography is allowed.

facts.label: Is Pappajohn Sculpture Park free?
facts.value: Yes. The outdoor park, artwork viewing, mobile guide, and virtual tour are free. Metered street parking, organized events, commercial activity, and nearby businesses have separate costs.

facts.label: What can restrict access at Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: Art conservation, lawn restoration, permitted events, severe weather, snow or ice, and downtown street closures can affect individual works or paths. Never cross barriers or touch artwork even when a sculpture appears durable.

facts.label: Can I picnic at Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: Yes. Picnicking is allowed, but food and drinks must stay away from the sculptures and waste belongs in receptacles around the park perimeter. Glass bottles are prohibited, and alcohol requires a permit.

facts.label: Is Pappajohn Sculpture Park good for children?
facts.value: Families are welcome, and the Art Center provides a printable exploration guide with movement, observation, and discussion activities for all ages. This is an art park rather than a playground: children must not climb, sit on, or touch sculptures except Scott Burton's Seating for Eight.

facts.label: Are there public restrooms at Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: Do not plan on a dedicated public restroom inside the open-air sculpture park; the official visitor page does not list one. The adjacent Central Library and nearby businesses have their own hours and access rules, so use a staffed downtown facility before entering the park if restroom access is important.

facts.label: Is there shade or weather shelter at Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: The 4.4-acre sculpture park is an open outdoor gallery of lawns, berms, paths, and monumental art with only limited young-tree shade. The official visitor guide identifies no pavilion, restroom, or indoor visitor building inside the park. The adjacent Central Library and nearby businesses have separate hours and access, while the Des Moines Art Center museum is several miles west; during dangerous heat, lightning, hail, or high wind, leave the park and use a confirmed-open downtown building rather than standing near trees or sculpture.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: Leashed dogs may accompany visitors in the outdoor city sculpture park, but it is not an off-leash area. Keep pets away from every artwork, pedestal, planting bed, and food setup, remove waste at the perimeter receptacles, and never allow climbing or contact with a sculpture. The separate Des Moines Art Center museum permits only service dogs indoors.
facts.sourceLabel: City of Des Moines Parks and Recreation

facts.label: Is there a splash pad or swimming area at Pappajohn Sculpture Park?
facts.value: No. Pappajohn is a 4.4-acre outdoor sculpture and landscape park with no listed pool, splash pad, or public water-play feature. Plan for art viewing, photography, a family exploration guide, or a picnic while keeping food, children, and pets away from the artworks. Use a separately listed Des Moines aquatic facility when cooling off in water is the purpose of the outing.

facts.label: Nomade
facts.value: Nomade is Jaume Plensa's monumental seated figure built from white steel letters and one of Pappajohn Sculpture Park's most recognizable works.

facts.label: Cost and fees

facts.label: Is parking free at Millennium Park?

facts.value: The park has nearly 18 miles of trails. Most allow walking, bicycles, rollerblades, and other human-powered use; surfaces include paved regional connections and park paths through rolling natural terrain.

facts.label: Where is Kids' City at Millennium Park?
facts.value: Kids' City is near both large open picnic shelters and is easy to reach from parking lots A and B, between the main recreation-area entrance and the beach. Playground access does not require beach admission.

facts.label: When is the Millennium Park splash pad open?
facts.value: For 2026, the splash pad operates 10:00 a.m.-7:00 p.m. through August 23, then 10:00 a.m.-6:00 p.m. through Labor Day. It is inside the paid beach area and may close for weather or maintenance.

facts.label: Are there changing rooms and restrooms at Millennium Park beach?
facts.value: Yes. The Van Andel Beach House provides restrooms, changing rooms, lockers, concessions, and plaza picnic space during beach operations. Other seasonal facilities may be limited outside the paid beach area.

facts.label: Is Millennium Park accessible?
facts.value: Developed lots, Kids' City, beach house, splash pad plaza, shelters, and portions of the trail network provide step-free access. Sand, water entry, rolling terrain, and natural routes vary; contact Kent County Parks for current beach accommodations.

facts.label: How much is Millennium Park beach?
facts.value: Daily beach and splash-pad admission is $4 for ages 16-62, $3 for age 63 and older, $2 for ages 3-15, and free for children 2 and under. General park and trail access remain free.

facts.label: Is Millennium Park open in winter?

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Millennium Park?

The playground also has a small toddler shade structure, while the beach, splash pad, courts, and many trail segments are exposed. Open shelters help with sun and ordinary rain but are not safe for lightning or high wind; the Beach House is available only during seasonal beach hours.

facts.label: Where can dogs go at Millennium Park, and what rules apply?

The park does not list a designated dog park, so no area should be treated as off leash; remove waste and obey posted exclusions at the paid beach, splash pad, playground, shelters, events, or other developed facilities. Service-animal access follows applicable law.

facts.label: Which picnic shelter should I use at Millennium Park?
facts.value: Open Shelters A and B are reservable, barrier-free shelters beside Kids' City; each holds up to 140 people and has 18 tables, two double charcoal grills, electricity, water, and nearby restrooms. A smaller family shelter near volleyball and a shelter inside the paid beach area are first come, first served. Shelter rental does not include beach or splash-pad admission.

facts.label: Is there a bus to Millennium Park?

Route to a named shelter or facility and check flood conditions before relying on low river-edge paths.

places.name: Lindenwood Park

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Lindenwood Park is available for public recreation with seasonal facility hours. The campground operates approximately May through October, weather permitting; its information center, rentals, restrooms, shelters, and groomed ski trails use separate schedules.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General park, parking, trails, playgrounds, adaptive kayak launch, fishing, picnic areas, and bridge access are free. Campsites are $38 nightly in 2026; bike and kayak rentals, shelters, firewood, concessions, and permits charge.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 1905 Roger Maris Drive, Fargo, ND 58103

facts.label: What address should I use for Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: Use 1905 Roger Maris Drive for the park, playgrounds, trails, shelters, and river access. Campground check-in and rentals are within the park; follow signs after entering rather than stopping at the first lot.

facts.label: Is parking free at Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: General park parking is free and distributed near playgrounds, shelters, trails, campground, and river access. Flooding, shelter events, and campground operations can close individual drives or lots.

facts.label: Is Lindenwood Park's playground accessible?
facts.value: Yes. The FM Rotary Universal Playground is designed for children of varied abilities and is a major regional play destination. A second playground and family picnic areas are also within the park.

facts.label: Is the Lindenwood kayak launch accessible?
facts.value: Yes. The fully ADA-compliant adaptive launch provides steady footing for nonmotorized watercraft and avoids the muddy riverbank. River level, current, debris, and seasonal rental operations still determine safe use.

facts.label: Can I bike from Lindenwood Park to Moorhead?
facts.value: Yes. Recreational paths and a pedestrian bridge connect Lindenwood Park to Gooseberry Park in Moorhead. Fargo's river trail network continues beyond the park, while winter grooming supports classic and skate skiing when conditions allow.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: Yes. Public restrooms serve developed park and shelter areas, while registered campers receive access to campground restrooms and hot showers. Seasonal operations, freezing weather, and flooding can affect individual buildings.

facts.label: Is Lindenwood Park free?
facts.value: General entry, parking, trails, playgrounds, adaptive launch, fishing, picnic areas, and bridge access are free. Camping is $38 nightly in 2026, and rentals, shelters, concessions, firewood, and permits charge.

facts.label: Does Lindenwood Park close when the Red River floods?
facts.value: Low roads, trails, campground areas, launch access, and facilities can close during high water, spring flooding, storms, or freeze conditions. Check Fargo Parks alerts before traveling during river events.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: Lindenwood has five covered picnic shelters: Main, Rotary, Ash, Elm, and Kost. The Main Shelter seats 150 to 200 people and has attached restrooms; mature river-bottom trees also shade portions of the park. Shelters can be reserved and are not severe-weather refuges, so use a substantial building or vehicle during lightning, dangerous wind, flooding, or winter emergencies.

facts.label: Can dogs go to Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: Yes. Dogs may use Lindenwood Park while controlled by a chain or leash, and the handler must carry supplies, collect solid waste, and place it in a refuse container or remove it from the park. Lindenwood is not one of Fargo's four fenced dog parks, so there is no off-leash exception here. Use Brandt Crossing, Dike East, Village West, or Yunker Farm when fenced off-leash exercise is the goal.

facts.label: Which picnic shelter should I use at Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: Lindenwood has five reservable shelters. The Main Shelter holds about 150-200 people and has electricity, a large charcoal grill, and attached restrooms; Rotary Shelter holds about 160 near the universal playground with electricity and a large grill. Ash, Elm, and Kost each hold about 20 and have electricity plus a small outdoor charcoal grill. An unreserved shelter may be used by the public, but only a reservation guarantees exclusive use; alcohol requires a separate group-consumption permit tied to a paid rental.

facts.label: Can I take MATBUS to Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: Yes, with a downtown transfer. MATBUS's rider guide directs park visitors to Route 13 for the Ground Transportation Center, then Route 14 or 16 for Island Park or Lindenwood Park. Enter the campground, main shelters, playground, or south park entrance in the live planner because Lindenwood stretches along the Red River and some amenities are far from another entrance. Confirm the return schedule before walking into the park.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad or swimming at Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: Fargo Parks does not list a splash pad, pool, or designated swimming area at Lindenwood Park. The park does provide an ADA-compliant kayak launch, seasonal kayak rentals, fishing, and a boat landing on the Red River, but those are river-access amenities rather than supervised water play. Use the launch only with appropriate watercraft and safety equipment; for a zero-depth splash pad, Fargo Parks lists Madison Pool and Splash Pad as a separate facility.

facts.label: What are the main landmarks in Lindenwood Park?
facts.value: The universal Rotary Playground and adjacent Rotary Shelter form the park's primary family landmark. The pedestrian lift bridge crosses the Red River to Gooseberry Park in Moorhead when river conditions allow, while the adaptive kayak launch, campground, Main Shelter, smaller picnic shelters, rental area, and recreational trails occupy other parts of Fargo's largest multi-use park. Check current flood and bridge status before planning a cross-river loop.

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Island Park is a year-round downtown park. The gazebo rents from 10:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m.; Island Park Pool's 2026 general admission is daily 12:00-7:00 p.m. during its summer season. Restrooms and winter trails vary seasonally.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General park, playgrounds, courts, paths, picnic areas, and Wergeland statue are free. Island Park Pool costs $10.25 for youth and $12.25 for adults in 2026; gazebo rentals, programs, and events charge.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 302 7th Street S, Fargo, ND 58103

facts.label: Where is Island Park in Fargo?
facts.value: Use 302 7th Street South for the general park and gazebo. The pool entrance is at 502 1st Avenue South on the park's north side; route there directly for swimming rather than the general park pin.

facts.label: Where should I park for Island Park?
facts.value: Use legal park-edge and downtown parking nearest the playground, courts, gazebo, or pool. Pool sessions, weddings, festivals, and downtown events can fill the closest spaces; follow posted time limits.

facts.label: Are there playgrounds at Island Park?
facts.value: Yes. Island Park lists separate playground equipment for ages 2-5 and 5-12, along with courts, paths, picnic areas, restrooms, and nearby pool water play.

facts.label: What water play is at Island Park Pool?
facts.value: The rebuilt pool includes zero-depth entry with interactive water features and two small slides, a lazy river, 50-meter pool, tube slide, high-speed FlyTyme slide, and diving. Large slides require a 48-inch minimum height; FlyTyme requires a waiver.

facts.label: Does Island Park Pool have a quieter time for young or sensory-sensitive children?
facts.value: Yes. Tot Time runs Monday-Friday from 10:30-11:50 a.m. for very young children and children with sensory needs, focused on the zero-depth play area. The 2026 Tot Time price is $2.25.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Island Park?
facts.value: Yes. Restrooms serve the park and reservable gazebo area, and the pool has its own restrooms and concessions during admission hours. Seasonal maintenance and winter operations can affect outdoor facilities.

facts.label: Is Island Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, playgrounds, courts, paths, picnic areas, and statue viewing are free. In 2026, pool daily admission is $10.25 for youth and $12.25 for adults; rentals, programs, and events charge separately.

facts.label: Are Island Park ski trails open in winter?
facts.value: The Island Park ski trail was closed for the 2025-2026 season because tree pruning prevented safe grooming. Check Fargo Parks' cross-country ski page for the current winter rather than assuming the route has reopened.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or shelter in Island Park?
facts.value: Mature trees shade many paths, picnic areas, and play spaces, while the reservable gazebo provides covered space with electricity and nearby restrooms. The gazebo may be occupied by a wedding or rental and is not a severe-weather shelter; use a substantial building or vehicle during lightning, dangerous wind, or winter emergencies.

facts.label: What are the walking surfaces and trail conditions at Island Park?
facts.value: Island Park's compact recreational-trail network connects the downtown perimeter, gazebo, playgrounds, pool, courts, picnic areas, and tree collection on generally developed walking routes. Lawn shortcuts and river-adjacent or winter recreation areas can be softer, uneven, wet, snowy, or icy. Cross-country ski and snowshoe trails are groomed only when conditions allow and can close for forestry work, as occurred during the 2025-2026 season; check Fargo Parks trail updates before relying on a winter route.

facts.label: Where can dogs go at Island Park, and what rules apply?
facts.value: Dogs may use Island Park's ordinary paths and grounds when controlled by a leash, and handlers must carry supplies, collect waste, and place it in a refuse container or remove it from the park. Island Park is not one of Fargo's four fenced dog parks, so leashes remain required throughout this park. Pets are not allowed inside facilities except service animals, and disruptive or aggressive dogs may be required to leave events or rentals.

facts.label: Where can I picnic at Island Park in Fargo?
facts.value: Picnic tables and grills are available in the park for casual use. The Island Park Gazebo is a separate reservable space for up to 30 people, with electricity and restrooms on site; it does not supply tables or chairs, so rental groups must bring their own. Check Fargo Parks availability before planning around the gazebo.

facts.label: Can I take MATBUS to Island Park?
facts.value: Yes. Island Park is immediately south of downtown Fargo, and MATBUS identifies it as a transit-accessible park through routes connecting at the Ground Transportation Center at 502 NP Avenue. Route 13 reaches the downtown hub, with Route 14 or 16 used for the park connection depending on direction and schedule. Enter Island Park Pool, the gazebo, tennis courts, or exact park edge in the live planner and check current downtown detours before leaving.

facts.label: What landmark should I look for in Island Park?
facts.value: The signature landmark is the bronze Henrik Wergeland statue on the park's primary north-south path. Sculptor Gustav Vigeland's work was unveiled here in 1908 before more than 3,500 people; an identical statue was unveiled in Oslo the same day. The gazebo and band shell are additional orientation points, but route to Island Park rather than the pool when visiting the statue.

facts.label: Cost and fees

facts.label: What address should I use for Falls Park?
facts.value: Use 131 E. Falls Park Drive for the main park and shelter or route directly to the Visitor Information Center for maps and the observation tower. Several free lots serve different overlooks and attractions.

facts.label: Is parking free at Falls Park?
facts.value: Yes. Multiple free surface lots serve the Visitor Center, overlooks, cafe, shelter, and park attractions. Farmers market, marathon, holiday lights, and major events can fill or redirect individual lots.

facts.label: Can I bike through Falls Park?
facts.value: Yes. Paved paths connect the overlooks and join Sioux Falls's 45-plus-mile recreation trail system. Falls Park and the Downtown River Greenway remain open until midnight, later than most trail sections.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Falls Park?
facts.value: Restrooms are available at developed facilities including the Visitor Center area during operating periods, with event or seasonal facilities elsewhere. Identify an open building before visiting early morning, late evening, or in winter.

facts.label: Can I see the falls without climbing stairs?
facts.value: Yes. Developed parking and paved paths reach several waterfall viewpoints, and the Visitor Center provides an observation-tower experience during seasonal hours. Individual overlooks, snow, ice, and slopes vary.

facts.label: What should I see at Falls Park besides the waterfalls?
facts.value: Visit the five-story observation tower, Queen Bee Mill ruins, Falls Overlook Cafe's historic hydroelectric building, Stockyards Ag Experience, public art, farmers market, river trail, and seasonal Winter Wonderland lights.

facts.label: Is Falls Park free?
facts.value: General entry, parking, waterfall viewpoints, trails, ruins, public art, Visitor Center, and observation tower are free. Cafe purchases, shelter reservations, vendors, tours, and special events may charge.

facts.label: When is the Falls Park observation tower open?
facts.value: Visitor Center and tower hours are seasonal: 9:00 a.m.-9:00 p.m. daily May 4-August 31, 9:00 a.m.-6:00 p.m. through October, and limited holiday-season hours later in the year. It closes on specified holidays and hours may change.

facts.label: Can I reserve a picnic shelter at Falls Park?
facts.value: Yes. Falls Park has an electrified open-air shelter with 14 tables, plus picnic tables elsewhere. Reservations guarantee use; an unreserved shelter is first come, first served. Grills must remain outside shelters, glass is prohibited, and special setups may require permits.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Falls Park?
facts.value: Yes. The City lists an accessible playground in Falls Park, along with nearby restrooms, drinking fountains, walking paths, and picnic facilities. Navigate to the playground rather than the general waterfall pin when play access is the priority.

facts.label: Is there an off-leash dog park at Falls Park?
facts.value: Pawsible Dog Park is at adjacent Jacobson Plaza in Falls Park West, not beside the main waterfall overlooks. Dogs must be leashed while entering and leaving designated dog areas and remain under control; ordinary Falls Park paths are not an off-leash zone.

facts.label: Where can I find shade or weather shelter at Falls Park?
facts.value: Falls Park has a reservable 20-by-40-foot picnic shelter and a larger open-air shelter with electricity. The Visitor Center, observation tower, Overlook Cafe, and Stockyards Ag Experience provide indoor or enclosed space only during their own posted hours. Waterfall overlooks, quartzite outcrops, bridges, playground, lawns, and much of the recreation trail are exposed. During lightning, flooding, high wind, or extreme cold or heat, leave the river and falls edge and use a confirmed-open substantial building or enclosed vehicle.

facts.label: Can visitors swim or use a splash pad at Falls Park?
facts.value: No current splash pad or designated swimming area is listed at Falls Park. The Big Sioux River, falls, quartzite ledges, and quarry water are not family water-play areas; wet rocks are slippery, currents strengthen rapidly, and people have died during high-water incidents. Renderings in long-range master-plan documents show possible future water features, not operating amenities. Use one of Sioux Falls' currently listed pools or spray parks instead.

facts.label: Which Sioux Area Metro bus stops at Falls Park?
facts.value: The Purple Line stops on Weber Avenue at both the east and west Falls Park entrances. It connects with the downtown bus terminal and normally runs hourly, so check live times before leaving and use the entrance closest to the Visitor Information Center, Overlook Cafe, Queen Bee Mill ruins, or Levitt event area.

facts.label: Middle Sioux Falls
facts.value: Middle Sioux Falls is the central mapped waterfall within Falls Park, where the Big Sioux River descends across exposed pink Sioux Quartzite beside the park's paved walking routes and overlooks.

facts.value: Queen Bee Mill Ruins preserve the visible remains of the seven-story flour mill that opened beside the falls in 1881 and was later damaged by fire, leaving historic stonework on the river's east bank.

facts.label: When is the Terrace Park Japanese Garden waterfall running?

facts.label: Can I reserve a picnic shelter at Terrace Park?

facts.label: Can I walk around Terrace Park and the Japanese Garden?
facts.value: Yes. The City lists accessible walking trails through the park and Japanese Garden area. Surfaces around formal garden features are developed, but grades, bridges, wet leaves, winter ice, and seasonal waterfall operations can affect the experience.

facts.label: Can I fish at Terrace Park?
facts.value: Yes. The City lists fishing access and a fishing dock on Covell Lake. South Dakota fishing-license and catch rules apply, and fishing access does not include swimming or entry into formal Japanese Garden water features.

facts.label: Where are the shaded or covered areas at Terrace Park?
facts.value: Terrace Park has two accessible picnic shelters with electricity: the 25-by-40-foot West Shelter and 20-by-30-foot Upper Shelter. Trees also shade portions of the Japanese Gardens, walking routes, and picnic landscape, while ballfields, playgrounds, lake edges, and the aquatic-center deck can be exposed. Shelter reservations may control group use, and neither shelter is safe in severe lightning or wind; use an open substantial building or enclosed vehicle during dangerous weather.

facts.label: Can I bring a dog to Terrace Park?
facts.value: Treat Terrace Park as an ordinary on-leash park, not an off-leash dog park. Keep dogs controlled and out of the Japanese Garden water, aquatic center, playground equipment, and any signed restricted area, and remove waste. Sioux Falls lists its designated off-leash facilities separately; a special advertised dog-swim event at the aquatic center does not create everyday off-leash or pool access.

facts.label: What water play is available at Terrace Park?

It has lifeguarded outdoor pools, zero-depth entry with children's play features, four drop slides, and body and tube slides; it is more than a free splash pad. Admission, capacity, weather closures, and swim hours apply, and general park hours do not guarantee pool access. Check the Sioux Falls app or aquatic-center page for same-day status before traveling.

facts.label: Which Sioux Area Metro route serves Terrace Park?

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Riverfront Park?

facts.label: Is Riverfront Park accessible?

facts.label: Can I reserve a shelter at Riverfront Park?

facts.label: Is Riverfront Park free?
facts.value: General entry, parking, lake and river trails, fishing, picnic sites, and open recreation are free. Shelter reservations, event permits, and programs may charge.

facts.label: Does Riverfront Park close during flooding?
facts.value: Yellowstone River high water can close low roads, paths, river access, restrooms, and parking. Check Billings park alerts after snowmelt or heavy rain.

facts.label: Is Riverfront Park in Billings an off-leash dog park?
facts.value: Riverfront Park itself is a mixed-use natural and picnic area, not a designated fenced dog park. Keep dogs under control and follow posted leash rules around lakes, wildlife, shelters, and trails. Norm's Island has separate conditions and should not be assumed to make all connected routes off leash.

facts.label: Is there shade at Billings Riverfront Park?
facts.value: Natural cottonwood and riverside vegetation provide shade on portions of the trails and picnic landscape, while lake edges, paved segments, and open shelter approaches can be exposed. Bring sun protection and water during hot, dry, or smoky conditions.

facts.label: Can I fish at Billings Riverfront Park?
facts.value: Yes. Fishing is a recognized use around the park's lakes and Yellowstone River access. Montana licensing and seasonal regulations apply, and high water, ice, algae, wildlife activity, or restoration work can temporarily make particular banks unsafe or unavailable.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Riverfront Park in Billings?
facts.value: Billings Parks and Recreation does not list a playground at Riverfront Park, and Riverfront is absent from the City's current playground directory. Plan this park for paved jogging paths, natural areas, picnics, shelters, horseshoes, lakes, and river access rather than swings or slides. For equipment play, choose a park from the official Billings playground directory; supervise children closely near water, natural banks, ice, and wildlife.

facts.label: Can visitors swim at Riverfront Park in Billings?
facts.value: Billings Parks and Recreation does not list a swimming beach, pool, or splash ground at Riverfront Park. Lake Josephine and the Yellowstone River provide fishing, scenery, shoreline, and water access, but they are natural waters without a listed supervised swim area. Do not treat the lake or river as children's water play; currents, cold water, changing depth, banks, debris, and water quality require separate judgment. Use a currently operated City pool or sprayground, or Lake Elmo State Park's designated beach, for planned swimming.

facts.label: Can I take MET Transit to Riverfront Park in Billings?

Use the MET Transit live system map with the park entrance at 7250 Highway 3 and verify both the nearest signed stop and the final walking route before leaving; Lake Josephine, the Yellowstone River access, shelters, trails, and dog area are spread across a large property. If the planner does not show a safe practical walk, arrange a ride and pickup.

facts.label: What are the main places to find in Riverfront Park in Billings?
facts.value: Lake Josephine anchors the developed park and shelter area, while the Yellowstone River and Norm Schoenthal Island, historically called Barbara Island, form a separate natural section reached through the broader trail network. Three reservable shelters, paved jogging routes, picnic areas, and natural areas are distributed across the property. Use the park map or a named shelter for arrival; the lake, island, and river access should not be treated as one parking destination.

Carry water and sun protection, and return to a vehicle before severe weather rather than relying on trees, cliff edges, or restroom structures.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Swords Park?
facts.value: No conventional playground is listed at Swords Park. Billings describes this as a 60-acre scenic and natural Rimrocks park with paved and unpaved jogging trails, a historic site, picnic area, and restrooms, and Swords does not appear on the City's maintained playground list. Choose one of Billings' 38 listed playground parks for swings or climbing equipment; at Swords, keep children close on overlook approaches and away from cliff edges, loose rock, and fast trail users.

facts.label: Where can I picnic at Swords Park?
facts.value: The City lists one picnic site within Swords Park's 60-acre scenic trail area, but it does not list a reservable shelter, grill, playground, or developed group facility there. Treat it as a simple first-come picnic stop and carry what you need. Alcohol permits are specifically unavailable at Swords Park. For a reservable covered gathering, choose one of Billings' separately listed park shelters instead.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad or swimming at Swords Park?
facts.value: No. Billings Parks and Recreation lists Swords Park as a scenic natural-area park with paved and unpaved jogging trails, historic sites, picnicking, and restrooms, but no pool, splash ground, beach, or designated swimming area. The Rimrocks are dry, exposed terrain; carry drinking water and do not treat drainage channels or stormwater as play features. Use a currently listed Billings pool or sprayground for managed water play.

facts.label: Can I take MET Transit to Swords Park?
facts.value: Billings' Downtown Circulator reaches the Skyline Trail stop on the east end of the Rimrocks corridor seasonally from May 1 through September 30, generally on weekdays. That provides a trail connection toward Swords Park rather than service to every overlook or parking area. Check the current MET schedule, choose the exact trail destination, and plan the return before starting; the exposed Skyline Trail and park extend for miles.

facts.label: What historic landmarks are along Swords Park?

Swords Park itself is a 60-acre natural and historic area with paved and unpaved jogging trails, picnic space, and restrooms rather than a single monument plaza. Choose the specific gravesite, cliff, overlook, or trailhead before navigating and expect exposed conditions on the rims.

facts.label: Is there an easy paved trail at Garden of the Gods?

facts.label: What can limit access at Garden of the Gods?
facts.value: Parking congestion, winter weather, wildfire conditions, construction, permitted events, and seasonal shuttle or restroom schedules can change a visit. The east face of North Gateway Rock currently has a climbing closure, and all technical climbing requires a permit and proper gear.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Garden of the Gods?
facts.value: Yes. Pets must remain on a leash no longer than six feet and stay on trail, and owners must remove waste. A designated off-leash area lies east of Rock Ledge Ranch and south of Gateway Road; dogs must still remain under control there.

facts.label: Where can I picnic at Garden of the Gods?
facts.value: Use the designated Scotsman or South Spring Canyon picnic areas. Receptions are not allowed elsewhere in the park, overnight stays are prohibited, and seasonal fire restrictions can limit cooking or open flame.
facts.sourceLabel: Garden of the Gods Visitor & Nature Center

facts.label: What are the main sights at Garden of the Gods?
facts.value: Major landmarks include North and South Gateway Rocks, Balanced Rock, Siamese Twins, Central Garden, High Point, and views of Pikes Peak. Start with the free Visitor and Nature Center for maps because parking and trail access differ by formation.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter at Garden of the Gods?
facts.value: Natural shade is limited and uneven among the exposed red-rock formations, paved Central Garden, overlooks, and many trails. Scotsman and South Spring Canyon picnic areas have scattered trees, but visitors should carry sun protection and water. The accessible Visitor and Nature Center provides indoor exhibits, cafe, water refill stations, and restrooms during posted hours, generally 9 a.m.-6 p.m. in summer. Rock overhangs and trees are not lightning shelters; return to the center or a vehicle before storms.
facts.sourceLabel: Garden of the Gods Visitor and Nature Center

facts.label: Is there a playground at Garden of the Gods?
facts.value: Garden of the Gods does not advertise a conventional playground. It is a protected National Natural Landmark focused on red-rock scenery, paved and natural trails, geology, wildlife, guided programs, and the Visitor and Nature Center's exhibits. For equipment play, choose a Colorado Springs neighborhood park rather than climbing on the formations, which is prohibited outside permitted technical climbing. For a child-friendly visit, start at the center, use the easy Central Garden route, carry water, and keep children on marked trails and away from roads and drop-offs.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad, pool, or lazy river at Garden of the Gods?
facts.value: No. Garden of the Gods has no public pool, splash pad, or lazy river; it is a protected dry-land natural landmark for trails, geology, climbing under permit rules, and scenic touring. A City post dated April 1, 2026 announcing a lazy river was an April Fools joke, not a real project. The completed waterline supplies fire protection and future restroom capacity, not recreational water play. Use a separately listed Colorado Springs pool or sprayground instead.

facts.label: Can I reach Garden of the Gods by city bus?

Plan a final walk or rideshare to the Visitor and Nature Center or selected trailhead. Do not confuse Route 34 on Garden of the Gods Road with direct service to the rock formations, and verify any seasonal internal shuttle separately.

facts.value: Check current fire restrictions, grill rules, weather, trail conditions, and posted notices. At roughly 6,500 feet the area is exposed to heat, sun, wind, storms, and winter conditions; wildlife and wilderness access require normal backcountry awareness.

facts.label: Where can I find shade at Elena Gallegos Open Space?
facts.value: Seven covered picnic areas provide the most dependable shade, and the reservable Kiwanis and Double Shelter areas offer larger roofs near restrooms and trailheads. Cottonwood Springs Trail also has shaded rest stops. Most trails cross exposed high-desert terrain with sparse piñon and juniper cover, so carry water and sun protection and leave ridges or open ground when thunderstorms approach.

facts.label: What are the walking surfaces and slopes at Elena Gallegos Open Space?
facts.value: Cottonwood Springs Trail is the easiest option: a roughly quarter-mile, ten-foot-wide concrete accessible trail with shaded rest stops leading to a pond and wildlife blind. The broader network is very different, using natural high-desert surfaces with rocks, loose gravel, roots, drainage crossings, and sustained climbs toward Sandia Mountain Wilderness. Multi-use routes also carry mountain bikes and horses, while two trails are foot-traffic only; use the official trail map and choose a route that matches mobility, footwear, heat, and weather conditions.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Elena Gallegos Open Space?
facts.value: The City does not list a conventional playground at Elena Gallegos. This is a mountain open-space and picnic destination centered on trails, wildlife viewing, outdoor education, reservable picnic areas, and natural terrain; the Kiwanis reservation area adds a volleyball net and horseshoe pit rather than children's play equipment. For the easiest family outing, use the short concrete Cottonwood Springs Trail and a developed picnic area, while supervising children closely around cactus, wildlife, heat, loose rock, and trail traffic.

facts.label: Can dogs hike at Elena Gallegos Open Space?
facts.value: Yes, but all pets must remain under direct supervision on a leash no longer than eight feet throughout Elena Gallegos and other Albuquerque Open Space lands. There is no off-leash exception on the trails or in picnic areas. Carry out waste, keep dogs away from wildlife, horses, cactus, and cliff or drainage edges, and note that guided wildlife programs may ask participants to leave pets at home even though ordinary leashed access is allowed.

facts.label: Can I take public transit to Elena Gallegos Open Space?
facts.value: No fixed-route bus enters Elena Gallegos Open Space. Albuquerque's official planning record identifies the nearest Route 1 stop at Academy Road and Lowell Street, about 2.5 miles away and roughly a 50-minute uphill walk from the recreation area. Do not plan this as an ordinary bus trip, especially in heat or after hiking; arrange a car, taxi, rideshare, bicycle approach, or pickup and confirm your return before entering the trails.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad or swimming at Elena Gallegos Open Space?
facts.value: No. Elena Gallegos is a high-desert trail and picnic area with covered shelters, restrooms, drinking water at developed facilities, and a small wildlife pond reached by the accessible Cottonwood Springs Trail, but it has no splash pad or public pool. The pond is for habitat observation and education, not swimming or wading. Carry more drinking water than expected and use a separately listed Albuquerque aquatic center for water play.

facts.label: What is the best short interpretive walk at Elena Gallegos Open Space?
facts.value: Use the accessible Cottonwood Springs Trail on the north side of the picnic area. It leads to a wildlife pond and blind, with shaded rest stops featuring original interpretive artwork by Margie O'Brien. For broad Sandia and city views, continue through the developed picnic loop or choose a longer signed trail. The Kiwanis and Double Shelter reservation areas are separate group facilities, not trailhead landmarks.

facts.label: Kiwanis Reservation Area
facts.value: Kiwanis Reservation Area is Elena Gallegos' large sheltered group-picnic destination, with room for up to 250 people, three coal grills, a volleyball net, horseshoes, running water, electricity, restrooms, and direct trail access.

places.name: Tingley Beach and Bosque

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: The fishing ponds, public restrooms, and trails are open daily from sunrise to sunset. The train station and cafe are currently closed.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: General access, parking, trails, and pond use are free. Anglers age 12 and older need a current New Mexico fishing license.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 1800 Tingley Drive SW, Albuquerque, NM 87102

facts.label: Where is the entrance to Tingley Beach?
facts.value: Navigate to 1800 Tingley Drive, just south of Central Avenue. Gated vehicle entrances from Tingley Drive serve lots north of the train station and between the Central and South ponds.

facts.label: Where should I park at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: Use either of the two lots entered from Tingley Drive or legal parallel spaces along the gravel road west of the ponds. Do not park on cement paths, landscaping, or the ditch maintenance road west of Tingley Drive.

facts.label: What hours is Tingley Beach open?
facts.value: The ponds, public restrooms, and trails are open every day from sunrise to sunset. The train station and cafe are currently closed, so bring water and food rather than relying on concessions.

facts.label: Is Tingley Beach free?
facts.value: Yes. Admission, parking, trails, and pond access are free and first-come, first-served. Anglers age 12 and older must separately obtain a current New Mexico fishing license; licenses are not sold on site.

facts.label: Where can a wheelchair user fish at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: The Children's Pond has an accessible ramp, the Central Pond has a wheelchair-accessible ramp in front of the train station, and the Model Boat Pond has a ramp to the water's edge. Fishing users with mobility disabilities receive preference at designated ramps.

facts.label: Can I reach the bosque trail from Tingley Beach?
facts.value: Yes. Paved walking and fitness paths around the ponds connect to the Paseo del Bosque Trail, with additional unpaved multi-use paths in the Rio Grande bosque. Use the official map to choose the pond or trail connection you need.

facts.label: Are restrooms open at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: Public restrooms are available during the posted sunrise-to-sunset park hours. Concession and train-station closures do not mean the outdoor park and public restrooms are closed.

facts.label: Can I swim or boat at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: No swimming or wading is allowed. Rafts and ordinary boats are prohibited; only designated model boats may use their specified pond. The Train Station and cafe are currently closed, and grills can close during fire restrictions.

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: Yes. Dogs are welcome but must remain leashed, and owners must remove all waste. Keep pets out of every pond and respect wildlife and anglers around narrow shoreline paths.

facts.label: Can I picnic or grill at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: Yes. Picnic tables, covered picnic areas, and charcoal grills are located around the ponds, and visitors may bring their own food. Grilling can be prohibited during fire season, no alcohol is allowed, and events over 50 people require permits.

facts.label: Which pond should I use at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: Central Pond allows anglers of all ages; Children's Pond is for anglers age 12 and under; Bob Gerding Pond is catch-and-release fly and lure fishing with single barbless hooks; and the separate Model Boat Pond is for qualifying model craft. Everyone age 12 or older needs a New Mexico fishing license to fish.

facts.label: Where can I find shade at Tingley Beach and in the Bosque?
facts.value: Tingley Beach has five shade structures: covered picnic tables on the Central Pond peninsula and at the Boat Pond, plus covered benches at the Boat Pond. Cottonwoods provide intermittent shade on bosque routes, but pond edges, parking, and long trail stretches remain exposed to high-desert sun. The seasonal cafe and train-station facilities are not dependable all-day refuges. Carry water and use an open substantial building or enclosed vehicle for lightning, high wind, dust, or dangerous heat.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: The City classifies Tingley Beach as open space and does not list playground equipment there. It is intended for fishing ponds, model boats, walking, wildlife, picnics, and Bosque access; swimming and wading are prohibited. Do not confuse it with the separate Tingley Park near Coal Avenue and 10th Street, which the City lists with shaded playgrounds, fields, picnic space, and restrooms. Use the exact destination name and address before navigating, and supervise children continuously beside every pond.

facts.label: Can visitors swim at Tingley Beach?
facts.value: No. Despite the name, Tingley Beach's ponds are for regulated fishing and designated model or rental boats; Albuquerque prohibits swimming and wading. The lakes, restrooms, and trails are free and open sunrise to sunset, but every child should remain supervised at the water's edge. Rio Grande Outdoor Pool is a separate seasonal City pool just east of Tingley Beach with admission, wristbands, and scheduled swim sessions.

facts.label: Which bus goes to Tingley Beach?
facts.value: ABQ RIDE Route 66 and ART Route 766 stop at Central Avenue and Tingley Drive, the official transit approach for Tingley Beach and the nearby Botanic Garden and Aquarium. From Central, walk south on Tingley Drive toward the fishing ponds; do not confuse Tingley Beach with Tingley Park near the Zoo. ABQ RIDE is zero-fare, and the City recommends its Transit app for live arrivals and construction-related changes.

facts.label: Central Pond
facts.value: Central Pond is Tingley Beach's largest fishing pond, open to anglers of all ages and bordered by walking paths, a fitness course, a grassy picnic peninsula, and a wheelchair-accessible fishing ramp in front of Tingley Station.

facts.label: Where should I enter Reid Park?
facts.value: Use 900 South Randolph Way for the general park. Use 800 South Concert Place for the outdoor performance center, 920 South Concert Place for the rose garden, 910 South Concert Place for Miko's Corner dog park, and 3400 East Camino Campestre for Hi Corbett Field.

facts.label: What hours is Reid Park open?
facts.value: General park hours are 6:00 a.m.-10:30 p.m. Miko's Corner dog park is open 7:00 a.m.-10:00 p.m. and closes Thursdays from 9:00 a.m. to noon for maintenance; other facilities follow separate schedules.

facts.label: Is there a playground at Reid Park?
facts.value: Yes. The city lists a public playground, picnic tables and ramadas, restrooms, drinking fountains, ponds, and broad recreation grounds. The zoo is adjacent but is a separate paid attraction.

facts.label: Where is the dog park at Reid Park?
facts.value: Miko's Corner Playground Dog Park is at 910 South Concert Place, reached from Picnic Place or Concert Place off South Country Club Road. It has separate large- and small-dog areas, lights, water fountains, double-entry gates, and a ramada.

facts.label: When is the Reid Park Rose Garden open?
facts.value: The Cele Peterson Rose Garden is at 920 South Concert Place. It closes annually from December 1 through March 31 for pruning and cleaning and can also close for reserved events.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Reid Park?
facts.value: Yes. Restrooms and drinking fountains are listed as general park amenities. Separate venues such as the zoo, stadium, performance center, and recreation facilities control their own building access.

facts.label: Where should I park at Reid Park?
facts.value: Choose parking near the exact facility address rather than the general park pin. Parking-lot maintenance, major games, zoo attendance, festivals, and performance events can restrict the closest sections.

facts.label: Is Reid Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, playground, ponds, picnic areas, paths, and rose-garden grounds are free. Reid Park Zoo, aquatic facilities, stadium events, reservations, classes, and special events may charge separately.

facts.label: Are parking areas or facilities closed at Reid Park?
facts.value: Targeted asphalt repairs are affecting selected high-priority sections of Reid Park parking lots in June 2026, with periodic limited access rather than full-lot closure. The Rose Garden also closes annually December 1-March 31, and Miko's Corner dog park closes Thursdays 9 a.m.-noon for maintenance.

facts.label: Can I reserve a picnic ramada at Reid Park?
facts.value: Yes. Reid Park has picnic tables, grills, and reservable ramadas. Ramada reservations cover the full day from 8 a.m.-7 p.m.; nearby power and table placement are not guaranteed, open-pit fires and personal gas grills are prohibited, and large events follow a separate process.

facts.label: Is there shade at Reid Park?
facts.value: Reid Park has trees, ramadas, and shaded seating in selected areas, including a ramada at Miko's Corner dog park, but broad lawns, sports areas, paths, and parking can be fully exposed. In Tucson heat, plan water, sun protection, and a shorter route between shaded destinations.

facts.label: What are the walking surfaces and routes at Reid Park?
facts.value: The David Bell Path and principal park connectors are paved, shared recreation routes used by walkers, runners, bicycles, and wheelchair athletes; they can be crowded at popular times. Garden and activity-area routes vary between concrete, compacted dirt, turf, and older uneven surfaces, with ongoing work to stabilize Rose Garden paths. The former east-side path through Zoo Court to the Adaptive Recreation Center and zoo is permanently closed; use the alternate route from 22nd Street west of Lakeshore Drive and follow new signs.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad or pool at Reid Park?
facts.value: Reid Park has accessible swimming at the Edith Ball Adaptive Recreation Center: its covered outdoor recreation pool includes a zero-depth area and play features, while the indoor therapy pool has separate eligibility and reservation rules. Both follow facility schedules rather than general park hours. A new interactive water feature or splash pad is planned near the north pond and playground, but current permit records extend into 2029 and Tucson's operating splash-pad list does not yet include Reid Park, so do not treat that future feature as open.

facts.label: Which Sun Tran routes serve Reid Park?

Because the park is large, choose Route 7 for the south side and Park & Ride area, then confirm the closest stop for the zoo, rose garden, ponds, or recreation center in Sun Tran's live planner.

places.name: Rillito River Park

facts.label: Hours
facts.value: Rillito River Park and the Chuck Huckelberry Loop are open from sunrise to sunset; nighttime use is prohibited. Trailheads, adjoining parks, construction zones, flood conditions, and emergency closures may further limit access.

facts.label: Cost and fees
facts.value: Trail and ordinary trailhead access are free. Nearby special facilities and events may charge.

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: Where should I start on Rillito River Park?
facts.value: There is no single main entrance. Choose a trailhead near the section you want to use. Rillito Racetrack and Rio Vista Park are practical starting points with parking and paved connections; consult the official interactive map for north- or south-bank access.

facts.label: Where can I park for Rillito River Park?
facts.value: Use a designated Loop or adjacent-park trailhead rather than neighborhood or business parking. The Rillito Racetrack area has substantial free parking with paved trail connections; Rio Vista Park also provides parking, water, restrooms, and playground access.

facts.label: Is Rillito River Park paved?
facts.value: The principal Loop route is a paved shared-use path, with parallel or connecting natural-surface and equestrian routes in some sections. The corridor runs on both banks in many areas, but crossings and bank changes matter; follow the current Loop map.

facts.label: Is Rillito River Park wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: Many primary paved sections and trailheads are accessible. Rillito Racetrack has free accessible parking and paved links; accessible restrooms are available at selected trailheads, including the Rio Vista Park area. Conditions vary along the long corridor.

facts.label: Where are restrooms on Rillito River Park?
facts.value: Restrooms and drinking water are available at selected trailheads and adjacent parks, not continuously along the corridor. Use the official interactive map and plan a known stop such as Rio Vista Park before beginning a long walk or ride.

facts.label: How far does the Rillito River Park trail go?
facts.value: The river-park path runs from Interstate 10 to Craycroft Road on the north and south banks and connects with the larger Chuck Huckelberry Loop network, including the Santa Cruz and Pantano river parks.

facts.label: Can dogs use Rillito River Park?
facts.value: Yes. Walking with dogs is an official listed activity. Keep dogs leashed, carry water in hot weather, clean up waste, yield on the shared path, and avoid hot pavement during extreme temperatures.

facts.label: When should I avoid Rillito River Park?
facts.value: Avoid the exposed corridor during extreme heat and do not enter the wash during storms or flooding. Construction, maintenance, high water, and emergency conditions can close individual segments; the regional map warns that trail conditions are subject to change.
facts.sourceLabel: City of Tucson and Pima County Loop Map

facts.label: What hours is Rillito River Park open?
facts.value: The Chuck Huckelberry Loop is open from sunrise to sunset, and nighttime use is prohibited. Adjacent parks and trailhead parking can have different posted closing times, so finish the route before the controlling facility closes.

facts.label: Who has the right of way on the Rillito shared path?
facts.value: Stay right and pass on the left, travel single file when passing, and do not block the path. Cyclists must slow around others and should stop and ask before passing a horse; all users yield to people with disabilities.

facts.label: Where do I check current Rillito River Park closures?
facts.value: Use Pima County's Loop notices immediately before the trip. In July 2026, maintenance affects multiple Rillito segments and the Swan restrooms and Paradise Falls parking lot have posted closures, so a familiar route may require a bank change or detour.

facts.label: Where can visitors find shade or weather shelter along Rillito River Park?
facts.value: Most of the paved river corridor is exposed desert trail with limited dependable shade. At the Rillito Regional Park and racetrack access, four reservable ramadas and a shaded playground provide nearby cover; shade varies at other trailheads. Ramadas are useful for sun but are not safe in lightning, flash flooding, dust storms, or dangerous wind. Avoid the wash, leave exposed trail early, and use an open substantial building or vehicle during severe weather.

facts.label: Where is the playground along Rillito River Park?
facts.value: A shaded playground is at Pima County's Rillito Regional Park and racetrack complex, together with ramadas, restrooms, and trail access; playgrounds are not present at every Rillito River Park trailhead. Route to the regional park rather than a generic point on the long river corridor when equipment play is the priority. Pima County does not publish age ranges on the park page, so supervise for the child's ability and avoid exposed equipment during dangerous heat.

facts.label: Which picnic ramada should I reserve at Rillito Regional Park?
facts.value: Ramada 1 or 2 costs $25 per day and has electricity, one table, and a grill. Ramada 3 costs $40 and has four tables, a grill, electricity, and nearby restrooms; Ramada 4 costs $40 and has the same setup beside the shaded playground. Holiday and premium dates add $20, and beer or wine requires a separate $25 permit tied to a valid rental.

facts.label: Can children swim or use a splash pad at Rillito River Park?
facts.value: No pool, splash pad, or designated swimming area is listed at Rillito River Park or Rillito Regional Park. The river channel is normally a desert wash but can become a fast, dangerous floodway during storms, including when skies nearby appear clear. Never enter a flowing wash or cross barriers. Use a separately listed Tucson or Pima County pool or splash pad for water play rather than the Rillito channel.

facts.label: Where should I start on Rillito River Park?
facts.value: Rillito River Park is a long corridor, not a central destination: paved Chuck Huckelberry Loop paths run on both banks from Interstate 10 to Craycroft Road and connect onward to other river parks. Choose a named trailhead, road crossing, restroom, or equestrian access in the interactive map before traveling. The river channel is a natural desert wash and floodway rather than a recreational landmark to enter; stay on the banks and never cross flowing water.

facts.label: Rillito River Park Path
facts.value: Rillito River Park Path is a paved, shared-use segment following the Rillito River corridor and connecting into Pima County's larger Chuck Huckelberry Loop network.
facts.positionQuality: reviewed-official-campus-placement
facts.sourceLabel: Pima County Natural Resources, Parks and Recreation

facts.label: Chuck Huckelberry Loop Connection
facts.value: The Chuck Huckelberry Loop connection links the Rillito corridor to a countywide network of paved shared-use paths used by people walking, rolling, running, cycling, and riding horses on designated sections.

facts.value: Parking is distributed among one-way Scenic Drive pullouts. Calico lots fill first; once you pass a stop you must continue around the 13-mile loop. Red Rock Overlook outside the fee drive is free but also fills.

facts.label: What is the best entrance for Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area?
facts.value: Navigate to the Red Rock Canyon Visitor Center or Scenic Drive entrance, not a generic canyon pin. Timed entry is required October 1-May 31 for arrivals from 8:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m.; no timed reservation is required June-September.

facts.label: Are there restrooms at Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area?
facts.value: Restrooms and water are most dependable at the visitor center, with vault toilets at selected trailheads. Do not assume every overlook or trailhead has water.

facts.label: Is Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area free?
facts.value: The Scenic Drive fee is $20 per private vehicle, $10 per motorcycle or $5 per pedestrian/bicycle, separate from any required timed-entry reservation service fee. Federal recreation passes are accepted under current BLM rules.

facts.label: How accessible is Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area?

facts.label: Are dogs allowed at Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area?

facts.label: Is Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area good for children?
facts.value: The visitor center, Calico overlooks and short walks work well for families. Trails quickly become exposed and rugged; carry water for every person and never leave children or pets in a vehicle.

facts.label: How do I reach Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area without a car?
facts.value: Public transportation does not reach Red Rock Canyon. BLM opened a designated rideshare drop-off and pickup area in 2026, but cellular service and return availability can still be uncertain and the 13-mile Scenic Drive remains one-way and dispersed.

facts.label: What should I know before visiting Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area?

facts.label: Cost and fees

facts.label: Accessibility
facts.value: Accessibility varies by entrance, route, terrain, and destination. Review the exact mapped subsite and its official source before relying on a specific accessible route.

facts.label: Which entrance should I use for Rancho San Rafael Park?
facts.value: Use 1595 North Sierra Street for the south park and one arboretum entrance. The Washington Street side is convenient for the Wilbur D. May Museum lot and the arboretum's second entrance. Trail users should choose the trailhead shown on the county map.

facts.label: Where should I park at Rancho San Rafael?
facts.value: Use the Sierra Street lot for the south park, playground, and nearby arboretum entrance, or the May Museum lot from the Washington Street side for the museum and opposite arboretum gate. Large festivals use special traffic and overflow plans.

facts.label: Is there an accessible playground at Rancho San Rafael?
facts.value: Yes. Washoe County completed its first all-inclusive playground here, designed to provide play opportunities for children of varied abilities. Follow the south-park map and parking signs to the playground area.

facts.label: How many trails are at Rancho San Rafael?
facts.value: The county lists five trails totaling about 5.5 miles. Routes cross developed parkland, pasture, ravine, and natural sage terrain; the official trail map documents surfaces, grades, permitted uses, restrooms, and parking.

facts.label: Is the Wilbur D. May Arboretum wheelchair accessible?
facts.value: The arboretum has paved and packed-gravel paths. Paved routes are usually wheelchair accessible; dry gravel may also be usable, but wet mud and snow can temporarily make either surface inaccessible.

facts.label: Is Rancho San Rafael Park free?
facts.value: General park entry, trails, playground, picnic areas, and Wilbur D. May Arboretum are free. The Wilbur D. May Museum, rotating exhibits, reservations, professional photography permits, and special events may charge.

facts.label: Can dogs visit Rancho San Rafael?
facts.value: Dogs are allowed on designated park trails according to posted restrictions, but pets are not allowed inside the Wilbur D. May Arboretum except service animals. Keep dogs controlled and verify the rules for the exact trail or event area.

facts.label: What can affect access at Rancho San Rafael?
facts.value: Snow, wet gravel, trail reroutes, maintenance, museum hours, and major events can affect parking and individual areas. Herman's Pond is not a swimming area, and bicycles are prohibited on the arboretum loop and nature trail.

facts.label: Can I reserve a picnic pavilion at Rancho San Rafael?
facts.value: Yes. Reservable options include Peavine, Chinese Pagoda, Lions Highland, Brahma, and Leghorn pavilions. Groups of 25 or more need a group-use permit and a designated reservable area; casual smaller groups may use available first-come picnic space under posted rules.

facts.label: Where are restrooms at Rancho San Rafael?
facts.value: Restrooms are available near developed destinations, including the Nevada Farms and Families entrance and pavilions, but some are seasonal. Long natural trails do not have evenly spaced facilities, so plan around the south park, May Museum, playground, or pavilion area before hiking.

facts.label: Which picnic pavilion has the most shade at Rancho San Rafael?
facts.value: Leghorn Pavilion is described as thoroughly shaded and sits beside the Nevada Farms and Families restroom and entrance. Brahma Pavilion is also covered and includes a barbecue grill; each holds up to 50 people and requires a reservation for guaranteed use.

facts.label: Is there a splash pad or swimming at Rancho San Rafael Regional Park?
facts.value: No current pool or splash park is listed at Rancho San Rafael. Herman's Pond is a fishing pond, not a swimming area, and the old Nevada Farms and Families water-flume ride has been closed since 2008. A splash pad appears in the park's long-range master plan as a proposed future project, not an operating amenity. Washoe County's active water-play facilities are at Bowers Mansion, North Valleys Regional Park, and Lazy 5 Regional Park; verify their seasonal status separately.

facts.label: Can I take RTC transit to Rancho San Rafael Regional Park?
facts.value: Do not assume ordinary RTC service enters the park. RTC has operated special early-morning extensions to Rancho San Rafael for the Great Reno Balloon Race, but those are event-specific. For a normal visit, use RTC's live planner with the exact park entrance and verify the final walk or arrange a ride; the Wilbur D. May Center, arboretum, playground, dog area, fields, and trails are spread across the property.
facts.sourceLabel: Regional Transportation Commission of Washoe County

facts.label: What are the main landmarks in Rancho San Rafael Regional Park?
facts.value: The developed core includes the Wilbur D. May Museum, free May Arboretum and Botanical Garden, historic Ranch House, Herman's Pond, Nevada Farms and Families area, playgrounds, picnic pavilions, and Basque Sheepherder Monument. The open pasture hosts the Great Reno Balloon Race, while longer trails extend north across McCarran Boulevard into sage and canyon terrain. Use the Sierra Street entrance for the May Center area and consult the trail map for northern routes.
facts.sourceLabel: Washoe County Regional Parks and Open Space
